subtopic: Direct data entry devices (bar codes, RFID, QR)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A public library in Lahore is replacing the bar code labels in its books with RFID tags. State two advantages to the library of using RFID tags rather than bar codes.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. several books can be read at the same time; no line of sight is needed so books need not be turned to face the reader; tags can be read through covers/bags; tags are harder to damage than printed labels; data on the tag can be changed/updated.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two distinct advantages. Do not accept 'faster' alone without a reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one disadvantage to the library of using RFID tags.
parts.answer: Any one, e.g. tags cost more than bar code labels; tags can be read by unauthorised readers nearby; signals can be blocked/jammed by metal or interference; tags on adjacent books may be read by mistake.
parts.working: 1 mark for one valid disadvantage.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Direct data entry devices (bar codes, RFID, QR)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Write down the direct data entry device that is most suitable for each task.
(i) Reading the account and cheque numbers printed in special ink at the bottom of a bank cheque.
(ii) Reading pencil marks on 2000 multiple-choice answer sheets in a school.
(iii) Reading the strip on the back of an old-style hotel room key card.
(iv) Reading the price label on a packet of biscuits at a supermarket checkout.
parts.answer:
(i) Magnetic ink character reader (MICR)
(ii) Optical mark reader (OMR)
(iii) Magnetic stripe reader
(iv) Bar code reader/scanner
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct device. Brand names not accepted.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Direct data entry devices (bar codes, RFID, QR)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A warehouse in Karachi stores boxes of spare parts. It is deciding whether to label the boxes with bar codes or with RFID tags. Compare the use of bar code readers and RFID readers for identifying the boxes.
parts.answer: Similarities and differences written as linked comparisons, e.g. both read data without typing so reduce errors; both identify the box and look up its record in the stock file. RFID reads by radio waves while a bar code reader uses light reflected from the code; RFID needs no line of sight but a bar code must face the reader; RFID can read many boxes at once whereas bar codes are scanned one at a time; RFID tags can be read from further away; RFID tag data can be rewritten but a printed bar code cannot be changed; RFID tags cost more than printed labels; bar codes are easily damaged/dirtied, RFID tags are more robust.
parts.working: 1 mark per valid point, max 6. At least one similarity needed for full marks. Points must compare the two (e.g. 'RFID…whereas bar code…'); a list of separate features in two columns max 4.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Direct data entry devices (bar codes, RFID, QR)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A museum in Istanbul places a QR code next to each exhibit. Describe how a visitor uses the QR code to see more information about an exhibit.
parts.answer: Visitor opens the camera/QR app on their smartphone; points the camera at the QR code; the app decodes the pattern (into a URL/text); the phone opens the web page/shows the information or plays a video/audio guide.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three steps in a sensible order.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two advantages to the museum of using QR codes rather than printed information boards.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. information can be updated online without reprinting; can link to video/audio/multiple languages; QR code takes very little wall space; cheap to produce; can store more data than a bar code.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one disadvantage of QR codes for visitors.
parts.answer: Any one, e.g. visitor needs a smartphone with a camera; needs internet access/mobile data to open the page; a QR code can be replaced by a fake one linking to a malicious site.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Direct data entry devices (bar codes, RFID, QR)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A café in Islamabad accepts contactless card payments for amounts up to a set limit. Describe how a contactless payment is made.
parts.answer: Total is entered on the card reader/till; customer holds the card (or phone) close to the reader; data is sent by radio waves (RFID/NFC) from the chip; the transaction is encrypted; the card details are checked with the bank and the payment is authorised; reader shows that the payment is accepted (beep/green light) and a receipt can be given. No PIN is needed below the limit.
parts.working: 1 mark per point, max 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two security concerns about contactless payments.
parts.answer: Any two explained, e.g. a stolen card can be used without knowing the PIN (up to the limit); a criminal with a hidden reader close by could read card data (skimming/eavesdropping); a customer might pay twice by mistake if the card is near the reader again.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two explained concerns.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Direct data entry devices (bar codes, RFID, QR)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the steps that take place when a cashier scans the bar code on a tin of beans at a supermarket checkout.
parts.answer: The reader shines (red/laser) light on the bar code; the light is reflected from the white spaces, not the black bars; the reflections are converted into a number (product code); the code is looked up in the stock database/file; the price and description are sent back to the till and shown/printed on the receipt; the stock level for the item is reduced by 1.
parts.working: 1 mark per step, max 4.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Direct data entry devices (bar codes, RFID, QR)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A national survey in Pakistan uses printed forms. Part of each form has answer boxes that people shade in with a pencil. Another part asks people to write their address in capital letters. Explain why an optical mark reader (OMR) is used for the shaded boxes.
parts.answer: OMR detects the position of the marks in set positions; very fast so thousands of forms are processed quickly; more accurate than a person typing the answers.
parts.working: 1 mark for how it works/what it detects, 1 mark for a linked benefit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the addresses are read using a scanner with optical character recognition (OCR) software and not an OMR.
parts.answer: OMR can only detect whether a box is shaded, not read letters; OCR converts the scanned image of the handwriting/characters into editable text that can be stored in the database.
parts.working: 1 mark for why OMR is unsuitable, 1 mark for what OCR does.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one disadvantage of using OCR to read the addresses.
parts.answer: Handwriting may be unclear so characters are misread/errors need checking; poor-quality forms are rejected.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Direct data entry devices (bar codes, RFID, QR)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A dairy farm near Sahiwal puts a passive RFID tag in each cow's ear. Describe how the reader obtains the data from a passive RFID tag.
parts.answer: The reader sends out radio waves; the tag's antenna picks up the radio signal, which provides the energy to power the tag (no battery); the tag sends back its stored data (unique ID) as radio waves; the reader receives the data and passes it to the computer (where the cow's record is looked up).
parts.working: 1 mark per point, max 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain three reasons why RFID tags are more suitable than bar code labels for identifying the cows.
parts.answer: Cows move, and RFID needs no line of sight so the cow does not need to be held still; many cows can be read at once as they pass through a gate; a tag works when covered in mud/dirt whereas a bar code would become unreadable; tags are tough/waterproof; data on the tag (e.g. vaccination date) can be updated.
parts.working: 1 mark for each explained reason, max 3.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Direct data entry devices (bar codes, RFID, QR)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A customer in a restaurant in Dubai pays by inserting a chip and PIN card into a hand-held card reader. Describe the steps involved in making this payment.
parts.answer: The waiter enters the amount; the card is inserted into the reader; the customer types the PIN on the keypad; the PIN is checked against the one stored on the chip; if correct, the card details are sent to the bank (securely/encrypted); the bank checks the account has enough funds; the payment is authorised and the money is transferred; the reader displays 'approved' and a receipt is printed; if the PIN is wrong the transaction is rejected (after limited attempts card locked).
parts.working: 1 mark per valid step in order, max 5.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Direct data entry devices (bar codes, RFID, QR)

parts.label: a
parts.text: An international airport is planning to attach RFID tags to all checked-in luggage instead of using printed bar code labels. Evaluate this plan.
parts.answer: Benefits: bags read automatically as they pass on conveyors without line of sight, so fewer lost/misrouted bags; many bags read at once speeds up sorting; tags readable at longer range and when label is creased/torn; passengers could track bags; data can be updated along the route. Drawbacks: tags cost more per bag than paper labels; all airports on the route need RFID readers or bags still need bar codes; radio signals can be blocked by metal/liquids in bags; tags may be read by unauthorised readers (privacy); setup costs of new readers and staff training. Conclusion with a justified judgement.
parts.working: Level marking: 5–6 marks: benefits and drawbacks both well developed with a reasoned conclusion; 3–4 marks: both sides with some development; 1–2 marks: one side or list-like points. Up to 1 mark per developed point, max 6.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Write down the most suitable input device for each task.
(i) A journalist recording a spoken interview to be stored on a laptop.
(ii) A passenger selecting a destination on a ticket machine at a railway station.
(iii) A pilot in training controlling a flight simulator.
(iv) A student copying a printed photograph into a school magazine file.
parts.answer:
(i) Microphone
(ii) Touch screen
(iii) Joystick
(iv) Scanner
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept keypad for (ii); do not accept mouse.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A fast-food restaurant in Lahore installs touch screens so that customers can place their own orders. Explain two advantages of using touch screens for this purpose.
parts.answer: Any two explained, e.g. easy to use by selecting pictures/icons so little training needed; no separate keyboard/mouse that can be stolen or damaged; options limited to the menu, so fewer input errors; can be cleaned/wiped easily; faster for customers so queues are shorter.
parts.working: 1 mark each for an advantage with a reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two disadvantages of using touch screens for this purpose.
parts.answer: Any two explained, e.g. screens get dirty/greasy and need regular cleaning (hygiene); limited options compared with a keyboard for special requests; screens can be scratched or cracked; people with poor eyesight/disabilities may find them hard to use; arm fatigue if used for a long time.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A teacher in Peshawar wants to put copies of her printed worksheets on the school website. Name the input device she should use.
parts.answer: Scanner (flatbed scanner).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: She uses optical character recognition (OCR) software with this device. Give two advantages of using OCR software instead of retyping the worksheets.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. faster than retyping; text can then be edited in a word processor; fewer typing errors; text can be searched; text can be converted to other formats/read aloud.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A doctor in a clinic is choosing between a keyboard and a microphone with speech recognition software to enter patient notes. Compare these two input methods for this task.
parts.answer: Both enter text into the patient record. A microphone is faster/hands-free so the doctor can examine the patient while speaking, whereas typing needs both hands; speech recognition may misrecognise medical words/accents and needs training, while typing is more accurate for unusual words; background noise in a busy clinic affects the microphone but not a keyboard; speaking aloud may let others hear confidential details, whereas typing is private; a keyboard is cheap and familiar.
parts.working: 1 mark per valid comparison point, max 4. Points must compare the two methods.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A fashion designer in Faisalabad currently draws designs with a mouse. Discuss the benefits and drawbacks of using a graphics tablet instead of a mouse.
parts.answer: Benefits: pen/stylus is held like a pencil so drawing is more natural and accurate; pressure sensitivity gives thicker/thinner lines; fine detail is easier; less strain on the wrist than gripping a mouse for long periods; hand-drawn designs can be traced. Drawbacks: more expensive than a mouse; takes time to learn because the hand moves on the tablet while looking at the screen; takes up more desk space; stylus can be lost; not as good for general tasks such as clicking menus. Conclusion, e.g. worthwhile for a designer who draws all day.
parts.working: Up to 1 mark per developed point, max 4 for one side only; 6 marks needs both sides and a conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State how a television remote control sends instructions to the television.
parts.answer: By infrared signals (accept Bluetooth/radio for some models).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two uses of a driving wheel as an input device.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. driving games; driving simulators for learner drivers; training lorry/bus drivers; remote control of model cars/drones.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A power station control room uses trackerballs instead of mice. Describe what a trackerball is.
parts.answer: A pointing device with a ball on top that the user rolls with the fingers/thumb/palm; the device itself stays still, and buttons are used to click/select.
parts.working: 1 mark for the rolled ball, 1 mark for staying stationary/buttons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why trackerballs are suitable for the control room.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. needs less desk space because the device does not move; can be fixed into the control desk so it cannot be knocked off/stolen; easier for people with limited hand/wrist movement; more accurate control of the pointer for fine positioning.
parts.working: 1 mark each for an explained reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why ATMs use a numeric keypad rather than a full keyboard.
parts.answer: Only numbers are needed (PIN, amount), so a small keypad is enough; it is smaller, tougher and easier to make weatherproof/vandal-proof; fewer keys means faster and fewer errors.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two explained points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two problems customers may have when using the numeric keypad at an ATM.
parts.answer: People nearby can watch the PIN being typed (shoulder surfing); keys are small, so people with large fingers or poor eyesight can press the wrong key; keypads can be fitted with fake overlays to record PINs; hard to use in bright sunlight.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one feature of the keypad that helps a customer who is blind or partially sighted.
parts.answer: A raised dot on the 5 key / braille on keys; or a headphone socket for spoken instructions; large high-contrast keys.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the type of sensor that is most suitable for each use.
(i) Checking whether the soil in a greenhouse is too dry.
(ii) Turning street lights on automatically at dusk.
(iii) Detecting a person entering a room in a burglar alarm system.
(iv) Checking how acidic the water is in a river near a factory.
parts.answer:
(i) Moisture sensor
(ii) Light sensor
(iii) Infrared (motion) sensor (accept pressure sensor under a mat, acoustic/sound sensor)
(iv) pH sensor
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A computer controls the temperature in a greenhouse. A temperature sensor sends readings to the computer. Explain why an analogue-to-digital converter (ADC) is needed.
parts.answer: The sensor produces analogue data (continuously varying voltage); the computer can only process digital (binary) data, so the readings must be converted.
parts.working: 1 mark for sensor output analogue, 1 mark for computer needs digital.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The computer opens a window using a motor. Explain why a digital-to-analogue converter (DAC) may be needed and name the type of device that the motor is.
parts.answer: The computer's digital signal must be converted to an analogue signal/voltage to drive the motor; the motor is an actuator.
parts.working: 1 mark for DAC reason, 1 mark for actuator.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A shopping centre car park has an automatic barrier that rises when a car drives up to it. Name a suitable sensor to detect the car.
parts.answer: Pressure sensor (in the road) / proximity sensor / magnetic field sensor / infrared sensor.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the role of an actuator in this system.
parts.answer: The microprocessor sends a signal to the actuator; the actuator (motor) converts the signal into movement to raise and lower the barrier.
parts.working: 1 mark for receiving signal from the processor, 1 mark for producing movement.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the sensor does not control the barrier by itself.
parts.answer: A sensor only measures/detects and sends data; a microprocessor must compare the data with stored values and decide what to do.
parts.working: 1 mark.

stem: A scientist leaves a temperature sensor connected to a data logger beside a glacier in Gilgit-Baltistan. The logger takes one reading every 30 seconds for 6 hours. Each reading is stored using 2 bytes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of readings taken.
parts.answer: 720 readings

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the storage space needed for the readings, in bytes.
parts.answer: 1440 bytes

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two reasons why a data logger is used instead of a person taking the readings.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. readings are taken at exact equal intervals; works in dangerous/very cold conditions; can run day and night without breaks; readings are more accurate (no human error); readings are stored automatically ready for analysis.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by an actuator.
parts.answer: A device that converts a signal from a computer/microprocessor into physical action/movement (or other output such as heat).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two examples of actuators used in a home.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. motor (in a fan, washing machine, automatic gate); pump; heater (element); solenoid/valve (in a water tap or door lock); buzzer.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A farm in Faisalabad uses a computerised irrigation system. Moisture sensors are placed in the soil and a pump supplies water. Describe how the system uses the sensors, conversion and actuator to keep the soil at the right moisture level.
parts.answer: Moisture sensor continuously measures the soil moisture; readings are analogue and sent to an ADC which converts them to digital; the microprocessor compares the reading with a pre-set value stored in memory; if the reading is below the pre-set value the processor sends a signal (through a DAC) to the actuator to switch on the pump/open a valve; if the reading is at or above the pre-set value the pump is switched off/valve closed; the process repeats continuously in a loop.
parts.working: 1 mark per correct point in a logical order, max 6. Do not credit 'the sensor turns on the pump'.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Write down the most suitable output device for each task.
(i) Printing 600 report cards in a school office in one afternoon.
(ii) Printing one high-quality colour photograph at home.
(iii) Making a plastic model of a replacement part for a bicycle.
(iv) Playing train announcements to passengers on a platform.
parts.answer:
(i) Laser printer
(ii) Inkjet printer
(iii) 3D printer
(iv) Speakers
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A small accounting office in Islamabad prints about 3000 pages of black-and-white letters and invoices each week. Compare laser printers and inkjet printers for this office.
parts.answer: Both are non-impact printers that print text and graphics from the computer on plain paper. Laser printers are faster than inkjet printers, which suits large volumes; laser toner cartridges print many more pages than ink cartridges so cost per page is lower; laser output does not smudge, whereas inkjet ink can smudge while wet; inkjet printers are cheaper to buy; laser printers are larger and produce ozone/toner particles; inkjet printers are better for high-quality photographs; laser paper trays hold more paper. Conclusion: laser more suitable for this office.
parts.working: 1 mark per comparison point, max 6. At least one similarity needed for full marks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a 3D printer produces a solid object.
parts.answer: A design is created with CAD software/file; the software slices the design into thin layers; the printer builds the object one layer at a time (additive manufacturing) from material such as plastic/resin/powder; each layer is melted/bonded or hardened onto the layer below.
parts.working: 1 mark per point, max 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two uses of 3D printers in medicine.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. prosthetic limbs; artificial joints/implants; dental crowns/braces; models of organs for surgeons to practise on; tissue engineering; medical tools/splints.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A teacher in Multan uses a multimedia projector in her classroom. Give two advantages of using a projector instead of a large monitor.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. produces a very large image so the whole class can see; cheaper than a monitor of the same size; portable/can be moved between rooms; can project onto an interactive whiteboard.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two disadvantages of using a projector.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. image is less clear in a bright room; bulb/lamp is expensive and may fail; fan can be noisy; people walking in front cast shadows; needs setting up/focusing.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the steps a laser printer goes through to print a page.
parts.answer: The page data is sent to the printer and stored in its memory/buffer; the drum is given a (positive) electrostatic charge; a laser beam scans the drum, removing the charge where the image will be (or vice versa), forming an electrostatic image; the drum is coated with charged toner, which sticks only to the charged/image areas; the paper is given an opposite charge and the toner is transferred to it as it passes the drum; the fuser heats and presses the toner so it melts onto the paper; the drum is discharged/cleaned for the next page.
parts.working: 1 mark per step, max 5.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a laser printer is suitable for printing a large number of copies of the same page.
parts.answer: The whole page image is formed on the drum at once so pages are printed very quickly/the toner lasts for many pages.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether each device is an input device, an output device, or both.
(i) Touch screen
(ii) Actuator
(iii) Light sensor
(iv) 3D printer
(v) Microphone
(vi) Multimedia projector
parts.answer:
(i) Both
(ii) Output
(iii) Input
(iv) Output
(v) Input
(vi) Output
parts.working: All six correct: 3 marks; four or five correct: 2 marks; two or three correct: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a touch screen can be described as both an input device and an output device.
parts.answer: It displays information/images to the user (output) and detects where the user touches the screen to make selections (input).
parts.working: 1 mark for both roles.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Write down the most suitable storage medium for each use.
(i) Backing up all the data on a bank's servers every night and keeping the copies for ten years.
(ii) Selling a high-definition feature film in shops.
(iii) Carrying homework files between home and school.
(iv) Storing the operating system in a thin, light laptop.
parts.answer:
(i) Magnetic tape
(ii) Blu-ray disc
(iii) USB flash drive / pen drive (accept memory card)
(iv) Solid-state drive (SSD)
parts.working: 1 mark each. Do not accept brand names.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how data is stored on a magnetic hard disk drive.
parts.answer: The disk has platters coated in a magnetic material; the platters spin at high speed; a read/write head moves across the surface on an arm; the head magnetises tiny areas in one of two directions to represent 1s and 0s; data is stored in concentric tracks/sectors.
parts.working: 1 mark per point, max 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Bilal is a university student who carries his laptop to lectures every day. He is choosing between a laptop with a magnetic hard disk drive (HDD) and one with a solid-state drive (SSD) of the same capacity. Compare HDDs and SSDs for Bilal's laptop.
parts.answer: Both are non-volatile backing storage that store the OS and files with direct access. An SSD has no moving parts whereas an HDD has spinning platters and a moving head, so the SSD is less likely to be damaged if the laptop is dropped while carried; an SSD reads and writes data faster so the laptop starts up and loads files quicker; an SSD uses less power so the battery lasts longer; an SSD is lighter and thinner; an SSD is silent and runs cooler; an HDD is cheaper per gigabyte, so more storage for the same price; an HDD can be rewritten more times/has a longer lifespan for frequent writes.
parts.working: 1 mark per comparison point, max 6. At least one similarity for full marks. Points must be linked to both devices.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how data is read from an optical disc such as a DVD.
parts.answer: The disc spins; a laser beam is shone onto the surface; the surface has pits and lands (in a spiral track); light reflects differently from pits and lands (or at the change between them); a sensor/light detector reads the reflections and converts them into 1s and 0s.
parts.working: 1 mark per point, max 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which colour of laser is used to read a DVD.
parts.answer: Red laser.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A single-layer Blu-ray disc can hold about five times as much data as a single-layer DVD, even though both discs are the same size. Explain why.
parts.answer: Blu-ray uses a blue/blue-violet laser which has a shorter wavelength than the red laser used for DVDs; the shorter wavelength can be focused to a smaller spot so the pits can be smaller; the tracks can be closer together; so more pits fit on the same area of disc.
parts.working: 1 mark per point, max 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one reason why films are often sold on Blu-ray rather than DVD.
parts.answer: Higher capacity allows high-definition (or 4K/3D) video/extra content on one disc; Blu-ray discs have a protective coating so are less easily scratched.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A large insurance company in Karachi backs up its database onto magnetic tape every night. Explain two reasons why magnetic tape is used for this.
parts.answer: Any two explained, e.g. very large capacity so the whole database fits on one/few tapes; low cost per gigabyte; tapes are robust and can be stored off-site for many years; fast to write large amounts of data in one continuous stream.
parts.working: 1 mark each for an explained reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why magnetic tape is not suitable for looking up one customer's record while the customer waits on the telephone.
parts.answer: Tape uses serial access; the tape must be wound through from the start until the record is reached, so finding one record is very slow.
parts.working: 1 mark for serial access, 1 mark for consequence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by direct access to data.
parts.answer: Data can be read straight from where it is stored without reading through all the data before it.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is meant by serial access to data.
parts.answer: Data is read in the order it was stored, starting from the beginning, until the required item is found.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one example of a storage medium that uses each type of access.
parts.answer: Direct: hard disk/SSD/DVD/Blu-ray/flash drive. Serial: magnetic tape.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: Ayesha is a wildlife photographer in Chitral. Her camera uses a 64 GB memory card. Each photo is stored as a 48 MB file. Use 1 GB = 1024 MB.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the largest number of whole photos that can be stored on the memory card.
parts.answer: 1365 photos

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the type of storage used by the memory card.
parts.answer: Solid-state (flash memory).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why this type of storage is suitable for use in a camera carried in the mountains.
parts.answer: No moving parts so it is not damaged by knocks/vibration; small and light; works in cold conditions; uses very little power so battery lasts longer.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two explained points.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a solid-state drive stores data.
parts.answer: It uses flash memory chips (NAND) made of transistors; electrons are trapped in each cell (in the floating gate) to represent 1 or 0; data stays when power is off; there are no moving parts.
parts.working: 1 mark per point, max 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why smartphones use solid-state storage.
parts.answer: Any two explained, e.g. very small and light so fits in a thin phone; no moving parts so not damaged when dropped; low power use so longer battery life; fast access so apps open quickly.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two advantages to students of using USB flash drives to store their school work.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. small/portable; robust (no moving parts); plugs into any computer with a USB port without extra software; large capacity for the size; fast to transfer files.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one disadvantage of using USB flash drives.
parts.answer: Easily lost or stolen (data may be seen by others); can transfer viruses between computers; can be damaged if removed while writing; limited number of write cycles.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a DVD-ROM, a DVD-R and a DVD-RW.
parts.answer: DVD-ROM: data is written when the disc is made and can only be read, not changed. DVD-R: can be written (recorded) once by the user, then only read. DVD-RW: can be written, erased and re-written many times.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct description.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a suitable use for a DVD-RW.
parts.answer: Any suitable use where data changes, e.g. regular backups that are overwritten; recording TV programmes to watch and then record over; moving files between computers.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A school in Rawalpindi plans to replace the hard disk drives in its file server with solid-state drives. Evaluate this plan.
parts.answer: Benefits: SSDs read/write faster so students' files open and save more quickly, especially when many users log on at once; no moving parts so less likely to fail/be damaged and quieter; lower power use and less heat so cheaper to run and cool; smaller. Drawbacks: SSDs cost more per gigabyte so the same budget buys less storage; files may need to be moved/server set up again, causing disruption; SSDs have a limited number of write cycles, which matters for a server that saves files all day; HDD capacity may be enough if current speed is acceptable. Conclusion with justification.
parts.working: 5–6: balanced, developed points with a conclusion; 3–4: both sides, some development; 1–2: simple points/one side only.

stem: A photography club in Lahore wants to back up 60 GB of photos onto single-layer DVD-R discs. Each disc holds 4.7 GB.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the smallest number of discs needed.
parts.answer: 13 discs
parts.working: 60 ÷ 4.7 = 12.77… (M1); round up to 13 discs because 12 discs only hold 56.4 GB (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a portable hard disk drive would be a better choice for this backup.
parts.answer: One portable HDD holds all 60 GB so there is no need to split files across 13 discs; it can be overwritten for each new backup whereas DVD-R can only be written once; it is quicker to copy to and to restore from.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two explained points.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two devices that use memory cards for storage.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. digital camera; smartphone/tablet; drone; dashboard camera; handheld games console.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether a memory card is magnetic, optical or solid-state storage.
parts.answer: Solid-state.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A team of geologists will spend three months in the Thar Desert collecting data on laptops. Temperatures are very high, there is fine dust, and the vehicles travel over rough tracks. Recommend the most suitable type of backing storage for the laptops and explain your choice by comparing it with the other two types of storage.
parts.answer: Recommend solid-state (SSD). No moving parts, so it is not damaged by vibration on rough tracks, whereas the heads of a magnetic disk could crash into the platters; dust can stop an optical drive working/scratch discs, but sealed flash memory is unaffected; SSDs cope better with heat and use less power, important when charging is limited; optical discs have low capacity and are slow to write.
parts.working: 1 mark for SSD with a reason, then 1 mark per comparison with magnetic or optical, max 4.

stem: A news reporter in Dhaka records video on a camera with a 32 GB memory card. One minute of video uses 120 MB. Use 1 GB = 1024 MB.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the largest number of whole minutes of video that can be stored on the card.
parts.answer: 273 minutes

parts.label: b
parts.text: The reporter copies the video to her laptop at the end of each day. Give one reason why she should also keep a second copy on a different storage device.
parts.answer: If the laptop is lost/stolen/fails the video is not lost (backup).
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether each storage medium is magnetic, optical or solid-state.
(i) Blu-ray disc
(ii) Hard disk drive
(iii) Magnetic tape
(iv) SD card
(v) DVD-RW
(vi) USB pen drive
parts.answer:
(i) Optical
(ii) Magnetic
(iii) Magnetic
(iv) Solid-state
(v) Optical
(vi) Solid-state
parts.working: All six correct: 3 marks; four or five: 2 marks; two or three: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a solid-state drive can find and read a file faster than a magnetic hard disk drive.
parts.answer: An HDD must wait for the read/write head to move to the correct track and for the platter to spin to the correct sector; an SSD has no moving parts and reads electronically from any memory cell almost instantly.
parts.working: 1 mark for the HDD mechanical delay, 1 mark for the SSD electronic access.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Video games are still sold on optical discs. Explain two reasons why.
parts.answer: Any two explained, e.g. discs are very cheap to mass-produce by pressing; ROM discs cannot be changed or erased by accident/by a virus; easy to sell and package in shops; large enough capacity (Blu-ray) for a game; buyers without fast internet do not need to download a very large file; the disc can be resold/lent.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Khan family want to back up 400 GB of photos and videos. Compare using a portable hard disk drive and USB flash drives for this backup.
parts.answer: Both are portable and connect by USB, and both can be overwritten. A portable HDD holds 400 GB or more on one device whereas several flash drives might be needed; an HDD is cheaper per GB; a flash drive has no moving parts so is less easily damaged if dropped; flash drives are smaller and lighter; an HDD may be slower to access/needs more power.
parts.working: 1 mark per comparison point, max 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two differences between RAM and ROM.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. RAM is volatile (contents lost when power is off) but ROM is non-volatile; RAM can be written to and read from but ROM can only be read; RAM stores the programs/data currently in use, ROM stores the start-up instructions (BIOS/boot program); RAM is usually much larger than ROM in a computer.
parts.working: 1 mark for each difference that refers to both.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is normally stored in ROM in a personal computer.
parts.answer: The start-up/boot instructions (BIOS/firmware) needed when the computer is switched on.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is stored in RAM while a computer is being used.
parts.answer: The parts of the operating system, applications and data currently in use.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the contents of RAM would be lost during a power cut.
parts.answer: RAM is volatile: it needs a constant power supply to keep its contents.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare internal memory with backing storage.
parts.answer: Both store data and programs. Internal memory (RAM/ROM) is accessed directly by the processor, whereas backing storage must be loaded into RAM first; RAM is volatile while backing storage is non-volatile, so it keeps files when switched off; backing storage has much larger capacity; RAM is faster to access; backing storage is cheaper per GB; backing storage may be removable/external, internal memory is on the motherboard.
parts.working: 1 mark per comparison point, max 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a computer needs both RAM and backing storage.
parts.answer: RAM holds the programs and data the processor is currently using; RAM is fast so the processor can work quickly; RAM is volatile so files would be lost when switched off; backing storage keeps files/programs permanently when the power is off; backing storage has a much larger capacity than RAM so it can store all programs and files; RAM is too expensive to provide that capacity.
parts.working: 1 mark per point, max 4. Must address both RAM and backing storage for full marks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sana's computer becomes very slow when she has a web browser, a spreadsheet and a video editor open at once. A technician says that adding more RAM will help. Explain why.
parts.answer: All open programs and their data must be held in RAM; when RAM is full, the operating system moves some data to backing storage (virtual memory) and back again; backing storage is much slower than RAM, so the computer slows down; more RAM means more programs/data can be held in fast memory at once, so less swapping is needed.
parts.working: 1 mark per point, max 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether each statement is true or false.
(i) ROM keeps its contents when the computer is switched off.
(ii) Data in RAM can be read but cannot be changed.
(iii) Backing storage is usually larger than RAM.
(iv) A solid-state drive is an example of internal memory.
parts.answer:
(i) True
(ii) False
(iii) True
(iv) False
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: A laptop is advertised with 16 GB of RAM and a 512 GB solid-state drive.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times larger the solid-state drive is than the RAM.
parts.answer: 32 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why computers have much less RAM than backing storage.
parts.answer: RAM costs much more per gigabyte than backing storage; RAM only needs to hold the programs and data currently in use, while backing storage holds every file and program.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: The program that controls a washing machine is stored in ROM. Explain why ROM is used for this program.
parts.answer: ROM is non-volatile so the program is still there when the machine is unplugged/switched on again; ROM cannot be changed so the program cannot be erased or altered by accident.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The washing machine also contains a small amount of RAM. Explain why RAM is needed.
parts.answer: To store data that changes during a wash, e.g. the user's chosen programme/temperature, the time remaining and current sensor readings; this data must be written and changed, which is not possible in ROM.
parts.working: 1 mark for an example of temporary data, 1 mark for needing to change it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Backing storage is described as non-volatile. State what this means.
parts.answer: It keeps its data when the power is switched off.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Usman is typing an essay when a power cut happens. He saved the file ten minutes earlier. Explain what he will find when the power returns and why.
parts.answer: The version saved ten minutes ago is still there because it was saved to non-volatile backing storage; the work typed since then is lost because it was only in volatile RAM.
parts.working: 1 mark for each half.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the type of storage described in each statement. Choose from RAM, ROM or backing storage.
(i) It holds the program the processor is running right now.
(ii) It holds the instructions used when the computer is first switched on.
(iii) It keeps the user's photos and documents when the computer is switched off.
parts.answer:
(i) RAM
(ii) ROM
(iii) Backing storage
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hira edits videos for a YouTube channel about Pakistani cooking. She has enough money either to double the RAM in her computer or to double the capacity of its backing storage, but not both. Discuss which upgrade she should choose.
parts.answer: RAM upgrade: video editing software and high-resolution video frames need lots of RAM; more RAM lets her preview/edit without the computer swapping data to slower storage, so editing is smoother and faster; allows other programs to stay open. Backing storage upgrade: video files are very large, so a full drive stops her saving new projects; more space lets her keep raw footage and finished videos; but extra storage does not make editing faster. Other points: she could store old videos on an external drive/cloud instead; the choice depends on whether her problem is speed or space. Conclusion justified from the points made.
parts.working: 5–6: both options discussed in detail with a justified conclusion; 3–4: both options with some explanation; 1–2: simple statements.

subtopic: Design: data capture forms and file structures

parts.label: a
parts.text: A systems analyst is designing an on-screen data capture form for new members of a sports club in Abbottabad. Give three features of a well-designed on-screen form.
parts.answer: Any three, e.g. a clear title so users know the purpose; clear instructions/labels for each field; drop-down lists or radio buttons for fixed choices; tick boxes for yes/no answers; boxes of a suitable size for the data; fields in a logical order; navigation buttons (next/back/submit); no unnecessary fields/uncluttered layout; consistent font and colours; help/error messages.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three distinct features.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Design: data capture forms and file structures
stem:
A school library in Quetta is setting up a database table called BOOKS. Sample data for one record is shown.
BookID: QL-0457
Title: Hills of the North
DatePurchased: 14/03/2025
Price: 1850.00 (Pakistani rupees)
OnLoan: Yes
Copies: 3

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the most suitable data type for each of the six fields.
parts.answer:
BookID: Text (alphanumeric)
Title: Text
DatePurchased: Date/Time
Price: Currency (accept Number with 2 decimal places)
OnLoan: Boolean (Yes/No)
Copies: Number – Integer
parts.working: All six correct: 3 marks; four or five: 2 marks; two or three: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which field should be the primary key and give a reason.
parts.answer: BookID, because it is unique for each record/no two books have the same ID (Title could be repeated).
parts.working: 1 mark for BookID, 1 mark for reason.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Design: data capture forms and file structures

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a file of customer details, the analyst stores telephone numbers such as 03001234567 in a text field, not a numeric field. Explain why.
parts.answer: A numeric field would remove the leading zero; telephone numbers may contain + or spaces/dashes; no calculations are carried out on them.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The analyst stores each customer's date of birth rather than their age. Explain why.
parts.answer: Age changes every year so the stored value would become wrong/need updating; age can always be calculated from the date of birth and today's date.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Design: data capture forms and file structures

parts.label: a
parts.text: A clinic in Hyderabad needs an on-screen form to register new patients. The data needed is: full name, gender, date of birth, blood group (one of 8 types), telephone number and whether the patient has any allergies. Describe how the form should be designed to make data entry quick and accurate. Refer to the fields listed.
parts.answer: Title such as 'New patient registration' and short instructions; full name in a text box large enough for long names, perhaps split into first name/family name; gender chosen with radio buttons; date of birth entered with a date picker or set format dd/mm/yyyy; blood group from a drop-down list of the 8 types so it cannot be mistyped; telephone number in a text box with a set format/input mask; allergies as a yes/no tick box with a text box for details only if yes; fields in a logical order; validation on fields with clear error messages; submit/clear/next buttons; consistent layout, no clutter.
parts.working: 1 mark per feature linked to a field or explained, max 6. Generic features without reference to the scenario max 3.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Design: data capture forms and file structures

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a primary key in a database table.
parts.answer: A field that uniquely identifies each record in the table.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A car hire company in Sharjah stores these fields about each car: Make, Model, Colour, RegistrationNumber, Seats. State which field should be the primary key.
parts.answer: RegistrationNumber.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Design: data capture forms and file structures

parts.label: a
parts.text: When designing a file of student records, an analyst decides to code some data, for example storing the city as LHR for Lahore and KHI for Karachi. Give two advantages of coding data.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. less storage space is needed; faster to type so data entry is quicker; fewer spelling errors/consistent entries; easier to validate against a list of codes; faster to search/sort.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one disadvantage of coding data.
parts.answer: Users must know or look up the meaning of codes; codes may be confusing/similar; information may be lost if the coding is too general; codes run out or need changing.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Design: data capture forms and file structures
stem:
An online bookshop in Lahore sends you a file ORDERS.csv to import into a new database table. These are the first two rows:
OrderNo,CustomerCode,OrderDate,Total,Delivered,Items
ORD7711,C1043,03/11/2026,2499.5,Y,3
ORD7712,C0098,04/11/2026,780,N,1

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each field, state the data type and any format you would set so that the data is stored and displayed correctly. Total must be shown in rupees with 2 decimal places and OrderDate as day/month/year.
parts.answer: OrderNo – Text (primary key); CustomerCode – Text (leading zero in C0098 kept); OrderDate – Date, format dd/mm/yyyy; Total – Currency (or Number, decimal) with 2 decimal places, shown with the Rs symbol; Delivered – Boolean (Yes/No); Items – Number, integer.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct pair, max 5 (six fields, any five correct).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the design of the output formats, such as the delivery report, must be tested before the system is used.
parts.answer: To check the report shows all the required data, correctly laid out and formatted, so that users can read and use it.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Describe what is meant by each type of test data.
(i) Normal data
(ii) Abnormal data
(iii) Extreme data
parts.answer:
(i) Data within the acceptable range/of the correct type that should be accepted.
(ii) Data outside the range or of the wrong type that should be rejected.
(iii) Data on the boundaries of the acceptable range (the largest and smallest acceptable values) that should be accepted.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A secondary school in Sialkot accepts students aged 11 to 18 inclusive. The Age field is validated. Give one example of normal data, two examples of extreme data and one example of abnormal data for this field, with the expected result for each.
parts.answer: Normal: any whole number 12–17 (e.g. 14) – accepted. Extreme: 11 – accepted and 18 – accepted. Abnormal: e.g. 9, 19, -3 or 'twelve' – rejected.
parts.working: 1 mark normal, 1 mark each extreme (both 11 and 18), 1 mark abnormal; expected results must be correct.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a new computer system must be tested before it is implemented.
parts.answer: To find and remove errors/bugs before real data is used; to make sure the system meets the requirements set in analysis; to check it works with real volumes of data; to avoid data loss or wrong results that would cost the company money.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the file structure of the new system must be tested.
parts.answer: To check that each field has the correct data type and size so that data can be stored without being cut short/rejected; to check the validation rules accept/reject the right data; to check links between tables/searching and sorting work.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two points.

stem: A field called ExamMark must contain a whole number from 0 to 100 inclusive. A tester uses these test values: 0, 57, 100, 101, −1, fifty.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each test value, state the type of test data and whether it should be accepted or rejected.
parts.answer:
0 – extreme, accepted
57 – normal, accepted
100 – extreme, accepted
101 – abnormal, rejected
−1 – abnormal, rejected
fifty – abnormal, rejected
parts.working: All six correct: 3 marks; four or five: 2 marks; two or three: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: After testing with test data, the system is tested with live data. Explain what live data is and why it is used.
parts.answer: Real data from the organisation that has known results (e.g. data used with the old system); used to check the new system produces the same results as the old system/works with real data and real volumes.
parts.working: 1 mark for meaning, 1 mark for reason.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a test plan.
parts.answer: A document listing each test to be carried out, the test data to be used and the expected outcome (with space for the actual outcome).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two items that are recorded for each test in a test plan.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. test number; what is being tested; test data; type of test data; expected outcome; actual outcome; remedial action.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: A hotel booking system in Murree only accepts a booking date from today up to and including 90 days after today. Today's date is 25/10/2026.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the two extreme test values for the booking date.
parts.working: 1 mark each. Days after today: 6 (rest of October) + 30 (November) + 31 (December) + 23 (January) = 90.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of abnormal data for this field and explain why it should be rejected.
parts.answer: E.g. 24/10/2026 – a date in the past; or 24/01/2027 – more than 90 days ahead; or 31/11/2026 – not a real date.
parts.working: 1 mark for value, 1 mark for reason.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name three methods a systems analyst can use to research the current system.
parts.answer: Any three of: observation; interviews; questionnaires; examining documents.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An analyst is studying how a busy hospital pharmacy in Lahore records medicines given to patients. Give two advantages of using observation to research the current system.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. the analyst sees what actually happens rather than what staff say happens; reliable first-hand information; sees the whole process, including problems staff may not mention; relatively cheap/does not take staff away from work.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two disadvantages of using observation in this pharmacy.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. staff may work differently/better when they know they are watched; time-consuming for the analyst; the analyst may be in the way in a busy area; patient confidentiality – analyst may see private information; may not see rare problems during the visit.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A textile company has 800 employees working in offices in Karachi, Lahore and Faisalabad. Compare using questionnaires and interviews to find out what the employees think of the current system.
parts.answer: Both collect the views of users. Questionnaires can reach all 800 employees in different cities quickly and cheaply, whereas interviews take much longer and need travel; questionnaires can be anonymous so answers may be more honest, while in interviews staff may say what they think the analyst wants; interviews let the analyst ask follow-up questions and explain, but questionnaires have fixed questions; questionnaires may not all be returned; questionnaire answers are easier to analyse.
parts.working: 1 mark per comparison point, max 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A courier company in Karachi records parcel deliveries on paper. A systems analyst has been asked to produce a new computerised system. Describe the tasks the analyst carries out in the analysis stage.
parts.answer: Research the current system using observation/interviews/questionnaires/examining documents; record the inputs (e.g. parcel details, addresses), processing (e.g. allocating parcels to drivers) and outputs (e.g. delivery lists, receipts) of the current system; identify problems with the current system (e.g. lost parcels, slow tracking); identify user requirements (what staff need the new system to do); identify information requirements; identify the hardware and software needed for the new system; produce a requirements specification/cost-benefit.
parts.working: 1 mark per task, max 6. Max 4 if no reference to the courier scenario.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two things a systems analyst can learn by examining the documents used in the current system.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. what data is input/collected; what outputs are produced; the format/layout of current forms and reports; how much data is handled/volumes of data; the processing that takes place.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one disadvantage of examining documents.
parts.answer: It can be time-consuming; documents may be out of date/incomplete; difficult to understand without knowing the business; does not show users' opinions.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the four methods of implementing a new system.
parts.answer: Direct changeover; parallel running; pilot running; phased implementation.
parts.working: All four: 2 marks; two or three: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe direct changeover.
parts.answer: The old system is stopped and the new system is started at the same time/immediately replaces it.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bank introduces a new payroll system using parallel running. Describe parallel running.
parts.answer: The old and new systems are both used together for a period, processing the same data, until the new system is shown to work.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two advantages and one disadvantage of parallel running for the bank.
parts.answer: Advantages (any two): if the new system fails, the old one is still running so no data/pay is lost; results of the two systems can be compared to check the new system is correct; staff can be trained gradually. Disadvantage (any one): expensive because data is entered twice/extra staff or overtime needed; extra workload for staff; takes longer to fully implement.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 2 advantages and 1 disadvantage.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A supermarket chain with 60 stores across Pakistan is introducing a new stock control system using pilot running. Describe pilot running in this context.
parts.answer: The new system is introduced in one store (or a few stores) first; when it works there it is introduced in the other stores.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of pilot running for the supermarket chain.
parts.answer: Advantage: if the system fails only one store is affected; staff in the pilot store can help train others; problems can be fixed before full roll-out; cheaper than parallel running across all stores. Disadvantage: takes longer to implement across all 60 stores; if the system fails, the pilot store is affected/loses data; the pilot store may not be typical of all stores.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Recommend the most suitable implementation method for each situation and explain your choice.
(i) A hospital's new patient records system, where no data must be lost.
(ii) A restaurant chain with 40 branches that all do the same work.
(iii) A factory's new system made of separate stock, payroll and sales modules.
parts.answer:
(i) Parallel running – the old system continues so if the new system fails records are not lost; results can be compared.
(ii) Pilot running – try it in one branch first; any problems affect only one branch before roll-out to the others.
(iii) Phased implementation – introduce one module at a time so each part can be tested and staff trained gradually; a failure affects only one part.
parts.working: For each: 1 mark for method, 1 mark for explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A small school in Murree is replacing its paper attendance registers with a computerised system. The head teacher wants to use direct changeover during the summer holidays. Evaluate this choice.
parts.answer: For: cheapest method – no duplication of work; the new system is used straight away so benefits are immediate; during the holidays no attendance is being taken, so there is time to set up and test before term; staff only have to learn one system. Against: if the new system fails at the start of term there is no backup, so attendance data could be lost (important for safety/fire registers); all staff need training before day one; any errors affect the whole school at once. Mitigations: test thoroughly; keep paper registers ready in case. Conclusion, e.g. suitable for a small school with a simple system, given the holiday timing.
parts.working: 5–6: both sides developed with conclusion linked to the scenario; 3–4: both sides with some development; 1–2: simple points.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the most suitable validation check for each field.
(i) StudentID must have exactly 6 characters.
(ii) Gender must be M, F or X.
(iii) Mark must be from 0 to 100.
(iv) Email address must contain one @ symbol followed by a dot.
parts.answer:
(i) Length check
(ii) Lookup check (list/table lookup)
(iii) Range check
(iv) Format check
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: A hardware shop in Gujranwala uses a database table called SALES. The field Quantity must be a whole number from 1 to 50.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the validation rule you would enter for the Quantity field.
parts.answer: >=1 And <=50 (accept Between 1 And 50)
parts.working: 1 mark for correct operators and both limits.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the data type and field size you would set so that only whole numbers are accepted.
parts.answer: Number – Integer (accept Long Integer/Byte).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write suitable validation text that would be shown if the rule is broken.
parts.answer: E.g. 'Quantity must be a whole number from 1 to 50.'
parts.working: 1 mark for a message that tells the user what to enter.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A car park system stores vehicle registrations in the form ABC-123: three capital letters, a hyphen, then three digits. Describe how a format check would validate this field.
parts.answer: It checks that the data matches the pattern: three letters, then '-', then three digits (in the right positions).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one registration that would pass the format check and one that would fail.
parts.answer: Pass e.g. LEB-472; fail e.g. LEB472 / 12-ABC / LE-4721.
parts.working: 1 mark for both correct.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a registration that passes the format check could still be wrong.
parts.answer: Validation only checks that data is sensible/matches the rules, not that it is correct; e.g. LEB-427 typed instead of LEB-472 would pass.
parts.working: 1 mark.

stem:
A bookshop checks book numbers using a check digit. The first 12 digits of a book number are 978627880415. The check digit is calculated like this:
• multiply the 1st, 3rd, 5th … 11th digits by 1 and the 2nd, 4th, 6th … 12th digits by 3
• add the results
• find the remainder when the total is divided by 10
• if the remainder is 0 the check digit is 0, otherwise the check digit is 10 minus the remainder.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the check digit for this book number. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A shop assistant types the number as 978627880451 followed by the check digit 1. Explain how the computer detects the error.
parts.answer: The computer recalculates the check digit from the 12 digits typed: total becomes 131, remainder 1, check digit 9; 9 does not match the typed check digit 1, so the number is rejected (transposition error found).
parts.working: 1 mark for recalculating and comparing, 1 mark for correct values 131/9.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give three items that are found in user documentation.
parts.answer: Any three, e.g. how to load/run the software; how to save and print; how to add, edit and delete records; how to search/sort; hardware and software requirements; error messages and what to do (troubleshooting); FAQs; glossary; tutorials; screenshots; index/contents.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two items that are found in technical documentation but not in user documentation.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. program listing/code; flowcharts/algorithms; file structures; validation rules; programming language used; system design/data flow diagrams; test plans and results; known bugs.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why technical documentation is produced for a new system and state who uses it.
parts.answer: Used by systems analysts/programmers/technicians; so that the system can be maintained, updated or repaired later; so that errors can be found and fixed by someone who did not write the system; so that the system can be upgraded/extended.
parts.working: 1 mark for who uses it, 2 marks for reasons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare user documentation and technical documentation.
parts.answer: Both describe the system and both include hardware/software requirements. User documentation is written for people who use the system, whereas technical documentation is for people who maintain/develop it; user documentation explains how to carry out tasks (save, print, search) in plain language, while technical documentation includes program code, file structures and validation rules; user documentation has tutorials/FAQs/troubleshooting, technical documentation has algorithms/flowcharts/test results.
parts.working: 1 mark per comparison point, max 4; at least one similarity for full marks.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why user documentation often includes a troubleshooting section.
parts.answer: Users can solve common problems/error messages themselves without needing a technician; this saves time and support costs and the user can continue working.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by validation.
parts.answer: An automatic check by the computer that data entered is sensible/reasonable/follows set rules.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is meant by verification.
parts.answer: A check that data has been copied/entered accurately from the source document (or transferred without change).
parts.working: 1 mark. Do not accept 'checks that data is correct'.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether each method is a validation check or a verification method.
(i) Range check
(ii) Double data entry
(iii) Visual check against the original form
(iv) Presence check
parts.answer:
(i) Validation
(ii) Verification
(iii) Verification
(iv) Validation
parts.working: All four correct: 2 marks; two or three correct: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A clerk is typing students' examination marks from paper mark sheets into a database. Explain why both validation and verification should be used.
parts.answer: Validation will reject marks that are impossible/unreasonable, e.g. 112 when the maximum is 100; but validation cannot detect a reasonable but wrong mark, e.g. 67 typed as 76; verification (double entry/visual check) compares the entry with the mark sheet so it finds these copying errors; but verification does not check the data is sensible – a mark copied correctly may still be impossible if the sheet is wrong; so together they reduce errors (although neither guarantees the data is correct).
parts.working: 1 mark per point, max 4. Must refer to both methods.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A receptionist copies a patient's date of birth from a handwritten form and then checks the screen against the form. The form says 12/07/1985 but the patient actually wrote it wrongly; the correct date is 21/07/1985. Explain why the visual check did not find the error.
parts.answer: Verification only checks that the data on screen matches the source document; the copy was accurate, but the source document itself was wrong.
parts.working: 1 mark for what verification compares, 1 mark for source being wrong.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a range check would also not have found this error.
parts.answer: 12/07/1985 is a valid, reasonable date within any sensible range, so it passes validation.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the clinic could reduce this kind of error.
parts.answer: Ask the patient to check the details shown on screen/printout; check against an ID document such as a CNIC.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bank in Karachi employs staff to type customer details from paper application forms into its computer system. Explain how validation and verification can be used to reduce errors in the data. Include examples relevant to the bank.
parts.answer: Validation: checks done by the computer as data is entered; presence check that the customer's name and CNIC number are entered; format check on the CNIC number (5 digits-7 digits-1 digit); range check on date of birth so the customer is at least 18; lookup check on branch code/account type; type check that the phone number contains only digits. Verification: double data entry – two staff type each form and the computer compares the two copies, flagging differences; visual check – the clerk compares the screen with the paper form. Validation finds unreasonable data but not wrongly copied reasonable data; verification finds copying errors but not wrong source data; neither guarantees data is correct.
parts.working: 1 mark per valid point with example, max 6. Max 4 if only one of validation/verification is covered.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A hospital uses an admission form. Name a suitable validation check for each field.
(i) PatientName must not be left blank.
(ii) WardNumber must be from 1 to 25.
(iii) BloodGroup must be one of A+, A−, B+, B−, AB+, AB−, O+, O−.
(iv) DischargeDate must not be before AdmissionDate.
parts.answer:
(i) Presence check
(ii) Range check
(iii) Lookup check (list/table lookup)
(iv) Consistency check (cross-field check)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name one verification method that could be used when the form is typed in.
parts.answer: Double data entry or visual check.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how double data entry is used to verify data.
parts.answer: The data is entered twice (often by two different people); the computer compares the two versions and flags/rejects any differences so they can be checked against the source.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one disadvantage of double data entry.
parts.answer: Takes twice as long/costs more in staff time; if both people make the same mistake it is not detected; it does not detect errors in the source document.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a visual check is carried out.
parts.answer: After data is entered, the person compares the data on the screen with the original source document, item by item, and corrects any differences.
parts.working: 1 mark for comparing with the source, 1 mark for correcting differences.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one disadvantage of a visual check.
parts.answer: The person may not notice errors (tiredness/boredom); slow for large amounts of data; the person who typed the data may make the same reading error again.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: When creating an account on an online learning website, a student must type a new password twice. Explain whether this is validation or verification.
parts.answer: Verification; it checks that the second entry matches the first, so the password has been typed accurately (it does not check whether the password is reasonable).
parts.working: 1 mark for verification, 1 mark for reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The website also rejects any password with fewer than 8 characters. Name this check and explain why the website uses it.
parts.answer: Length check (validation); short passwords are easier to guess/crack, so a minimum length makes accounts more secure.
parts.working: 1 mark for length check, 1 mark for reason.

stem: A college in Lahore stores students' results in a database table. The field Grade must contain only A, B, C, D, E or U.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a validation rule for the Grade field.
parts.answer: "A" Or "B" Or "C" Or "D" Or "E" Or "U" (accept In ("A","B","C","D","E","U"))
parts.working: 1 mark for all six values correctly combined.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the field size you would set for Grade.
parts.answer: 1 (one character).
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A Pakistani CNIC number has the form 12345-1234567-1 (five digits, a hyphen, seven digits, a hyphen, one digit). Name the most suitable validation check for this field and describe what it checks.
parts.answer: Format check; it checks that the characters are in the pattern 5 digits, '-', 7 digits, '-', 1 digit (15 characters in total).
parts.working: 1 mark for format check, 1 mark for description.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a numeric type check would not be suitable for this field.
parts.answer: The CNIC contains hyphens, which are not numbers, so valid entries would be rejected (and a number field could not check the pattern).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each error made when typing data from a paper form, state whether it would be found by validation, by verification, or by both. Give the name of a suitable check or method for each.
(i) Age typed as 150.
(ii) Telephone number 03001234567 typed as 03001234576.
(iii) Surname field left blank by mistake.
(iv) Date of birth typed as 31/02/2010.
(v) Quantity 18 typed as 81 when quantities from 1 to 100 are allowed.
parts.answer:
(i) Validation (range check) – also found by verification
(ii) Verification only (double entry/visual check) – passes format and length checks
(iii) Validation (presence check) – also found by verification
(iv) Validation (type check – a Date field rejects 31/02 because it is not a real date; a simple dd/mm/yyyy format check alone would not) – also found by verification
(v) Verification only (double entry/visual check) – 81 is within range
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct answer with suitable check/method. Accept 'both' for (i), (iii), (iv).

parts.label: a
parts.text: An online shop in Lahore asks customers to type their email address twice when they register. Name the type of check this is.
parts.answer: Verification (double entry).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two validation checks the shop could carry out on the delivery details, stating the field each applies to.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. presence check on name/address; format check on email/phone number; length check on phone number (11 digits); lookup check on city; type check that postcode contains digits.
parts.working: 1 mark for each check correctly matched to a field.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what a character check does. Give an example of a field where it could be used.
parts.answer: It checks that the data contains only allowed characters (e.g. letters, spaces, hyphens, apostrophes) and no invalid ones; e.g. a person's name field such as 'Bushra Al-Saud' should not contain digits.
parts.working: 1 mark for description, 1 mark for suitable example.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a name that passes the character check may still be incorrect.
parts.answer: Validation only checks the characters are allowed, not that the name is spelt correctly, e.g. 'Busra' would pass.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A university in Doha asks applicants to type their email address twice, and also checks that it contains an @ symbol followed by a full stop later in the address. Explain what kind of error each of these two checks can detect.
parts.answer: Typing it twice (verification) detects a typing/copying slip where the two entries are different; the @ and full stop check (format check, validation) detects entries that cannot be email addresses, e.g. missing @.
parts.working: 1 mark for each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: An applicant types ahmed.raza@gmial.com in both boxes. Explain why neither check detects the error and what effect this will have.
parts.answer: Both entries are identical so verification passes; the address has the correct format so validation passes; the university's emails will go to a non-existent/wrong address so the applicant will not receive them.
parts.working: 1 mark for why both checks pass, 1 mark for effect.

stem: A sports club database has a table MEMBERS. The field JoinDate stores the date the member joined. The field Surname must always be completed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a validation rule that prevents a JoinDate later than today's date.
parts.answer: <=Date() (accept <=Now())
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how you would make sure the Surname field is never left blank, and name this type of check.
parts.answer: Set the field's Required property to Yes (accept validation rule Is Not Null); presence check.
parts.working: 1 mark for both.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what a consistency check is. Give an example from a school database.
parts.answer: It checks that data in two (or more) fields agrees/makes sense together; e.g. if Title is 'Mrs' then Gender must be F; or LeavingDate must be after JoiningDate; or a student in Year 7 cannot have an age of 17.
parts.working: 1 mark for description, 1 mark for example.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a consistency check is different from a range check.
parts.answer: A range check compares one field with fixed upper and lower limits; a consistency check compares the value in one field with the value in another field.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why data that passes all validation and verification checks may still be wrong.
parts.answer: Checks only find data that is unreasonable or wrongly copied; the source data itself could be wrong (e.g. the person gave the wrong information).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why an online shop validates data on its checkout page. Give one example of a validation check it might use.
parts.answer: To stop unreasonable/impossible data being stored (e.g. so orders are not sent to incomplete addresses); e.g. presence check on the delivery address, or range check that quantity is at least 1.
parts.working: 1 mark for purpose, 1 mark for example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Contrast validation and verification.
parts.answer: Validation is carried out automatically by the computer, whereas verification is often done by a person (visual check) or by entering data twice; validation checks data is reasonable/follows rules, while verification checks data has been copied accurately from the source; validation can reject impossible values (e.g. 32/13/2026) but not correctly formatted wrong data, while verification can find copying mistakes but not errors in the source; validation uses checks such as range/presence/format, verification uses double entry/visual check.
