parts.working: 1 mark per contrasting point, max 4. Points must refer to both methods.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by proofreading a document.
parts.answer: Reading through a document carefully (by a person) to find and correct errors in spelling, grammar, punctuation, layout and content/consistency.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two types of error that a spell checker would not find.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. a correctly spelt word used in the wrong place (their/there, form/from); missing words; wrong facts/numbers; correctly spelt names typed incorrectly; layout errors such as inconsistent fonts.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: This sentence was typed into a newsletter: "The prize giving will be held in the mane hall on Mondey at 10 am, and all parents are invited to there celebration."

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the three spelling or word errors in the sentence and give the correct word for each.
parts.answer: mane → main; Mondey → Monday; there → their
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which of these errors a spell checker would detect and explain why the others would not be detected.
parts.answer: Only 'Mondey' would be detected because it is not in the dictionary; 'mane' and 'there' are real words, so the spell checker accepts them even though they are wrong in this context.
parts.working: 1 mark for Mondey, 1 mark for explanation.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: When proofreading a document you must make sure there are no widows or orphans. State what is meant by a widow and an orphan.
parts.answer: Widow: the last line of a paragraph appears on its own at the top of a new page/column. Orphan: the first line of a paragraph appears on its own at the bottom of a page/column.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe one way to prevent widows and orphans in a word-processed document.
parts.answer: Turn on widow/orphan control in the paragraph settings (or insert a page/column break before the paragraph; keep lines together).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Before printing a word-processed report, a student proofreads the layout. Give three layout problems the student should check for.
parts.answer: Any three, e.g. blank pages; widows and orphans; tables split across pages/columns; headings separated from the text that follows; images overlapping text or outside margins; inconsistent styles, fonts or spacing; inconsistent bullet/numbering; text not aligned as required.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student types a travel guide about Pakistan. The spell checker underlines the correctly spelt place names Peshawar, Hunza and Skardu. Explain what the student should do with each place name and why she should not choose 'Change' or 'Change All'.
parts.answer: Choose 'Ignore All' (or 'Add to dictionary' if the names will be used again); the names are correct but are not in the software's dictionary; 'Change'/'Change All' would replace the correct names with the suggested (wrong) words throughout the document.
parts.working: 1 mark for ignore/add, 1 mark for why flagged, 1 mark for danger of Change All.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The guide is written for a British publisher. State which dictionary language the student should set and why.
parts.answer: English (UK), so that British spellings such as 'colour' and 'centre' are accepted and US spellings are flagged.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a visual check needs the original source document.
parts.answer: The data on screen must be compared with the original to see whether it has been copied accurately; without the source there is nothing to check it against, so only obvious errors could be spotted.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why it is better for a different person to carry out the visual check.
parts.answer: The person who typed the data may repeat the same misreading; a second person is more likely to spot mistakes.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A research organisation in Islamabad must enter the answers from 5000 paper survey forms. Compare double data entry and visual checking as methods of verifying the data.
parts.answer: Both compare the entered data with the source to find copying errors and neither finds errors in the source. Double entry is automatic in the comparison so it finds almost all differences, whereas a visual check relies on a person noticing errors and may miss some through tiredness; double entry needs each form typed twice so costs more staff time, while a visual check is a single re-read; for 5000 forms a visual check would be very tiring, so double entry is more reliable; double entry cannot detect the same mistake made twice.
parts.working: 1 mark per comparison point, max 4; at least one similarity for full marks.

stem:
A school office types this notice:
"the annual sports day will be held on on Friday 13 November at the Model town ground. Parents are welcome too attend. Refreshments will be avalable from 10:00"

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify five errors in the notice and state how each should be corrected.
parts.answer:
1. 'the' at the start should have a capital T.
2. 'on on' – remove the repeated word.
3. 'Model town' should be 'Model Town' (proper noun).
4. 'too' should be 'to'.
5. 'avalable' should be 'available'.
6. A full stop is missing at the end.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five correctly identified and corrected errors.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two types of error that a grammar checker can detect.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. subject–verb agreement (they was); repeated words; missing capital at the start of a sentence; incorrect punctuation/spacing; sentence fragments; some wrong word choices (your/you're).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a user should not accept every suggestion made by a grammar checker.
parts.answer: The checker does not understand meaning/context and can suggest changes that make the sentence wrong or change its meaning (e.g. in technical terms or quotes).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A document is set out in two columns. After proofreading, a student notices that the subheading 'Visiting Lahore Fort' is the last line of the first column while its paragraph starts at the top of the second column. Explain why this is a problem and describe how to fix it.
parts.answer: A heading should stay with the text it introduces – the reader sees it separated from its content (unprofessional/harder to read); fix by setting 'Keep with next' on the heading/heading style or by inserting a column break before the subheading.
parts.working: 1 mark for problem, 2 marks for a correct method described.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A table in the same document is split across two pages. Describe two ways to make the table easier to read.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. move the table/insert a page break so it is on one page; set table rows not to break across pages/keep with next; repeat the header row on the second page.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A company has a corporate house style. While proofreading a report, an employee checks that all headings, body text and line spacing match the house style. Give two reasons why this consistency is important.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. gives a professional appearance; makes the company's documents instantly recognisable (brand identity); makes documents easier to read/navigate; staff do not need to make layout decisions/documents from different people match.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Write down the most suitable generic file extension for each file.
(i) Plain text with no formatting, such as a list of names.
(ii) A table of data with the values separated by commas.
(iii) A formatted letter that can be opened and edited in most word processors.
(iv) A leaflet whose layout must look exactly the same on every computer and printer.
parts.answer:
(i) .txt
(ii) .csv
(iii) .rtf
(iv) .pdf
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Write the full name of each file format.
(i) .css
(ii) .pdf
(iii) .rtf
(iv) .csv
parts.answer:
(i) Cascading Style Sheet(s)
(ii) Portable Document Format
(iii) Rich Text Format
(iv) Comma Separated Values
parts.working: 1 mark each; spelling must be recognisable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why generic file formats are needed when files are shared between people.
parts.answer: Different people use different software/operating systems; a generic format can be opened by many different applications on any platform, so the receiver does not need the same software as the sender.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give an example of a situation where a generic file format would be used.
parts.answer: E.g. a school sending a timetable as .pdf to all parents; a company exporting sales data as .csv to import into a different database; sending a report as .rtf to someone with different word-processing software.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A web designer in Islamabad is choosing between .jpg and .png files for the images on a travel website. Compare the two formats.
parts.answer: Both are compressed image formats supported by all web browsers. JPG uses lossy compression so files are smaller and load faster, while PNG uses lossless compression so no detail is lost but files are larger; JPG suits photographs with many colours, PNG suits logos/text/diagrams with sharp edges; PNG supports transparent backgrounds whereas JPG does not; repeatedly editing and saving a JPG lowers its quality.
parts.working: 1 mark per comparison point, max 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two uses of .gif files on websites.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. short simple animations/animated banners; small icons/buttons; simple graphics with few colours; images with a transparent background.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why .gif is not suitable for a detailed colour photograph.
parts.answer: GIF can only store a limited palette of 256 colours, so photos with many shades would lose quality.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between lossy and lossless compression.
parts.answer: Lossy compression permanently removes some data (detail that is least noticeable), so the original cannot be restored exactly; lossless compression reduces the file size without losing any data, so the original can be rebuilt exactly.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
State which type of compression should be used for each file and give a reason.
(i) A spreadsheet of bank account balances.
(ii) A song to be streamed to mobile phones.
parts.answer:
(i) Lossless – every digit must be kept exactly/losing data would change the balances.
(ii) Lossy (e.g. .mp3) – much smaller file so it streams quickly using less data; the lost sounds are hard for people to hear.
parts.working: (i) 1 mark for lossless with reason; (ii) 1 mark for lossy, 1 mark for reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a .zip file.
parts.answer: A compressed file (archive) that can contain one or more files/folders in a smaller size (lossless).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two reasons for zipping a folder of files before emailing it.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. smaller file is quicker to upload/download; may fit within the email attachment size limit; many files are sent as one attachment; uses less storage space; can be password protected.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State what type of data is stored in each format.
(i) .mp3
(ii) .mp4
parts.answer:
(i) Audio/sound (music)
(ii) Video (with sound) – multimedia
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how an .mp3 file is made much smaller than the original recording.
parts.answer: Lossy compression removes sounds that humans cannot hear or are unlikely to notice (e.g. very high/low frequencies, quieter sounds masked by louder ones).
parts.working: 1 mark.

stem: A recording of a qawwali performance is stored as a 40 MB uncompressed audio file. Converting it to .mp3 reduces the file size by 85%. Use 1 GB = 1024 MB.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the size of the .mp3 file in MB.
parts.answer: 6 MB

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many whole .mp3 files of this size can be stored in 2 GB.
parts.answer: 341 files

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one drawback of using .mp3 for this recording.
parts.answer: Some sound quality is lost permanently and cannot be recovered (lossy).
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a practical task you are given a file called NEWSLETTER.rtf to edit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why you should save the file in your word processor's own format before you start editing.
parts.answer: The software's own format keeps all the features you add (styles, headers/footers with automated fields, section breaks, wrapped images); some of these may be lost or changed if the document is saved as .rtf.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The finished newsletter is to be sent to a printing company as a .pdf file. Give two reasons why .pdf is used.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. layout, fonts and images appear exactly as designed on any computer/printer; the printer does not need the same word processor; the file cannot be easily edited by mistake; the file is compact; fonts can be embedded.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A file called MARKS.csv contains lines such as:
Ali Raza,Lahore,85
Sara Khan,Karachi,92

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what the commas in the file do.
parts.answer: They separate the values/fields in each record (each comma marks the end of one field).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two types of software that can open this file.
parts.answer: Any two of: spreadsheet; database; text editor; word processor.
parts.working: 1 mark for two.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A website uses an external stylesheet. State what is stored in the .css file and what is stored in the .htm file.
parts.answer: .css: the styles/presentation rules (fonts, colours, sizes, alignment) for elements; .htm: the content and structure of the page (text, tables, images, links) in HTML.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the HTML element, placed in the head section, that attaches a stylesheet called style1.css stored in the same folder as the web page.
parts.answer: <link rel="stylesheet" type="text/css" href="style1.css">
parts.working: 1 mark: rel="stylesheet" and href="style1.css" required; type attribute optional; filename case must match.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student types CSS rules in a word processor and saves the file as house.rtf. He renames it house.css and attaches it to his web page, but none of the styles appear. Explain why.
parts.answer: The .rtf file contains formatting codes/control words as well as the CSS text; renaming does not remove them, so the browser cannot read the rules (invalid CSS).
parts.working: 1 mark for formatting codes in rtf, 1 mark for browser cannot interpret them.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how he should create the stylesheet so that it works.
parts.answer: Type the rules in a text editor (or the web-authoring software) and save as plain text with the .css extension.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Write down the most suitable file format for each file.
(i) A photograph of Badshahi Mosque on a website.
(ii) A school logo that must have a transparent background.
(iii) A short looping animated banner with a few colours.
(iv) A podcast episode for download.
(v) A video clip of a cricket match.
parts.answer:
(i) .jpg
(ii) .png (accept .gif)
(iii) .gif
(iv) .mp3
(v) .mp4
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare .txt and .rtf files.
parts.answer: Both are generic text formats that can be opened by most word processors/text editors. A .txt file stores only the characters with no formatting, whereas .rtf keeps formatting such as fonts, bold, colours and alignment; .txt files are smaller; .rtf can include tables/images while .txt cannot; .txt is used for simple notes/data/code, .rtf for formatted documents shared between different word processors.
parts.working: 1 mark per comparison point, max 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A school in Rawalpindi plans to email its 20-page prospectus to parents as a .pdf file instead of a word-processed file. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using .pdf.
parts.answer: Advantages: parents can open it on any device with a free reader/web browser; layout, fonts and images look exactly as designed; parents cannot easily change the content; can be compressed to a smaller file for emailing; can include links/bookmarks; can be printed accurately. Disadvantages: hard for the school or parents to edit/update – a new PDF must be made from the original; large if it contains many high-quality images; text may be hard to read on small phone screens because it does not reflow; screen readers may not read it well if not tagged; fill-in sections need special software. Conclusion.
parts.working: 5–6: both sides developed and linked to the prospectus, with conclusion; 3–4: both sides with some development; 1–2: simple points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A shop manager saves her sales spreadsheet in .csv format so that it can be imported into an accounts system. Describe three things that will be lost when the spreadsheet is saved as .csv.
parts.answer: Any three, e.g. formulas – only the calculated values are saved; cell formatting such as fonts, colours, borders, currency symbols; charts and images; additional worksheets – only the active sheet is saved; column widths/merged cells; named ranges/conditional formatting.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why .csv is still a good choice for transferring the data.
parts.answer: It is plain text that almost any spreadsheet/database/accounts software can import, whatever software created it.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a file name has an extension such as .docx or .png.
parts.answer: The extension tells the operating system what type of file it is and therefore which software to use to open it; it also lets the user see the file type.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: A school photographer has a photo of a science fair stored as a 2.88 MB file. After saving it as a .jpg the file is 0.36 MB.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage reduction in file size.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the photographer should keep a copy of the original file as well as the .jpg.
parts.answer: JPG compression is lossy, so detail removed cannot be recovered; the original is needed for high-quality printing/later editing, and re-saving a JPG reduces quality further.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a database task you are given data in .csv files to import. Explain why the data is supplied in .csv format.
parts.answer: CSV is a generic, plain-text format; it can be imported into any database software, whichever package the candidate uses.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: When importing a .csv file, the first row contains the field names. State the setting you choose during import so that these become field names and not a record.
parts.answer: Select 'First row contains field names/headings'.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether each file normally stores an image, audio, video or text.
(i) .png
(ii) .mp3
(iii) .mp4
(iv) .txt
(v) .gif
(vi) .csv
parts.answer:
(i) Image
(ii) Audio
(iii) Video
(iv) Text
(v) Image
(vi) Text (data)
parts.working: All six: 3 marks; four or five: 2 marks; two or three: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is stored in an .htm file and name one type of software that can open it.
parts.answer: The HTML code (tags and content) of a web page; opened by a web browser (or a text editor/web-authoring software).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A web page refers to its images using relative file paths such as . Explain why the image files must be copied into the same folder when the website is moved to a new computer.
parts.answer: A relative path tells the browser to look for the file in the same folder as the page; if the image is not there it cannot be found and will not display.
parts.working: 1 mark.

stem: Imran wants to email 25 holiday photos from Swat to his cousin in Toronto. The photos are .jpg files with a total size of 180 MB. His email service allows attachments of up to 25 MB per email.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the smallest number of emails needed if the photos are sent without changing them.
parts.answer: 8 emails
parts.working: 180 ÷ 25 = 7.2, so round up to 8 emails.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Imran zips the photos but the zip file is still about 175 MB. Explain why.
parts.answer: JPG files are already compressed (lossy), so lossless zip compression can make them only slightly smaller.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe two other ways Imran could send the photos.
parts.answer: Reduce the resolution/quality of the photos (lossy) so they fit in fewer emails; upload them to cloud storage and email a link with shared access; use a file-transfer service.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: You are given these files: banner.jpg, notes.txt, style4.css, map.png, logo.jpg, prices.csv. You are told to copy only the image files with a .jpg extension and the stylesheet into a new folder. List the files you copy.
parts.answer: banner.jpg, logo.jpg, style4.css
parts.working: 1 mark for both .jpg files only, 1 mark for style4.css; lose 1 mark for each extra file.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one reason why web page file names should not contain spaces.
parts.answer: Spaces can cause broken links on some web servers/browsers (they become %20 in the URL); file names must match exactly.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A college in Hyderabad publishes its examination timetable as a .pdf file on its website. Give two advantages of using .pdf.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. students can open it on any device without the original software; layout looks the same on every device/printer; students cannot easily change the times; small file size quick to download.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A video-streaming service stores films as compressed .mp4 files. Describe how lossy compression reduces the size of a video file.
parts.answer: Removes detail that viewers are unlikely to notice (e.g. small colour differences); stores only the parts of each frame that change from the previous frame instead of every whole frame; reduces the resolution/frame rate/bit rate; removes inaudible sounds from the soundtrack.
parts.working: 1 mark per point, max 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why the service uses lossy rather than lossless compression.
parts.answer: Lossy compression gives much smaller files, so films stream without buffering and use less data/storage; the small loss of quality is hardly noticed.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A teacher opens the file SCORES.csv in a text editor and then in a spreadsheet. Describe what she sees in each case.
parts.answer: Text editor: plain lines of text with the values separated by commas (one record per line). Spreadsheet: each value placed in its own cell, in rows and columns.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: She had typed a formula to total the scores before saving as .csv. Explain what happens to the formula.
parts.answer: Only the result/value is saved; the formula itself is lost.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Write down the most suitable file format for each purpose.
(i) An application form attached to an email that must look the same for everyone and should not be edited.
(ii) Data moved from one database package to a different database package.
(iii) A file holding the colours and fonts used by every page of a website.
parts.answer:
(i) .pdf
(ii) .csv
(iii) .css
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A photographer in Hunza is sending landscape photos to a magazine that will print them on large pages. Discuss whether she should send the photos as highly compressed .jpg files or in a lossless format such as .png.
parts.answer: JPG (high compression): much smaller files, quick to upload over a slow mountain internet connection, fit email limits, use less storage; but lossy – fine detail and colour gradients (sky) may show blocks/artefacts when printed large, and quality cannot be recovered. Lossless (.png): keeps every pixel, best quality for large printing and further editing by the magazine; but files are much larger, slow to upload, may need cloud storage/file transfer. Middle way: JPG at high quality/low compression, or send small previews first then full files of chosen photos. Conclusion, e.g. lossless/high-quality files because print quality is the priority.
parts.working: 5–6: both formats discussed in context with justified conclusion; 3–4: both sides with some development; 1–2: simple points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A web page must show the video clip tour.mp4 with controls that the user can use to play and pause it. If the browser cannot play the video, the text 'Video not supported' must be shown. Write the HTML to do this.
parts.answer:
<video controls>
  <source src="tour.mp4" type="video/mp4">
  Video not supported
</video>
parts.working: 1 mark for <video controls> … </video>; 1 mark for source with src="tour.mp4" (type="video/mp4"); 1 mark for fallback text placed inside the video element. Accept <video src="tour.mp4" controls>Video not supported</video>.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why .mp4 is a suitable format for video on a web page.
parts.answer: It is supported by almost all browsers/devices and is compressed so it downloads/streams quickly.
parts.working: 1 mark.

topic: Networks and the effects of using them
stem: Ayesha uses the password ayesha2009 for her school email account.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why this is a weak password.
parts.answer: It is easy to guess because it uses her own name and probably her year of birth, and it has no capital letters or symbols.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: contains personal information (her name) | number looks like a birth year/date, easily found | no upper-case letters | no special characters/symbols | all lower case so fewer combinations to try | could be cracked quickly by software trying names/dates.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two features of a strong password.
parts.answer: At least 8 characters long; a mix of upper case, lower case, digits and symbols (and no personal information or dictionary words).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: at least 8 (or more) characters | mixes upper and lower case letters | includes numbers | includes special characters such as # or ! | not a dictionary word | no personal details such as names or dates.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two other actions Ayesha should take to keep her password secure.
parts.answer: Change it regularly; never tell it to anyone or write it down (and use a different password for each account).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: change it regularly | do not share it | do not write it down / store it where others can see | use a different password for each account | log out on shared computers | do not let browser remember it on a shared device | watch for shoulder surfing when typing it.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Networks and the effects of using them

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bank's mobile app asks a customer for a password and then sends a six-digit code by text message to the customer's phone. State the name of this method of authentication.
parts.answer: Two-factor authentication (2FA).
parts.working: B1 two-factor authentication / two-step verification / multi-factor authentication.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this method is more secure than using a password alone.
parts.answer: Two different factors are needed: something the user knows (password) and something they have (the phone). A hacker who has stolen the password still cannot log in without the phone, and the code changes every time and expires quickly.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: needs two separate pieces of evidence | something you know plus something you have | stolen/guessed password alone is not enough | code is sent only to the registered phone | code is one-time / changes every login | code expires after a short time | user is alerted if a code arrives that they did not request.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Networks and the effects of using them
stem: A hospital in Karachi wants staff to use biometric methods instead of passwords to unlock the computers that hold patient records.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two biometric methods the hospital could use.
parts.answer: Fingerprint recognition; face (facial) recognition.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: fingerprint | facial recognition | retina scan | iris scan | voice recognition | hand/palm vein recognition.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two advantages of biometric methods over passwords for the hospital staff.
parts.answer: Staff cannot forget or lose their fingerprint/face, so no resets are needed; biometrics are unique and very hard to copy or share, so only authorised staff can open records.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two expanded points: cannot be forgotten | cannot be lost or left behind | unique to each person so harder to fake | cannot be shared with or lent to a colleague | faster to log in during emergencies | no need to remember many passwords | stops shoulder surfing of a typed password.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe two disadvantages of biometric methods in a hospital.
parts.answer: Gloves, masks or injuries (cuts, dirty hands) can stop the fingerprint or face being recognised; the scanners are expensive to buy and set up, and the biometric data is personal data that must be protected.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: surgical gloves/masks may block recognition | cuts, burns or dirt on fingers cause rejection | false rejections delay staff | expensive hardware | data is very personal – privacy concerns | if the stored biometric data is stolen it cannot be changed like a password | takes time to enrol every member of staff.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Networks and the effects of using them
stem: A company gives each employee a small physical token. When pressed, it shows a number that changes every 30 seconds. Employees type this number after their password to log in from home.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the physical token and the company's system make sure the number is accepted only once.
parts.answer: The token and the server share a secret and both run the same algorithm using the current time, so they generate the same number; the server checks the typed number matches the one it calculates for that time period, and once used (or after 30 seconds) it is no longer valid.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: token generates a one-time password (OTP) | token and server use the same algorithm/secret key | the number is linked to the time / changes every 30 s | server generates the same number and compares | if they match access is granted | the number expires and cannot be reused.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Compare a physical token with an electronic token (an authenticator app on a smartphone).
parts.answer: Both generate one-time codes used as a second factor and both must be in the user's possession. A physical token is a separate device that can be lost and costs money to issue, whereas the electronic token is software on a phone the user already owns, so it costs less, but it depends on the phone being charged and secure.
parts.working: 1 mark for a similarity: both create one-time passcodes / both are 'something you have' / both used for two-factor authentication. Up to 2 marks for differences: physical is extra hardware vs app on existing phone | physical costs the company to buy/replace vs app is free/cheap | physical has no network or battery dependence on phone vs app needs a working phone | phone can be infected with malware whereas token is a closed device.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Networks and the effects of using them
stem: A school is choosing a way for students to log on to the library computers. The options are: (1) user ID and password, (2) a smart card with a PIN, (3) zero login using face recognition.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by zero login.
parts.answer: The system authenticates the user without them typing anything, by using biometrics and behaviour (for example face, location or how they use the device) to recognise them automatically.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: no username or password is entered | user is recognised automatically by biometrics / behavioural patterns / known device or location.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the use of smart cards with a PIN for the students rather than user IDs and passwords.
parts.answer: Smart cards are quick and need two factors, but cards can be lost, forgotten or swapped and cost money; passwords cost nothing but are often weak or shared. Conclusion: smart cards with PINs are more secure if the school can afford the readers and replacement cards.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for benefits/drawbacks, max 4 on one side; 1–2 marks for a reasoned conclusion. Benefits: two factors (card + PIN) so a stolen card alone is useless | chip data is hard to copy | short PIN easier to remember than complex password | quicker log on | card can also be used for library loans/ID. Drawbacks: cards lost/forgotten so students cannot log on | cost of cards and readers | students may share card and PIN | PIN can be seen by shoulder surfing | replacement takes time. Passwords: no extra cost but often weak/written down/shared. Conclusion must weigh security against cost/convenience.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Networks and the effects of using them

parts.label: a
parts.text: A user receives a message that says their online account has been locked after three wrong password attempts. Explain why systems lock an account after a small number of failed attempts.
parts.answer: To stop a hacker using software to try thousands of possible passwords (a brute-force attack); locking after a few attempts makes guessing impractical and alerts the real owner.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: prevents repeated guessing / brute-force attacks by programs | limits the number of tries so the chance of guessing is tiny / alerts the owner and administrator.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Magnetic stripe cards and smart cards (chip cards) are both used to authenticate users. Describe two reasons why smart cards are more secure.
parts.answer: The chip data is encrypted and much harder to copy (clone) than a magnetic stripe; a smart card normally needs a PIN as well, and the chip can create a different code for each transaction.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: chip data is encrypted | magnetic stripe data is easily read and cloned (skimming) | chip used with a PIN = two factors | chip can generate a unique code each use | magnetic stripe can be damaged by magnets / easier to tamper with.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two reasons why a user should not use the same password for every online account.
parts.answer: If one website is hacked and passwords are leaked, criminals can use that password to get into all the user's other accounts; one stolen password then exposes everything (email, bank, social media).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: a data breach at one site exposes all accounts | criminals try leaked passwords on other sites | the email account could be used to reset other passwords | damage from one phishing attack is multiplied.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Networks and the effects of using them

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by cloud storage.
parts.answer: Files are saved on remote servers owned by a provider and accessed over the internet through an account; the data is usually copied on several servers.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: data stored on remote/off-site servers | owned/managed by a third-party provider | accessed via the internet using an account/login | data may be duplicated across many servers in different places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the three types of cloud storage.
parts.answer: Public cloud, private cloud, hybrid cloud.
parts.working: 1 mark each: public | private | hybrid.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Networks and the effects of using them
stem: Bilal is a university student in Lahore. He saves all his assignments to a cloud storage service instead of his laptop's hard disk.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give three advantages to Bilal of using cloud storage.
parts.answer: He can open his files from any device with internet access, e.g. a university computer; his files are backed up on the provider's servers so they are safe if his laptop is lost or damaged; he can easily share files with classmates.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: access from anywhere / any device with internet | no need to carry a storage device | automatic backup by provider | files safe if laptop is lost/stolen/broken | easy sharing and collaborating on the same file | extra storage can be bought as needed | files synchronise across devices.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two disadvantages to Bilal of using cloud storage.
parts.answer: He cannot reach his files without an internet connection; his data is held by a third party, so it could be hacked or lost if the provider has problems.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: needs an internet connection | slow upload/download on a poor connection | security risk – provider could be hacked | he loses control of his data | provider could go out of business / service outage | ongoing subscription cost for more space | uses mobile data allowance.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Networks and the effects of using them
stem: A small architecture firm in Islamabad has eight employees. It is deciding whether to use a public cloud service or to keep a server in its own office.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the difference between a public cloud and a private cloud.
parts.answer: A public cloud is run by a third-party provider and its servers are shared by many customers over the internet; a private cloud is used by one organisation only, often behind its own firewall and controlled by that organisation.
parts.working: 1 mark for public: third-party provider / storage shared by many customers / accessed over the internet. 1 mark for private: dedicated to one organisation / controlled by the organisation / behind its firewall.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages to the firm of using a public cloud service rather than a server in its office.
parts.answer: Public cloud: no server to buy or maintain, provider handles backups and security updates, staff can work from site visits and home, storage can grow easily; but monthly fees continue, a fast reliable internet connection is essential, large drawing files are slow to upload, the firm depends on the provider and client data is held by a third party. Conclusion based on cost and connectivity.
parts.working: Max 4 marks for one side; 6th mark for a reasoned conclusion. Advantages: no hardware purchase | no IT staff needed for maintenance | backups done by provider in several locations | access from anywhere (site visits) | easy to increase storage | software/security updated by provider. Disadvantages: needs reliable internet | large CAD files slow to transfer | ongoing subscription | less control over data security | provider outage stops work | legal concerns about where client data is stored.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Networks and the effects of using them

parts.label: a
parts.text: Three students are writing a group report. They each edit the same document saved in cloud storage at the same time. Describe two benefits of working this way compared with emailing copies of the file to each other.
parts.answer: Everyone works on one up-to-date copy, so there is no confusion about which version is newest and no need to merge changes; edits appear immediately and the version history lets them see who changed what and restore earlier versions.
parts.working: Two benefits, each 1 mark for identification + 1 mark for expansion: single shared copy – no conflicting versions to merge | real-time editing – see each other's changes instantly | version history – can undo/restore and see who edited | no attachment size limits | comments can be added for discussion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two security precautions the students should take when sharing the file.
parts.answer: Share only with named people (not 'anyone with the link'), giving view-only access where editing is not needed; use strong passwords with two-factor authentication on their cloud accounts.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: share with specific accounts only | set appropriate permissions (view/comment/edit) | do not post the share link publicly | strong passwords on accounts | two-factor authentication | log out on shared computers.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Networks and the effects of using them
stem: A manufacturing company keeps its customer database on servers in its own building but stores its marketing videos and staff training files with a cloud provider. Both systems are linked so staff can reach either from the same software.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the type of cloud storage the company is using and justify your answer.
parts.answer: Hybrid cloud – it combines a private cloud (the customer database on its own servers) with a public cloud (videos and training files at a provider).
parts.working: B1 hybrid. B1 justification: mixture of private (in-house, sensitive data) and public (third party, less sensitive data) linked together.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the company may have chosen to keep the customer database on its own servers.
parts.answer: The customer data is personal and sensitive; keeping it in-house gives the company full control over security and access and helps it meet data protection laws.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: personal/sensitive data | full control of security | less risk from a third party being hacked | meets data protection rules about where data is held | fast access on the local network without depending on internet.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why public cloud storage is suitable for the videos and training files.
parts.answer: These files are large and not sensitive, so the provider can store them cheaply and staff in any branch or at home can stream them over the internet without the company buying extra storage.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: large files would need expensive in-house storage | not confidential, so lower risk | accessible by staff anywhere | provider scales storage as more videos are added | provider handles backups.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Networks and the effects of using them

parts.label: a
parts.text: A freelance graphic designer in Dubai syncs her work folder between her laptop and a cloud service. Explain what happens when she edits a file on her laptop while it is offline and then reconnects.
parts.answer: The change is saved locally first; when the laptop reconnects the sync software detects the file has changed and uploads the new version to the cloud servers; other synced devices then download the updated version (if the file was also changed elsewhere, a conflict copy may be created).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: edit stored on the local copy | sync software monitors for changes | on reconnection the new version is uploaded | cloud copy is replaced/updated (old version kept in history) | other devices download the update | if edited in two places a conflicted copy is made.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why cloud storage on its own should not be her only backup.
parts.answer: Syncing copies mistakes too: if she deletes or corrupts a file, or ransomware encrypts it, the damaged version is synced to the cloud. The provider could also suffer an outage or close her account, so she should keep a separate backup, for example on an external drive.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: deletions/corruption are synced across | ransomware-encrypted files overwrite good copies | provider outage or account lock-out means no access | provider could close / lose data | needs internet to recover | a second, independent backup (external drive/another service) is good practice.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Networks and the effects of using them

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Match each device to its description by writing the correct letter next to each number.
Devices: 1 Router, 2 Switch, 3 Network interface card (NIC)
Descriptions:
P Lets a single computer connect to a network and has a unique MAC address
Q Connects a LAN to another network such as the internet and directs packets using IP addresses
R Connects devices within a LAN and sends data only to the device it is addressed to
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct match.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Networks and the effects of using them
stem: A family home in Peshawar has a laptop, two smartphones, a smart TV and a printer. All of them use the internet through one box supplied by the internet provider.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the name of the device that allows all the devices to share the single internet connection.
parts.answer: Router.
parts.working: B1 router (accept wireless router).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two functions of this device.
parts.answer: It forwards data packets between the home network and the internet using IP addresses; it gives each device on the home network a local IP address (and often provides Wi-Fi and a firewall).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: connects the LAN to the internet/WAN | routes/forwards packets to the correct destination using IP addresses | assigns local IP addresses to devices | stores a routing table | can act as a wireless access point | may include a firewall.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Networks and the effects of using them

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a hub and a switch.
parts.answer: Both connect devices in a LAN. A hub sends every data packet it receives to all connected devices, whereas a switch reads the MAC address of the destination and sends the packet only to that device, so a switch reduces unnecessary traffic and is more secure.
parts.working: 1 mark for a similarity: both connect devices on a LAN. 1 mark: hub broadcasts packets to all devices. 1 mark: switch uses MAC addresses / a lookup table to send only to the intended device. (Max 3; accept 'switch is more secure / less traffic' as expansion.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is meant by a MAC address.
parts.answer: A unique identifier given to a network interface card by the manufacturer, normally written as 12 hexadecimal digits (48 bits).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: unique number identifying a device/NIC | set by the manufacturer | made up of 48 bits / 12 hexadecimal digits / 6 pairs | part identifies manufacturer, part identifies device.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Networks and the effects of using them
stem: A school computer room has 30 desktop computers connected by cables. The network technician says the room needs a switch, and each computer needs a NIC.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why each computer needs a NIC.
parts.answer: The NIC is the hardware that physically connects the computer to the network (cable or wireless) and gives it a unique MAC address so data can be sent to it.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: provides the connection/interface to the network | has a unique MAC address so the device can be identified.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The school wants students' laptops to join the same network without cables. Name the extra device needed and describe what it does.
parts.answer: A wireless access point (WAP); it connects to the wired network (for example to the switch) and sends and receives data to and from devices by radio waves (Wi-Fi), so wireless devices become part of the LAN.
parts.working: B1 wireless access point. Then 1 mark each for any two of: connects to the wired LAN/switch | transmits/receives data using radio waves/Wi-Fi | allows wireless devices to join the LAN | can require a password/encryption key.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Networks and the effects of using them
stem: A company has two office buildings in different cities. Each building has its own LAN of about 50 computers connected through switches.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a document sent from a computer in the first office reaches a computer in the second office. Refer to switches and routers in your answer.
parts.answer: The document is split into packets. The switch in the first office reads the MAC address and forwards the packets to the router. The router reads the destination IP address and sends the packets out over the internet/WAN, where other routers pass them on. The router at the second office receives them and passes them to its switch, which uses the MAC address to deliver them only to the destination computer, where they are reassembled.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: data split into packets | switch forwards packets within the LAN using MAC addresses | router connects the LAN to the WAN/internet | router uses IP address to route the packets | packets may travel different routes via other routers | receiving router passes packets to its LAN | switch sends to correct computer | packets reassembled in order.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The company replaced its old hubs with switches. Give two benefits of doing this.
parts.answer: Less network traffic, because data goes only to the intended computer so the network is faster; better security, because other computers do not receive data meant for someone else.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: less unnecessary traffic | fewer collisions / faster network | more secure as data not broadcast to all | better performance as more devices are added.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Networks and the effects of using them

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name three items of hardware a person needs to take part in a video conference from home, other than a computer.
parts.answer: Webcam, microphone, speakers (or headphones).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: webcam/video camera | microphone | speakers | headphones/headset | large monitor/screen | router/internet connection device. Do not accept 'computer' or 'laptop'.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one item of software needed for video conferencing.
parts.answer: Video conferencing software (with a codec to compress the video).
parts.working: B1 video conferencing software/app | codec / compression software | webcam/microphone drivers | echo cancellation software.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Networks and the effects of using them
stem: A charity has volunteers in Pakistan, Kenya and the UK. The manager wants to hold monthly meetings by video conference instead of flying volunteers to one place.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe three advantages to the charity of using video conferencing.
parts.answer: It saves the cost of flights and hotels; no time is lost travelling, so meetings can be arranged quickly; volunteers can see each other's faces and share documents on screen during the meeting.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: no travel costs | no travel time | meetings can be arranged at short notice | people do not have to leave family/home | less carbon emission | can see facial expressions/body language | documents/screens can be shared | meetings can be recorded.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe three disadvantages of video conferencing for this charity.
parts.answer: Different time zones make it hard to find a time that suits everyone; a slow or unreliable internet connection causes lag or dropped calls; some volunteers may need to buy equipment or need training, and it is harder to build personal relationships.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: time zone differences | poor/unreliable connection causes lag, freezing or dropped calls | cost of equipment / data | volunteers need training to use the software | less personal than meeting face-to-face | security risk of uninvited people joining | power cuts in some areas.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Networks and the effects of using them

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by audio conferencing.
parts.answer: A meeting held between people in different places using only sound, through telephones, mobile phones or computers (VoIP); a host usually sets it up with a number and PIN for others to join.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: meeting using sound/voice only | people in different locations | uses telephones/mobile phones or internet calling (VoIP) | organiser gives participants a phone number/PIN to join.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two features of web conferencing that are not available in audio conferencing.
parts.answer: Participants can share their screen or slides so everyone sees the same document; they can use text chat, polls or a shared whiteboard during the meeting.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: screen sharing / presentations | video of participants | instant messaging/chat | shared whiteboard | polls/voting | file transfer | breakout rooms.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Networks and the effects of using them
stem: A secondary school in Quetta wants to hold parent–teacher meetings by web conferencing instead of in the school hall.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using web conferencing for parent–teacher meetings.
parts.answer: Advantages: parents do not need to travel or take time off work, meetings can be scheduled flexibly and parents in other cities can join, teachers can share the student's work on screen. Disadvantages: some families have no device or reliable internet, power cuts and poor connections cause problems, it is harder to discuss sensitive issues, some parents lack the skills, and privacy must be protected. Conclusion: offer web meetings as an option alongside in-person meetings.
parts.working: Max 4 marks for one side; 1–2 marks for a reasoned conclusion. Advantages: no travel time/cost | flexible times | working parents/those far away can attend | screen-share student work | shorter queues / timed slots | can be recorded with consent. Disadvantages: not all parents have devices/internet | poor connection/load-shedding | less personal, harder to read body language | parents may need help to use software | security/privacy of meeting links | staff need training.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Networks and the effects of using them

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Tick (✓) the correct network type for each description.
(i) Covers a small area such as one building and uses cables. LAN / WLAN / WAN
(ii) Covers a large geographical area, such as a country, and may use public communication links. LAN / WLAN / WAN
(iii) Covers a small area and uses radio waves to connect devices. LAN / WLAN / WAN
parts.answer: (i) LAN; (ii) WAN; (iii) WLAN.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct tick.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Networks and the effects of using them
stem: A coffee shop in Karachi offers free internet to customers through a WLAN.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two advantages to customers of using a WLAN rather than a cabled LAN.
parts.answer: They can connect their own phones and laptops without any cables, and they can move around the shop and stay connected.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: no cables needed | can move around while connected | easy to connect personal devices | many devices can join at once.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two disadvantages of a WLAN compared with a cabled LAN.
parts.answer: Data transfer is usually slower and less reliable because of interference from walls and other devices; it is less secure because signals can be intercepted by people nearby.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: slower data transfer rate | signal weakened by walls/distance | interference from other devices | less secure – signals can be intercepted | limited range | more devices sharing the connection reduces speed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe one way the coffee shop can stop people outside the shop using its WLAN.
parts.answer: Protect the network with WPA2/WPA3 encryption and a password that is given only to paying customers (and changed regularly).
parts.working: 1 mark for the method + 1 mark for expansion: password/encryption (WPA2/WPA3) + only given to customers / changed regularly | reduce transmitter power so signal does not reach outside | captive login page with a code on the receipt.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Networks and the effects of using them

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bank has 400 branches across Pakistan. Each branch has its own LAN. Explain why the bank also needs a WAN.
parts.answer: The branches are spread over a large area, so a WAN is needed to link all the branch LANs to each other and to head office, so customer account data can be shared and updated everywhere.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: branches far apart / large geographical area | WAN connects the separate LANs so data (customer accounts) can be shared/accessed centrally.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Compare a LAN with a WAN.
parts.answer: Both connect computers so they can share data and resources. A LAN covers a small area such as one building, whereas a WAN covers a large area such as a country. A LAN normally uses the organisation's own cables and equipment, but a WAN uses leased lines, telephone networks or satellites owned by other companies. LANs usually have faster data transfer than WANs.
parts.working: 1 mark for a similarity (both share data/resources / both can use routers/switches). Up to 3 marks for linked differences: small area vs large area | own cables/equipment vs public/leased links | faster vs slower | cheaper vs more expensive to run | fewer vs very many connected devices. Comparisons must state both sides.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Networks and the effects of using them
stem: A hospital is replacing its cabled LAN on the wards with a WLAN so doctors can use tablet computers at patients' bedsides.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the decision to use a WLAN on the wards.
parts.answer: Benefits: doctors can update patient records at the bedside immediately, no trailing cables, tablets can be moved between wards, cheaper to add new devices. Drawbacks: signals may be intercepted so strong encryption is needed for confidential data, interference from medical equipment or thick walls may cause dead spots, slower than cable for large scans, tablets need charging and can be lost or stolen. Conclusion: suitable if access points are planned carefully and data is encrypted.
parts.working: Max 4 for one side; 1–2 marks for a reasoned conclusion. Benefits: bedside access/updating records | fewer errors from copying notes later | no cables to trip over | flexible/mobile | easy to add devices. Drawbacks: security of patient data – interception | need encryption/strong authentication | interference/dead spots | slower for large image files | coverage needs many access points | device loss/theft | battery life.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Networks and the effects of using them

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two similarities between Wi-Fi and Bluetooth.
parts.answer: Both are wireless technologies that send data using radio waves; both can be secured using encryption/passwords.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: both wireless | both use radio waves (both can use the 2.4 GHz band) | both use encryption/security keys | both connect devices without cables | both have limited range.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two differences between Wi-Fi and Bluetooth.
parts.answer: Wi-Fi has a greater range (up to about 100 m) than Bluetooth (about 10–30 m); Wi-Fi has a faster data transfer rate, so it suits larger files and internet access, while Bluetooth suits a small number of nearby devices.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two differences, both sides stated: Wi-Fi longer range vs Bluetooth shorter | Wi-Fi faster vs Bluetooth slower | Wi-Fi connects many devices to a network/internet vs Bluetooth pairs a few devices directly (WPAN) | Bluetooth uses less power.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Networks and the effects of using them
stem: Zainab wants to send a photo from her smartphone to her friend's phone, which is next to her, using Bluetooth.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the steps involved in connecting the two phones using Bluetooth.
parts.answer: Turn Bluetooth on in both phones; set the friend's phone to be discoverable; Zainab's phone searches for nearby devices and selects her friend's phone; a pairing code/PIN is shown and confirmed on both phones; the phones are paired and the photo can be sent.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: switch Bluetooth on on both devices | make receiving device discoverable/visible | sending device searches/scans for devices | select the device from the list | pairing code/PIN is displayed/entered | code confirmed on both devices (matching) | devices paired and connection made | file sent and accepted.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Bluetooth uses spread-spectrum frequency hopping.
parts.answer: Bluetooth changes randomly between many channels (79) many times a second, which reduces interference from other devices using the same frequencies and makes the transmission harder to intercept.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: channel/frequency is changed rapidly/randomly among many channels | reduces interference from other devices / makes eavesdropping more difficult.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Networks and the effects of using them

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each situation, state whether Wi-Fi or Bluetooth is more suitable and give a reason.
(i) Connecting wireless earbuds to a phone.
(ii) Giving 25 laptops in a classroom access to the internet.
(iii) Streaming high-definition video from a home network storage device to a smart TV in another room.
parts.answer: (i) Bluetooth – short range, low power, one device paired directly to the phone. (ii) Wi-Fi – many devices can connect to the network/internet through an access point. (iii) Wi-Fi – needs a high data transfer rate and greater range through walls.
parts.working: 1 mark per situation; choice and matching reason required.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe one security risk of leaving Bluetooth switched on and discoverable in a public place, and one precaution.
parts.answer: A hacker nearby could try to pair with the phone or send unwanted files/malware; precaution: switch Bluetooth off or set the device to non-discoverable, and never accept pairing requests from unknown devices.
parts.working: 1 mark for risk: unauthorised pairing / data stolen / malware sent / unsolicited messages. 1 mark for precaution: turn off or non-discoverable when not in use | reject unknown pairing requests | keep software updated.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Networks and the effects of using them

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by an intranet.
parts.answer: A private network used inside one organisation, which uses internet technologies such as web pages, and can only be accessed by the organisation's staff (with a login).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: private network | belongs to one organisation | uses the same protocols/technology as the internet (web pages, browsers) | only accessible by authorised members/employees | usually behind a firewall.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give three differences between the internet and an intranet.
parts.answer: The internet is public and can be used by anyone, an intranet only by members of the organisation; internet information is not controlled and may be unreliable, intranet content is checked and relevant to the organisation; the internet is a worldwide network of networks, an intranet is usually within one organisation's buildings.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three linked differences: public vs private | open to anyone vs needs login/authorised | worldwide vs organisation-only | information not moderated vs controlled/policed | huge amount of general information vs company-specific information | intranet more secure/behind firewall.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one example of information a school might put on its intranet.
parts.answer: Homework timetables and class notes for students.
parts.working: B1 any suitable internal item: timetables, homework, staff notices, policies, internal forms, exam schedules.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Networks and the effects of using them
stem: A car manufacturer allows its parts suppliers to log in to part of its private network to check stock levels and place delivery schedules.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the type of network the suppliers are using and explain your answer.
parts.answer: An extranet – it is part of the company's intranet that has been opened to authorised people outside the organisation (the suppliers) through a secure login.
parts.working: B1 extranet. B1 explanation: private network extended to selected outside users / suppliers given restricted access via login.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss the benefits and drawbacks to the manufacturer of giving suppliers this access.
parts.answer: Benefits: suppliers see stock levels in real time so parts arrive just in time, fewer phone calls and emails, fewer ordering errors, faster reordering. Drawbacks: security risk if a supplier's login is stolen, cost of setting up secure access and firewalls, must limit what each supplier can see, competitors' information must be protected, dependence on the system working. Conclusion: beneficial if access is controlled and monitored.
parts.working: Max 4 for one side; 1–2 marks for conclusion. Benefits: real-time stock information | automatic/just-in-time deliveries | lower admin cost/time | fewer errors | stronger supplier relationship | available 24/7. Drawbacks: unauthorised access/hacking via supplier accounts | set-up and maintenance cost | need strict permissions | confidential data could leak to rival suppliers | downtime stops ordering.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by phishing.
parts.answer: The criminal sends a legitimate-looking email (or message) that contains a link to a fake website, to trick the user into entering personal details such as passwords or bank details.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: email/message that appears to come from a genuine organisation | contains a link/attachment | link leads to a fake website | user tricked into giving personal/financial data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two ways a user can protect themselves from phishing.
parts.answer: Do not click links in unexpected emails – type the organisation's web address yourself; check the sender's address and look for spelling mistakes or urgent threats; use a spam filter.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: do not click links/open attachments from unknown senders | type the URL directly / use bookmarks | check the sender's email address carefully | look for poor spelling/grammar, generic greetings, urgency | use anti-spam/phishing filters | check for https/padlock before entering details | contact the organisation directly to confirm.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete each sentence using the correct term from this list: smishing, vishing, pharming, shoulder surfing.
(i) A fake text message that tries to get a person to call a number or visit a website is called ……
(ii) Watching a person type their PIN at a cash machine is called ……
(iii) A phone call in which a criminal pretends to be from the bank is called ……
(iv) Malicious code that redirects a user from a genuine website to a fake one is called ……
parts.answer: (i) smishing; (ii) shoulder surfing; (iii) vishing; (iv) pharming.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct term.

stem: Usman's computer has started running slowly, files are disappearing and strange messages appear on screen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a computer virus.
parts.answer: A program that copies (replicates) itself and is designed to cause harm, such as deleting or corrupting files or making the computer malfunction.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: program/software that replicates itself | causes damage – deletes/corrupts data or makes the computer crash/run slowly. Accept: attaches itself to other files.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how anti-virus software helps protect Usman's computer.
parts.answer: It scans files and compares them with a database of known virus signatures; it also looks for suspicious behaviour (heuristics); infected files are quarantined or deleted, and the database must be updated regularly.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: scans files/memory/downloads | compares against a database of known virus signatures | heuristic checking for suspicious behaviour | quarantines or deletes infected files | warns the user | runs in the background / scans automatically | needs regular updates to recognise new viruses.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between phishing and pharming.
parts.answer: Both try to get personal data using a fake website. In phishing the user must open an email and click a link to reach the fake site. In pharming, malicious code installed on the computer (or a corrupted DNS server) redirects the user to the fake site even when they type the correct web address, so the user does not need to click anything.
parts.working: 1 mark for similarity: both aim to obtain personal data via fake websites. 1 mark: phishing relies on the user clicking a link in an email/message. 1 mark: pharming uses malicious code/altered DNS so a correctly typed URL is redirected without user action.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two methods that can be used to prevent pharming.
parts.answer: Use anti-malware software that can detect and remove pharming code; check that the website uses https and look at its certificate/address before entering details.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: up-to-date anti-malware/anti-spyware software | check URL is correct in the address bar | look for https/padlock and check digital certificate | use a trusted DNS service | be suspicious if a familiar site looks different.

stem: A shop owner in Faisalabad finds that customers' card details have been stolen after they used the card reader at the shop counter.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe card cloning and explain how it could have happened at the shop.
parts.answer: Card cloning is copying the data from a card's magnetic stripe to make a fake card. A criminal could have attached a skimmer (a small reading device) to the card reader so that each card's stripe data was read when swiped, and a hidden camera or overlay keypad recorded the PIN.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: copying data from the card's magnetic stripe | to create a duplicate card | a skimmer fitted to/inside the reader | captures data when card is swiped | PIN recorded by hidden camera/fake keypad/shoulder surfing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what is meant by key-logging software and how it could be used to commit card fraud.
parts.answer: Spyware that records every key pressed on a keyboard and sends the log to a criminal; it could capture card numbers, PINs and passwords typed into online shopping or banking sites, which are then used to make purchases.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: a type of spyware | records keystrokes | sends the recorded data to a third party | captures card numbers/PINs/passwords typed by user | criminal uses the stolen details for purchases/withdrawals. Prevention not required.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a firewall protects a computer network.
parts.answer: A firewall sits between the network and the internet and examines all incoming and outgoing traffic. It checks each packet against rules set by the user or administrator and blocks traffic that does not meet them, such as from undesirable websites or unknown IP addresses. It can log attempted attacks and warn the user, and helps stop hackers gaining access.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: between the computer/network and the external network | monitors incoming and outgoing traffic | checks against a set of rules/criteria | blocks traffic that fails the rules | can block specified IP addresses/websites | keeps a log of traffic | warns the user of attempted access | helps prevent hacking/unauthorised access. Can be hardware or software.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two things a firewall cannot prevent.
parts.answer: It cannot stop a user deliberately sharing their password or data (or an employee misusing access); it cannot stop a virus brought in on a USB stick or one that is already on the computer.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: users bypassing it e.g. with their own modem | viruses on removable media | individuals within the network misusing access | social engineering / phishing where user gives away details | attacks via encrypted traffic it cannot inspect.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each type of malware, describe what it does.
(i) Trojan horse
(ii) Ransomware
(iii) Adware
parts.answer: (i) Malicious code disguised as useful or legitimate software, which installs harmful programs (such as spyware) once run. (ii) Encrypts the user's files and demands payment before the decryption key is given. (iii) Displays unwanted advertisements on screen, often by redirecting the browser to advertising sites.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct description.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A worm does not need to attach itself to a file. Explain why worms can spread faster across a network than viruses.
parts.answer: A worm is a stand-alone program that replicates itself and spreads through networks automatically by exploiting security holes, without needing a user to open or run an infected file.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: stand-alone / does not need a host program | spreads by itself through the network / does not need user action.

stem: A user posts to an online forum, but finds that the forum is full of offensive posts and links to dangerous downloads.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the difference between a moderated forum and an unmoderated forum.
parts.answer: In a moderated forum an administrator checks posts and removes those that break the rules before or after they appear; in an unmoderated forum posts are not checked, so anything can be posted.
parts.working: 1 mark each: moderated – posts checked/filtered by an administrator, rule-breaking posts removed, users can be banned | unmoderated – no checks, posts appear without control.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two problems caused by spam and one way to reduce spam.
parts.answer: Spam fills inboxes and wastes users' time and storage; it may contain phishing links or malware. To reduce it, use a spam filter (or never reply to spam / do not publish your email address).
parts.working: 1 mark each for two problems: clogs inbox / wastes time deleting | uses storage/bandwidth | may contain phishing links / malware | replying confirms address is active. 1 mark for one reduction: spam filter | do not reply or click 'unsubscribe' on unknown mail | keep email address private | block senders | untick marketing opt-in boxes.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A company's network administrator reports that someone outside the company gained unauthorised access to the server and changed customer records.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by hacking and give one effect it could have on the company.
parts.answer: Hacking is gaining unauthorised access to a computer system. It can lead to data being deleted, changed or stolen, to identity theft of customers, and to loss of reputation and possible fines for the company.
parts.working: 1 mark for definition (unauthorised access to a computer system). 1 mark for one effect: data deleted/corrupted/changed | data stolen / identity theft | malicious software planted | loss of customer trust/reputation | legal action/fines.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the use of user IDs with passwords, firewalls and two-factor authentication as methods for preventing hacking at this company.
parts.answer: User IDs and passwords are cheap and give each user their own access level, but weak, reused or stolen passwords are easily exploited. Firewalls block traffic from unknown sources and log attempts but cannot stop an attacker using stolen valid credentials. Two-factor authentication means a stolen password alone is not enough, though it adds cost and inconvenience. Conclusion: a combination of all three, with strong password policies, gives much better protection than any single method.
parts.working: Max 4 marks for comments on methods, at least one benefit and one drawback required; 1–2 marks for reasoned conclusion. Passwords: cheap, levels of access | weak/reused/shared/phished. Firewall: blocks unauthorised incoming traffic, logs attempts | does not stop insiders or stolen credentials, needs correct configuration. 2FA: stolen password insufficient | extra device/cost, staff inconvenience, phone lost. Conclusion: layered security / combination best.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A message arrives on Hamza's phone: 'Your parcel could not be delivered. Pay the Rs 150 redelivery fee within 2 hours at this link.' Hamza has not ordered anything. Explain why this message is likely to be smishing and what Hamza should do.
parts.answer: It is unexpected (he ordered nothing), it creates urgency with a 2-hour deadline, and it asks for payment through a link, which would take him to a fake site to steal his card details. He should not click the link or reply, delete or report the message, and if unsure contact the courier using its official number or website.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for reasons: unsolicited/he has no parcel | urgency/deadline pressure | link to unknown site | asks for card/payment details | small fee to make it seem harmless. Up to 2 marks for actions: do not click link | do not reply | delete/block/report as spam | check with company via official channels | install security software on phone.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why criminals ask for a small payment such as Rs 150 rather than a large amount.
parts.answer: A small amount seems believable and not worth worrying about, so more people pay without checking; the real aim is to capture the full card details, which are then used for much larger fraudulent payments.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: small amount lowers suspicion / seems genuine | the goal is the card details / personal data, which are misused for larger amounts.
