stem: An online games company stores the account details of two million players, including email addresses, dates of birth and saved payment cards.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe three different security threats to this data.
parts.answer: Hackers breaking into the servers to steal the database; staff being tricked by phishing emails into revealing administrator passwords; ransomware encrypting the database and demanding payment.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three different threats applied to the company: hacking | phishing/social engineering of staff | malware/spyware | ransomware | pharming of players to fake login pages | key-loggers on players' computers | insider misuse | card fraud with stolen saved cards.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe three measures the company should take to protect the data, explaining how each one helps.
parts.answer: Encrypt the stored data so that if it is stolen it cannot be read without the key; use firewalls and keep server software patched to block unauthorised access; require two-factor authentication for staff logins so stolen passwords are not enough.
parts.working: 1 mark per measure with how it helps, any three: encryption – data unreadable if stolen | firewall – blocks unauthorised traffic | 2FA/strong passwords for staff | access rights – staff see only what they need | anti-malware – detects malicious software | staff training on phishing | regular backups – recover after ransomware | do not store full card numbers / use payment provider.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two signs that an email may be a phishing email.
parts.answer: It starts with a general greeting such as 'Dear customer', and it urges you to act quickly or your account will be closed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: generic greeting | spelling/grammar mistakes | urgent or threatening tone | sender address does not match the organisation | asks for personal details/passwords | link address differs from the displayed text | unexpected attachment | offer too good to be true.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason why a bank will never ask a customer to send their PIN by email.
parts.answer: The bank already holds what it needs to verify the customer; a PIN must stay secret, and email is not secure, so any request for a PIN must be a scam.
parts.working: B1: PIN must be known only to the customer | email is not secure/can be intercepted | banks have other ways of verifying – any such request is fraud.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three examples of personal data.
parts.answer: Name, home address, date of birth.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: name | address | date of birth | phone number | email address | ID card/passport number | bank details | photograph | medical history | school name. Sensitive personal data such as religion or ethnicity also accepted.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a student should not post their home address and school name on a social media profile.
parts.answer: Strangers could use the information to find where the student lives or studies, putting them at risk of being stalked or harmed, and it could be used for identity theft.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: can be located by strangers/predators | risk of physical harm/stalking/grooming | identity theft | information stays online and is hard to remove.

stem: Sana, aged 14, has just joined an online gaming community.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe three precautions Sana should take to stay safe while playing online games.
parts.answer: Use a nickname that does not reveal her real name; never give out personal details such as her address or school; do not agree to meet anyone she has met through the game (and report or block players who are abusive).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: use a username that is not her real name | do not reveal personal information | do not share photos | turn off location settings | do not meet online friends in person | use privacy settings | block and report abusive players | only use voice/video chat with known friends | be wary of links/downloads offered in-game | tell a trusted adult about anything upsetting.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two risks of online gaming, other than strangers finding personal information.
parts.answer: Cyberbullying by other players; downloading malware disguised as game add-ons or cheats.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: cyberbullying | grooming by predators | malware/viruses in downloads/cheats | phishing for game accounts | in-game purchases/financial loss | addiction | violence in games.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe four ways to stay safe when using email.
parts.answer: Only open emails and attachments from known senders; never reply to or forward emails asking for personal details; check the sender's address and do not click on links in suspicious emails; use a spam filter and report phishing emails.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: open emails only from known sources | do not open unknown attachments | do not click links in suspicious emails | never give personal details by email | use spam/junk filters | do not reply to spam | check sender address | use strong password on email account | be wary of emails asking for urgent action | do not forward chain emails.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a user should use bcc rather than cc when sending one email to 50 parents.
parts.answer: With bcc, recipients cannot see each other's email addresses, so the parents' personal data is protected and their addresses cannot be harvested for spam or misused.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: bcc hides recipients' addresses from each other | protects personal data/privacy / prevents addresses being collected for spam / avoids 'reply all' to everyone.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Data protection legislation sets out principles that organisations must follow. Describe three of these principles.
parts.answer: Data must be processed fairly and lawfully; it must be collected for a specified purpose and not used in other ways; it must be accurate and kept up to date.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: processed fairly and lawfully | used only for the purpose it was collected for | adequate, relevant and not excessive | accurate and up to date | not kept longer than necessary | processed in line with the data subject's rights | kept secure | not transferred to countries without adequate protection.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why data protection legislation is needed.
parts.answer: It protects people's personal data from being misused, sold, lost or stolen, and gives people rights to see and correct the data held about them.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: protects individuals from misuse of their data | prevents data being shared/sold without consent | makes organisations keep data secure | gives individuals rights to view/correct data | reduces identity theft risk.

stem: A private clinic in Lahore keeps patients' names, addresses, phone numbers and medical histories on its computer system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the clinic must take extra care with medical histories compared with phone numbers.
parts.answer: Medical history is sensitive personal data; if it is leaked it could lead to discrimination, embarrassment or harm to the patient, so the law requires stronger protection.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: medical history is sensitive personal data | misuse could cause discrimination/embarrassment/harm (e.g. by employers or insurers) | stricter legal requirements.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe three ways the clinic can keep the patient data secure.
parts.answer: Encrypt the data so it cannot be read if stolen; give each staff member a user ID and strong password with access only to the records they need; keep the server in a locked room and make regular backups.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: encryption | user IDs and strong passwords | access levels / permissions | firewall | anti-malware | physical security of the server room | regular backups stored securely | audit logs of who accessed records | staff training | two-factor authentication.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe three ways a person can stay safe when using social networking sites.
parts.answer: Set the profile to private so only friends can see posts; accept friend requests only from people they know in real life; never post personal details such as their address, phone number or holiday plans.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: privacy settings / private profile | only accept friends known in real life | do not post personal information | do not post location/check-ins or holiday plans | think before posting photos | do not meet online friends alone | block and report bullying or abuse | use a strong password | be wary of links in messages.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why posting a photo of yourself in school uniform outside your house is a risk.
parts.answer: The uniform identifies the school and the house shows where you live, so a stranger could work out where to find you; once posted, the photo can be copied and shared beyond your control.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: identifies school and home location | allows strangers to find/track you | photo can be copied/shared and is permanent.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A teenager receives friendly messages from someone who claims to be the same age and asks to keep their chats secret. Explain why this could be dangerous and what the teenager should do.
parts.answer: The person may not be who they claim – this could be grooming by an adult who builds trust and asks for secrecy to stop parents finding out, possibly leading to requests for photos or a meeting. The teenager should not share personal information or photos, should not agree to meet, should keep evidence, block and report the account, and tell a trusted adult.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for dangers: identity cannot be verified / could be an adult pretending | secrecy is a warning sign of grooming | may lead to requests for photos/personal details/meeting. Up to 2 marks for actions: tell a trusted adult | do not share personal data/images | do not meet | block and report | save the messages as evidence.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two reasons why it is hard to remove information once it has been posted online.
parts.answer: Others may have taken screenshots or shared it before it is deleted; copies may be stored on servers, caches or archives that the person cannot control.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: screenshots/copies made by others | shared/reposted on other sites | stored in backups/caches/archives | search engines index it.

stem: A school wants to put photographs of students taking part in sports day on its public website, with each student's full name under the photo.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the eSafety and data protection issues the school should consider before doing this.
parts.answer: Photos with full names are personal data, so the school needs consent from parents (and students) and must use the images only for the stated purpose. Naming students alongside their school lets strangers identify and locate children, creating a risk of grooming. Images on a public site can be copied and misused. Some students may have safeguarding reasons not to be shown. Benefits: celebrating achievement and promoting the school. Conclusion: publish only with written consent, use first names or no names, avoid close-ups, or use a password-protected area.
parts.working: Up to 5 marks for issues/benefits, 1 mark for reasoned conclusion. Points: personal data requires consent | purpose limitation | identifying children + school location = safeguarding risk | images copied/edited/misused | permanent once online | some students must not be identifiable (custody/safeguarding) | right to withdraw consent | benefit – celebrates students, promotes school. Conclusion: consent, no surnames, private area, review regularly.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why it is safer to use a website that the user knows is trustworthy when buying items online.
parts.answer: A trusted website is more likely to protect payment details with encryption and to deliver the goods; unknown sites may be fake and steal card details or take money without sending anything.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: trusted sites secure/encrypt payment data | unknown/fake sites may steal personal or card data | risk of not receiving goods / fraud.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a user should not let the browser save their card details when shopping on a shared computer.
parts.answer: Anyone who uses the computer later could make purchases with the saved card, or malware/other users could read the stored details, so the card could be used fraudulently.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: other users of the shared computer can see/use the saved details | could make purchases without permission | stored details may be stolen by spyware/hackers | user may forget to log out, leaving the account open.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two ways a user can tell that a website is using SSL.
parts.answer: The web address starts with https:// instead of http://; a padlock symbol appears in the browser's address bar.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: https at start of URL | padlock icon | can click padlock to view the digital certificate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what is meant by encryption.
parts.answer: Scrambling data using an encryption key/algorithm so that it is unreadable if intercepted; only someone with the correct key can decrypt it back to its original form.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: data is scrambled/converted into a form that cannot be understood (cipher text) | a key is needed to decrypt / unauthorised people cannot read it. Encryption does not stop data being intercepted.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the steps that take place when a browser connects to a web server that uses SSL.
parts.answer: The browser asks the web server to identify itself; the server sends a copy of its SSL (digital) certificate; the browser checks that the certificate is valid and issued by a trusted authority; if it trusts it, the browser tells the server, and the server acknowledges; an encrypted session then starts and data sent between them is encrypted.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: browser requests server to identify itself | server sends its SSL certificate | browser checks certificate is authentic/trusted/in date | browser sends a message to the server confirming trust | server sends back a digitally signed acknowledgement | encrypted session begins | data exchanged is encrypted with session key.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two items contained in a digital certificate.
parts.answer: The name of the organisation it belongs to, and the expiry date of the certificate.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: organisation/owner name | serial number | expiry date | public key | name of the certificate authority (issuer) | digital signature of the issuer.

stem: A student in Rawalpindi has a laptop with an encrypted hard disk. He also emails coursework to his teacher.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why encrypting the hard disk is useful if the laptop is stolen.
parts.answer: The thief cannot read any files on the disk without the decryption key/password, so personal data remains protected even though the laptop is gone.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: data is scrambled/unreadable | cannot be decrypted without the key/password, so data stays private.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why encryption does not stop an email being intercepted, and why it is still useful.
parts.answer: Encryption does not prevent a hacker copying the data as it travels across the network, but the copied data is meaningless to them without the key.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: data can still be intercepted/copied | but cannot be understood without the decryption key.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two other situations where encryption is used.
parts.answer: Online banking transactions; storing data on a USB memory stick.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: online banking/shopping (https) | encrypting email | encrypting backups/USB drives | cloud storage | Wi-Fi (WPA2/WPA3) | messaging apps (end-to-end).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the purpose of a certificate authority (CA) in the use of digital certificates.
parts.answer: A CA is a trusted organisation that checks the identity of the website owner before issuing a digital certificate and digitally signs it. Browsers trust certificates signed by known CAs, so users can be confident that the website really belongs to the organisation named and is not a fake.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: trusted third party | verifies identity of organisation before issuing | issues and digitally signs certificate | browsers hold list of trusted CAs to check signature | gives users confidence site is authentic | can revoke certificates.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A user sees a browser warning: 'Your connection is not private – the certificate has expired.' Explain what this means and what the user should do.
parts.answer: The website's certificate is no longer valid, so the browser cannot confirm that the website is genuine or that the connection is safe; it may be a fake site or poorly maintained. The user should not enter any personal or payment details and should leave the site (or contact the organisation by another method).
parts.working: 1 mark: certificate out of date/not valid. 1 mark: identity of site/secure connection cannot be guaranteed – possibly fake/pharming. 1 mark: do not enter personal details / leave site / check URL / contact organisation another way.

stem: An online bookshop in Lahore wants customers to trust its website when they pay by card.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how SSL and digital certificates together protect customers when they buy from the bookshop.
parts.answer: The digital certificate, issued by a certificate authority, proves that the website really belongs to the bookshop, so customers know they are not on a fake site. SSL then creates an encrypted link between the browser and the web server, so card numbers and personal details are scrambled while they travel and cannot be read if intercepted. The padlock and https show customers the protection is in use.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: certificate authenticates the website/proves identity | issued/verified by a trusted certificate authority | protects against fake sites | SSL encrypts data between browser and server | card details unreadable if intercepted | https/padlock visible to reassure customers | data integrity – changes in transit detected.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the bookshop still needs other security measures even though it uses SSL.
parts.answer: SSL only protects data while it is being transmitted; once the card data is stored on the bookshop's server it must be protected with firewalls, encryption and access controls, and SSL cannot stop a customer giving details to a phishing site.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: SSL protects data in transit only | stored data on server needs encryption/firewall/access control | does not prevent hacking of the server | does not stop phishing/malware on customer's computer.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each physical safety risk in a computer room, give one way to prevent it.
(i) Electrocution
(ii) Fire from overloaded sockets
(iii) Tripping over trailing cables
parts.answer: (i) Do not bring drinks near computers / check cables for damage. (ii) Do not plug too many devices into one socket. (iii) Use cable ducts or tie cables together and keep them under desks.
parts.working: 1 mark each, any suitable prevention: (i) no drinks/liquids near equipment, check insulation, use RCCB, don't open casings while on | (ii) avoid overloading sockets, ventilate equipment, have CO₂ extinguishers, check wiring | (iii) cable ducts, cable ties, cables under floor/along walls, use wireless.

stem: A small office in Multan has computers on narrow desks, several extension leads plugged into each other and a kettle placed beside a printer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three safety hazards in this office and explain why each is dangerous.
parts.answer: Computers on narrow desks may fall and injure someone; extension leads plugged into each other overload the sockets and can overheat and cause a fire; the kettle could spill water onto the printer, causing electrocution.
parts.working: 1 mark per hazard with reason, any three: heavy equipment on narrow/unstable desk – may fall and injure | daisy-chained extension leads – overload, overheating, fire | kettle/liquids next to equipment – spill, electrocution/short circuit | trailing leads – tripping.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why water extinguishers should not be used on electrical fires, and state a suitable type.
parts.answer: Water conducts electricity, so the user could be electrocuted; a carbon dioxide (CO₂) extinguisher should be used instead.
parts.working: 1 mark: water conducts electricity / risk of electrocution. 1 mark: CO₂ (accept dry powder) extinguisher.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a health risk and a safety risk when using computers. Give one example of each.
parts.answer: A health risk is something that causes illness over time from using computers, such as repetitive strain injury (RSI) from long periods of typing. A safety risk is an immediate danger that could cause an accident or injury, such as electrocution from damaged cables.
parts.working: 1 mark: health risk – harm to the body built up over time from use. 1 mark: example (RSI, back pain, eye strain, headaches). 1 mark: safety risk – accident/immediate danger from the equipment. 1 mark: example (electrocution, fire, tripping, heavy equipment falling).

stem: A school is setting up a new computer room with 32 computers, a projector and two laser printers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe four measures the school should take to reduce physical safety risks in the new room, giving a reason for each.
parts.answer: Use cable ducts or floor channels so cables are not trailing and students cannot trip; provide enough sockets so extension leads are not overloaded, which reduces fire risk; ban food and drink so spills cannot cause electrocution; place the printers and projector on strong, wide tables or fixed mounts so they cannot fall and injure anyone.
parts.working: 1 mark per measure with reason, any four: cable management – tripping | sufficient sockets/no daisy-chaining – overheating/fire | no drinks – electrocution/short circuit | sturdy desks / heavy items at the back – falling equipment | ventilation/air conditioning – overheating | CO₂ extinguishers – electrical fires | regular PAT testing of equipment – faulty wiring | RCCB/circuit breakers – electrocution | clear walkways/fire exits.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why laser printers should be placed away from students' desks.
parts.answer: Laser printers become hot (the fuser) and give off ozone and fine toner particles, which can irritate breathing, so they should be in a well-ventilated area away from where students sit; it also reduces noise.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: hot fuser – burn risk | ozone/toner particle emissions – breathing problems | needs ventilation | heavy – needs a stable base | noise/distraction.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by a flat-file database.
parts.answer: A database that stores all its data in a single table, so data about different things (for example customers and their orders) is held together in one file.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: data held in one table/file | each record holds all the data / no links to other tables (data often repeated).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what is meant by a relational database.
parts.answer: A database made of two or more tables that are linked by relationships using key fields (a primary key in one table matching a foreign key in another).
parts.working: 1 mark each for: data stored in more than one table | tables linked using common/key fields (primary key – foreign key).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two advantages of a relational database over a flat-file database.
parts.answer: Data is stored only once, so there is less duplication (redundancy) and less storage is used; updating data in one place keeps it consistent everywhere, so there are fewer errors.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: less data redundancy/duplication | less storage needed | data consistency/integrity – change once | fewer data entry errors | more complex queries/reports across tables | easier to add new types of data | better security – access to tables can be restricted.

stem: A sports club in Sialkot stores these fields about each member: MemberID, FirstName, DateOfBirth, PhoneNumber, FeesPaid (whether this year's fees are paid), FeeAmount (in rupees, e.g. 3500.00).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the most suitable data type for each field: MemberID (e.g. M0451), DateOfBirth, PhoneNumber (e.g. 03001234567), FeesPaid, FeeAmount.
parts.answer: MemberID – text/alphanumeric; DateOfBirth – date/time; PhoneNumber – text/alphanumeric; FeesPaid – Boolean (logical, Yes/No); FeeAmount – currency (or numeric, 2 decimal places).
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct data type.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why PhoneNumber should not be stored as a numeric field.
parts.answer: A numeric field would remove the leading zero, and phone numbers are never used in calculations (they may also contain + or spaces).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: leading zero would be lost | no calculations are carried out on it | may contain symbols such as + or spaces/dashes | may be longer than some number formats allow.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a primary key.
parts.answer: A field that holds a unique value for every record, so it can be used to identify each record.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: a field (key field) | unique value for each record / identifies each record. Cannot be empty.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A supermarket stores data about products with these fields: ProductName, Barcode, Category, Price, Supplier. Identify the most suitable primary key and explain why ProductName would not be suitable.
parts.answer: Barcode – every product has a different barcode number. ProductName is unsuitable because two products (e.g. different sizes) can share the same name.
parts.working: 1 mark: Barcode. 1 mark: two products (e.g. different sizes/brands) can have the same name, so ProductName is not unique.

stem: A teacher in Karachi keeps records of 400 students' marks in a spreadsheet. The school's IT manager suggests moving the records into a relational database.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare using a database with using a spreadsheet to store and process the student records.
parts.answer: Both store data in rows and columns and can sort and search it. A spreadsheet is better for calculations, what-if modelling and charts, whereas a database is better for storing large amounts of related data. A database can use validation and forms to control data entry more strongly and links several tables (students, subjects, marks) so data is stored once, whereas a spreadsheet often repeats data. A database is better for complex queries and reports and allows multiple users to edit records at the same time, while a spreadsheet is easier to set up and learn.
parts.working: 1 mark for a similarity (both rows/columns, sort, search, filter, charts/reports). Up to 5 marks for linked differences: database handles large volumes of related data vs spreadsheet better for numerical calculation/modelling | database tables linked – less redundancy vs spreadsheet data duplicated | database queries on multiple criteria/reports easier | database forms and validation control input | database supports many simultaneous users/access rights | spreadsheet quicker to set up/easier to learn | spreadsheet better for graphs/what-if. Each difference must refer to both.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A small taxi company in Islamabad stores all its data in one table. Part of the table is shown.
Table BOOKINGS:
BookingID | Date | CustomerName | CustomerPhone | DriverName | DriverPhone
B201 | 03/03/2026 | Faiza Khan | 03215550101 | Imran Ali | 03335550919
B202 | 03/03/2026 | Omar Shah | 03015550244 | Imran Ali | 03335550919
B203 | 04/03/2026 | Faiza Khan | 03215550101 | Nadia Riaz | 03455550377
B204 | 05/03/2026 | Faiza Khan | 03215550110 | Imran Ali | 03335550919

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two examples of data redundancy in this table.
parts.answer: Imran Ali's name and phone number are stored three times; Faiza Khan's name is stored three times (and her phone number twice).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: driver Imran Ali + 03335550919 repeated | customer Faiza Khan repeated | Faiza Khan's phone repeated | date 03/03/2026 repeated (accept).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the problem shown by booking B204.
parts.answer: Faiza Khan's phone number is different from the other two records (03215550110 instead of 03215550101), so the data is inconsistent – it is not clear which number is correct, probably caused by typing the repeated data again.
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies inconsistent phone number for the same customer. 1 mark: caused by re-entering duplicated data / impossible to know which is correct (data integrity problem).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how the data could be stored as a relational database to remove these problems.
parts.answer: Split it into three tables: CUSTOMERS (CustomerID primary key, name, phone), DRIVERS (DriverID primary key, name, phone) and BOOKINGS (BookingID, Date, CustomerID, DriverID). CustomerID and DriverID are foreign keys in BOOKINGS, creating one-to-many relationships, so each customer's and driver's details are stored only once.
parts.working: 1 mark: separate CUSTOMERS and DRIVERS tables (and BOOKINGS). 1 mark: each with its own primary key (CustomerID, DriverID). 1 mark: BOOKINGS holds foreign keys / one-to-many relationships so details stored once.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A hospital database has two tables.
PATIENT (PatientID, Name, DateOfBirth, Ward)
APPOINTMENT (AppointmentID, PatientID, AppointmentDate, Doctor)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the primary key in each table.
parts.answer: PATIENT: PatientID; APPOINTMENT: AppointmentID.
parts.working: 1 mark for each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the foreign key and state which table it is in.
parts.answer: PatientID in the APPOINTMENT table.
parts.working: 1 mark: PatientID. 1 mark: in APPOINTMENT.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the type of relationship between PATIENT and APPOINTMENT and explain why.
parts.answer: One-to-many – one patient can have many appointments, but each appointment belongs to only one patient.
parts.working: 1 mark: one-to-many (PATIENT one side). 1 mark: one patient many appointments, each appointment one patient.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A dental clinic in Hyderabad stores patient details and appointment history on paper record cards kept in filing cabinets. The owner is considering a computerised database.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the use of a computerised database rather than paper record cards for the clinic.
parts.answer: A database lets staff search for a patient instantly, sort and produce reports such as all appointments for tomorrow, uses validation to reduce errors, can be backed up and needs less physical space, and access can be restricted with passwords. However it costs money for hardware, software and training, needs electricity (load-shedding is a problem), data could be hacked or lost if not backed up, and data protection rules apply. Conclusion: the database is better in the long term if backups and security are in place.
parts.working: Max 4 marks for one side; 1–2 marks for reasoned conclusion. Benefits: faster searching | easy sorting/queries/reports | validation reduces errors | backups possible – cards can be lost/destroyed by fire | less storage space | several staff can access at once | easier to update | password-protected. Drawbacks: initial cost of hardware/software | staff training | data entry of existing cards takes time | power cuts/system failure stop access | hacking/malware risk | must comply with data protection.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A school stores data about students and the clubs they join. A student can join many clubs and each club has many students. The designer proposes three tables: STUDENT (StudentID, Name, Class), CLUB (ClubID, ClubName, Teacher) and MEMBERSHIP (StudentID, ClubID, DateJoined).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the MEMBERSHIP table is needed.
parts.answer: The relationship between students and clubs is many-to-many, which cannot be linked directly. MEMBERSHIP holds one record for each student joining each club, linking StudentID and ClubID, so it turns the relationship into two one-to-many relationships (STUDENT to MEMBERSHIP and CLUB to MEMBERSHIP) without repeating student or club details.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: relationship is many-to-many | cannot be stored directly without repeating data | MEMBERSHIP has one record per student per club | contains StudentID and ClubID as foreign keys | creates two one-to-many relationships | stores data about the joining (DateJoined).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why StudentID alone cannot be the primary key of MEMBERSHIP, and suggest a suitable primary key.
parts.answer: A student who joins several clubs appears in several records, so StudentID is not unique; a composite key of StudentID and ClubID together (or a new MembershipID field) is unique.
parts.working: 1 mark: StudentID repeated – not unique. 1 mark: StudentID + ClubID combined (composite key) or a new unique MembershipID.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A data entry form is used to add records to a database. Describe three features of a well-designed data entry form.
parts.answer: Clear labels or instructions next to each box; drop-down lists or option buttons for fields with fixed choices; validation that shows an error message when invalid data is entered.

parts.label: a

stem:

parts.label: a

parts.answer: Error 1: RAM_GB > 8 should be >= 8 – laptops with exactly 8 GB of RAM are wrongly excluded. Error 2: the RAM and InStock criteria are missing from row 2 – every Brand B laptop is selected, even those with less than 8 GB RAM or out of stock.
parts.working: 1 mark for each error identified + 1 mark for each effect: > instead of >= excludes 8 GB laptops | row 2 has only Brand so all Brand B laptops are shown regardless of RAM/stock.

parts.label: b

parts.answer:
Row 1: Brand = "Brand A", RAM_GB >= 8, InStock = Yes
Row 2: Brand = "Brand B", RAM_GB >= 8, InStock = Yes
(or Brand: "Brand A" OR "Brand B" with RAM_GB >= 8 AND InStock = Yes on one row)
parts.working: 1 mark: >= 8 on both rows. 1 mark: InStock = Yes repeated on row 2 / single row with Brand A OR Brand B.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by a corporate house style.
parts.answer: A set of rules an organisation uses for all its documents and media, fixing items such as the logo, fonts, font sizes, colour scheme and layout, so that everything it produces looks the same.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: a standard/consistent style for all documents | set by the organisation | specifies fonts/sizes/colours/logo/layout/spacing | so all documents look the same / are recognisable.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give three items that a corporate house style might specify.
parts.answer: The company logo and its position; the font type and sizes for headings and body text; the colour scheme.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: logo (size/position) | font/typeface | font sizes | colour scheme | margins | line spacing | paragraph spacing | text alignment | header/footer contents | page orientation/size | slogan/strapline.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give three reasons why a company uses a corporate house style.
parts.answer: Documents are consistent, so customers instantly recognise the brand; the company looks professional; staff save time because templates already have the styles set up.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: consistency across all documents | brand identity/recognition | professional image | saves time – templates/styles reused | fewer formatting decisions/errors | easy for new staff to follow | builds customer trust.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the difference between a serif font and a sans-serif font.
parts.answer: A serif font has small extra strokes (serifs) at the ends of the letters; a sans-serif font has no such strokes, giving plain, clean letter ends.
parts.working: 1 mark each: serif has small lines/'feet'/tails on the ends of characters | sans-serif has none.

stem: A chain of pharmacies in Pakistan has 60 branches. Each branch manager currently designs their own posters and leaflets.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the benefits to the chain of introducing a corporate house style for all branch posters and leaflets.
parts.answer: Customers will recognise any branch's material immediately because it looks the same everywhere, which strengthens the brand; it gives a professional, trustworthy image, important for a health business; managers save time by using ready-made templates with the styles built in; and errors such as wrong logos or colours are reduced.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four expanded points: brand recognition across all branches | consistent/professional image builds trust | templates save managers' time | less training needed | fewer mistakes with logo/colours | material from head office and branches matches | easier to update all documents when style changes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two drawbacks of introducing the house style.
parts.answer: It takes time and money to design the style and train all managers to use it; it limits managers' creativity and their ability to adapt posters for local customers.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: cost/time to design and set up templates | staff need training | less creative freedom | may not suit every type of document/local language | existing materials must be redone.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why using paragraph styles is better than formatting each paragraph by hand.
parts.answer: Every paragraph with the same style looks identical, so the document is consistent; if the house style changes, modifying the style updates every paragraph that uses it at once; applying a style in one click is faster than setting font, size, spacing and alignment each time; and heading styles can be used to build an automatic table of contents.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: consistency | changing a style updates all text using it | faster to apply | fewer errors/forgotten settings | can be saved in a template and shared | headings styles allow automatic contents/navigation pane | reduces file editing effort for long documents.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two settings that can be stored in a paragraph style.
parts.answer: Font size and alignment.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: font/typeface | font size | font colour | bold/italic/underline | alignment | line spacing | space before/after | indentation | bullets/numbering.

stem: A university in Islamabad publishes a prospectus, a website and slide presentations. Its house style says: logo top right; headings in a sans-serif font, dark green; body text in a serif font, 11 pt, black; all pages have the university name in the footer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the university can make sure that staff follow the house style in documents, presentations and web pages.
parts.answer: Provide word-processing templates with the paragraph styles and footer already set up; provide a master slide for presentations containing the logo, fonts and colours; use one external stylesheet (CSS) for all web pages so every page uses the same fonts and colours; and train staff and check documents before they are published.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: document templates with styles | locked/predefined styles | master slide for presentations | external CSS stylesheet for all web pages | style guide document | staff training | proofreading/approval before publication | logo provided as a fixed image file in the templates.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether a serif font or a sans-serif font is more suitable for the body text on the university's website.
parts.answer: Sans-serif fonts are usually clearer on screens because the plain letter shapes display well at low resolution, whereas serif fonts are traditionally easier to read in long printed text; so the website may use sans-serif body text even though the printed prospectus uses serif, but this breaks consistency with the house style unless the house style allows it.
parts.working: 1 mark: sans-serif clearer on screen / serif better for long printed text. 1 mark: conclusion weighing readability against consistency with the house style.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A designer says: 'A house style should use no more than two fonts.' Explain why.
parts.answer: Too many fonts make a document look cluttered and unprofessional and harder to read; limiting fonts keeps documents consistent and recognisable.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: many fonts look messy/unprofessional/distracting | two fonts (e.g. one for headings, one for body) give consistency/readability/brand identity.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a house style might specify colours as exact codes (such as #1B5E20) rather than names such as 'dark green'.
parts.answer: 'Dark green' can be interpreted differently by different people and software, giving many slightly different greens; an exact code gives exactly the same colour in every document, slide and web page, protecting brand consistency.
parts.working: 1 mark: names are vague/different shades. 1 mark: code gives an identical colour everywhere / consistency of brand.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two reasons why a corporate logo is usually supplied as a file rather than recreated by staff.
parts.answer: Recreated logos would vary in shape, proportion and colour; supplying a fixed file ensures every document shows the identical, correctly proportioned logo and saves staff time.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: consistency | correct colours/proportions | prevents distortion | saves time | protects trademark/brand.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by each of these text alignments: left aligned, centre aligned, fully justified.
parts.answer: Left aligned: each line starts at the left margin and the right edge is uneven (ragged). Centre aligned: each line is centred between the margins. Fully justified: spacing between words is adjusted so lines are straight at both the left and right margins.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct description.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a newspaper house style uses fully justified text in columns.
parts.answer: Straight edges on both sides make narrow columns look neat and tidy and fit more text.
parts.working: B1: neat/straight edges on both sides / tidy columns / professional appearance.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Tick the TWO statements that are true about corporate house style.
A It is only used for printed documents.
B It helps customers recognise an organisation.
C It means every document must have the same text.
D It can be applied using templates and styles.
E It allows each employee to choose their favourite font.
parts.answer: B and D.
parts.working: 1 mark each for B and D. Deduct for extra ticks (max 2).

stem: You are told to create a new paragraph style called HL-body with these settings: sans-serif font, 11 point, left aligned, single line spacing, 0 pt space before and 6 pt space after.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to create this style in a word processor.
parts.answer: Open the Styles pane and choose New Style; name it HL-body and set the style type to paragraph; choose a sans-serif font and 11 pt; set alignment to left and, in Paragraph settings, line spacing single, spacing before 0 pt and after 6 pt; save the style.
parts.working: 1 mark: create new style and name it exactly HL-body. 1 mark: font sans-serif 11 pt. 1 mark: paragraph settings – left, single, 0 pt before, 6 pt after.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how you would apply the style to all the body text in the document.
parts.answer: Select all the body text paragraphs and click HL-body in the styles list.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the style name must be typed exactly as given, including the capital letters and hyphen.
parts.answer: A style is identified by its name; a name spelt differently (e.g. HL Body or hl-body) is a different style, so the document would not match the house style and others could not find or apply the correct style.
parts.working: B1: styles identified by exact name / different spelling = different style, so house style not followed (accuracy).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A house style for a school magazine is:
- Title: serif font, 28 pt, bold, centre aligned
- Subheading: sans-serif font, 16 pt, italic, left aligned
- Body: serif font, 12 pt, fully justified, 1.15 line spacing

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student's title is in a serif font, 28 pt, bold and left aligned. Identify the error and how to correct it.
parts.answer: The title is left aligned instead of centre aligned; apply/modify the Title style so the alignment is centre.
parts.working: 1 mark: error is alignment. 1 mark: change to centre (via style).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A subheading appears in a serif font, 16 pt, italic, left aligned. Identify the error.
parts.answer: The font should be sans-serif, not serif.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the alignment and line spacing for the body text.
parts.answer: Fully justified; 1.15 line spacing.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A document already uses the style Heading 1 for twelve headings. The house style changes: Heading 1 must now be 20 pt, dark blue, with 18 pt space before and 6 pt space after.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the most efficient way to update all twelve headings.
parts.answer: Modify the Heading 1 style itself (right-click the style → Modify) and change the size, colour and spacing; every heading using Heading 1 updates automatically.
parts.working: 1 mark: modify the style (not each heading). 1 mark: all headings using that style update automatically.

parts.label: b
parts.text: One heading did not change after the style was modified. Suggest a reason and how to fix it.
parts.answer: That heading had manual (direct) formatting applied, or a different style, which overrides the style; select it, clear the direct formatting and reapply Heading 1.
parts.working: 1 mark: direct/manual formatting or wrong style applied. 1 mark: clear formatting and reapply Heading 1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why spacing is set in the style rather than by pressing Enter to add blank lines.
parts.answer: Blank lines are extra empty paragraphs that give inconsistent gaps and can cause blank pages or poor page breaks; style spacing gives exact, consistent gaps that change automatically if the style is changed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: consistent exact spacing | no empty paragraphs/unwanted blank lines or pages | spacing updates when the style changes | easier to edit.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A house style states that the heading style Brand-H1 must have 36 pt space before and 18 pt space after. One point (pt) is 1/72 of an inch, and 1 inch = 2.54 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the space before in centimetres, correct to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the space after in centimetres, correct to 3 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the house style specifies spacing in points rather than as 'one blank line'.
parts.answer: A blank line's height depends on the font size used, so it varies; points are an exact measurement, so every document gets exactly the same spacing.
parts.working: 1 mark each: blank line size varies with font/size | points exact/consistent across documents.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A company's house style for newsletters states: A4 portrait page 21.0 cm wide; left and right margins 2.0 cm each; body text in two equal columns with 1.0 cm spacing between them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the width of each column.
parts.answer: 8.0 cm

parts.label: b
parts.text: The title of the newsletter must stretch across the full page width above the two columns. Describe how this is done.
parts.answer: Keep the title in a single column and insert a continuous section break after it; set the section below the break to two columns, so the title section stays one column wide.
parts.working: 1 mark: continuous section break after the title. 1 mark: two columns applied only to the section after the break.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The left margin is changed to 2.5 cm but the right margin stays at 2.0 cm. Calculate the new column width.

author: HomiLabs

stem: You have been asked to create a style called Note-bullet based on the body text style. It must use the same font and size as the body text, be indented 1 cm from the left margin, and use a square bullet. Each paragraph must be followed by 3 pt space.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what 'based on the body text style' means and one benefit of this.
parts.answer: The new style inherits all the settings of the body text style and only the listed differences are changed; if the body text font or size is later modified, Note-bullet changes automatically too, keeping them consistent.
parts.working: 1 mark: inherits settings from the parent style. 1 mark: changes to the parent automatically carry through.

parts.label: b
parts.text: List the settings that must be changed in Note-bullet.
parts.answer: Left indent 1 cm; square bullet; space after 3 pt.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A table in a report must follow this house style: header row in a sans-serif font, 12 pt, bold, white text on a dark grey background, centre aligned; all other cells in 11 pt, left aligned; all borders visible.

parts.label: a
parts.text: List four formatting changes needed for the header row.
parts.answer: Set the font to sans-serif 12 pt; make it bold; set the text colour to white and the cell shading to dark grey; centre align the text.
parts.working: 1 mark each: sans-serif 12 pt | bold | white text + dark grey shading | centre aligned.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one check to make after formatting the table.
parts.answer: Check that all borders are visible on every cell (and that no text has wrapped awkwardly or been cut off).
parts.working: B1: borders visible | text fits / no unwanted wrapping | body cells 11 pt left aligned | table fits within margins.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Part of a corporate style sheet for a travel company in Lahore is:
TT-Title: sans-serif, 26 pt, bold, centre, 0 pt before, 12 pt after
TT-Sub: sans-serif, 14 pt, bold, italic, left, 12 pt before, 6 pt after
TT-Body: serif, 11 pt, fully justified, 0 pt before, 6 pt after, single spacing
A student's document shows:
Paragraph 1 (TT-Title): sans-serif, 26 pt, bold, centre, 12 pt before, 12 pt after
Paragraph 2 (TT-Sub): sans-serif, 14 pt, bold, left, 12 pt before, 6 pt after
Paragraph 3 (TT-Body): serif, 11 pt, left aligned, 0 pt before, 6 pt after, single spacing

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the three errors in the student's document.
parts.answer: TT-Title has 12 pt space before instead of 0 pt; TT-Sub is not italic; TT-Body is left aligned instead of fully justified.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the student should correct these errors by modifying the styles rather than the individual paragraphs.
parts.answer: Every paragraph that uses the style is then corrected at once, and any paragraphs added later automatically have the correct settings, keeping the whole document consistent.
parts.working: 1 mark each: all paragraphs with that style fixed together | future text consistent / no direct formatting overrides.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A house style requires every document to have: the company name in the header, left aligned; the page number in the footer, right aligned; the file name and path in the footer, left aligned; all in the same font as the body text.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the page number and file name should be inserted as automated fields rather than typed.
parts.answer: Fields update automatically, so each page shows its correct number and the file name/path changes if the document is renamed or moved; typed text would be the same on every page and become wrong.
parts.working: 1 mark each: page numbers change automatically on each page | file name/path updates when the file is saved/moved/renamed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how to place the file name on the left and the page number on the right of the same footer line.
parts.answer: Insert the file name field at the left of the footer, then use the right-aligned tab stop (at the right margin) or press Tab to move to the right and insert the page number field.
parts.working: 1 mark: file name field at left. 1 mark: right tab stop aligned with right margin used for page number.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why the header and footer must align with the page margins.
parts.answer: So that they line up with the body text and look consistent and professional, as the house style requires.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each description, state whether it describes a serif or a sans-serif font.
(i) Letters have plain ends with no small strokes.
(ii) Letters have small tails or feet at the ends of the strokes.
(iii) Often chosen for headings on posters to be read from a distance.
parts.answer: (i) sans-serif; (ii) serif; (iii) sans-serif.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: A presentation for a cricket academy in Karachi must follow the academy's house style: dark blue background, logo in the bottom right corner of every slide, titles in a white sans-serif font, 40 pt, and slide numbers on every slide except the title slide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the logo and colours should be set on the master slide.
parts.answer: Items on the master slide appear on every slide automatically in exactly the same position, so the house style is consistent and the logo does not have to be added and positioned on each slide.
parts.working: 1 mark each: appears on all slides | consistent position/format | saves time | changes in one place update all slides.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how to show slide numbers on every slide except the title slide.
parts.answer: In Header and Footer settings, tick slide number and tick 'Don't show on title slide', then apply to all slides.
parts.working: 1 mark: turn on slide numbers for all slides. 1 mark: option to hide on title slide.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one setting in the house style that would be hard to read if the background were changed to white.
parts.answer: The white title text would be invisible against a white background.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student is told: 'Create a style called Quote-box: serif, 12 pt, italic, centre aligned, 1 cm indent from both left and right margins, a 1 pt black border around the paragraph, 6 pt space before and after. Apply this style to the paragraph beginning "Our mission".'

parts.label: a
parts.text: List the settings that are paragraph settings and those that are font (character) settings.
parts.answer: Font settings: serif, 12 pt, italic. Paragraph settings: centre alignment, 1 cm left and right indents, 1 pt black border, 6 pt space before and after.
parts.working: 2 marks for all font settings correctly listed (1 mark if one wrong/missing); 2 marks for all paragraph settings (1 mark if one wrong/missing).

parts.label: b
parts.text: After applying the style, the border appears around two paragraphs. Explain the likely cause.
parts.answer: The student selected (or placed the cursor across) two paragraphs when applying the style, or the next paragraph's style is also Quote-box because 'style for following paragraph' was set to Quote-box; borders on adjacent paragraphs with identical settings merge into one box.
parts.working: 1 mark: two paragraphs selected / following paragraph also uses the style. 1 mark: identical adjacent bordered paragraphs are joined in one box.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A charity's house style says all bulleted lists must use: round bullet, bullet at 0.6 cm, text indented to 1.2 cm, 3 pt space after each item, and the last item followed by 12 pt space.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the last item is treated differently and how this could be achieved.
parts.answer: Extra space after the last item separates the list from the next paragraph; it can be done by modifying the spacing after for the final item only, or by setting the next paragraph's space before.
parts.working: 1 mark: separates the list from following text. 1 mark: set 12 pt after on the last item (or space before next paragraph).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student changes a numbered list into a bulleted list. State two ways the student can check that the list now matches the house style.
parts.answer: Look at the bullet character and indent markers on the ruler; open the paragraph settings for an item to check the indents and spacing values.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: visual check of bullet shape | ruler indent markers at 0.6/1.2 cm | paragraph dialog values | show formatting/reveal formatting pane | compare with a correct example.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A letter template for an engineering firm in Islamabad must use the house style: logo top left; firm name, address and phone number top right; body text 11 pt sans-serif; margins of 2.5 cm on all sides.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the firm saves the letter as a template.
parts.answer: Each new letter starts with the logo, header details, styles and margins already set, so staff save time and every letter follows the house style; the original template is not overwritten.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: settings already applied | consistency | saves time | original not overwritten / new file created each time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two ways to position the logo top left and the address top right on the same line.
parts.answer: Use a two-column table without borders in the header (logo in left cell, address in right cell, right aligned); or insert the logo with square wrapping at the left and right-align the address text.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: borderless table | text wrapping on the image + right aligned text | right tab stop | text box positioned at right.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A long report (60 pages) for a water research institute uses the styles Report-H1, Report-H2 and Report-body. The director asks for a table of contents and wants all Report-H2 headings to start on a new page.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the heading styles make it possible to create the table of contents automatically.
parts.answer: The table of contents tool finds every paragraph using the heading styles (set as outline levels 1 and 2) and lists them with their page numbers; it can be updated if headings or pages change.
parts.working: 1 mark: TOC built from paragraphs with heading styles/outline levels. 1 mark: page numbers added automatically / can be updated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the most efficient way to make every Report-H2 heading start on a new page.
parts.answer: Modify the Report-H2 style and turn on 'page break before' in its line and page break settings; every Report-H2 heading then moves to the top of a new page.
parts.working: 1 mark: modify the style (not insert breaks manually). 1 mark: page break before option.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two settings in the heading styles that help avoid a heading being left alone at the bottom of a page.
parts.answer: 'Keep with next' so the heading stays on the same page as the following paragraph; 'keep lines together' so a multi-line heading is not split.
parts.working: 1 mark each: keep with next | keep lines together (accept widow/orphan control).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student must apply this house style to the title 'Annual Science Fair 2026': sans-serif, 24 pt, bold, centre aligned, all text in capital letters.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the title exactly as it should appear after formatting.
parts.answer: ANNUAL SCIENCE FAIR 2026
parts.working: B1 exact, including the year and spaces.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage of using the 'All caps' font effect rather than retyping the title in capitals.
parts.answer: The original text and spelling are kept, so there is less risk of typing errors, and if the style changes the text can be shown in normal case without retyping.
parts.working: 1 mark: no retyping so no new errors. 1 mark: effect can be removed/changed in the style.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A company's corporate colours are dark red (red 139, green 0, blue 0) and gold (red 255, green 204, blue 0). Its house style also requires all body text to be dark grey (red 64, green 64, blue 64).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Convert each colour to a six-digit hexadecimal colour code.
parts.answer: Dark red #8B0000; gold #FFCC00; dark grey #404040.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why dark grey body text on a white page is still readable.
parts.answer: There is a strong contrast between the dark grey text and the white background.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A document contains two styles: Body-text (serif, 11 pt) and Caption (sans-serif, 9 pt, italic). The house style says every image must have a caption directly below it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a student should add a caption under an image so it follows the house style.
parts.answer: Type the caption text in a new paragraph directly below the image and apply the Caption style to it.
parts.working: 1 mark: caption placed directly below the image. 1 mark: Caption style applied.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two features of the Caption style that make it different from Body-text.
parts.answer: It is sans-serif rather than serif, and it is 9 pt italic rather than 11 pt.
parts.working: 1 mark each: font type | size/italic.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a leaflet for a bakery in Hyderabad, the house style says the phrase 'freshly baked every morning' must be bold and italic wherever it appears in the body text, and the rest of the body text must have no enhancement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the two text enhancements required for the phrase.
parts.answer: Bold; italic.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student makes the whole paragraph containing the phrase bold and italic. Explain why this does not follow the house style.
parts.answer: Only the phrase itself should be enhanced; the rest of the body text must be plain, so the paragraph is now inconsistent with the other body text.
parts.working: 1 mark: enhancement applied to too much text. 1 mark: rest of body text must have no enhancement / inconsistent.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A 40-page annual report for a textile company in Faisalabad mentions the company name 'Indus Weave' 85 times. The new house style says the company name must always appear in bold, dark green, small capitals, but the surrounding text must keep its own paragraph style.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a character style is more suitable than a paragraph style for this requirement.
parts.answer: A character style applies only to the selected words, so the paragraph keeps its own style (spacing, alignment, font for other text); a paragraph style would change the whole paragraph.
parts.working: 1 mark: character style affects only selected text. 1 mark: paragraph style would reformat the entire paragraph.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe an efficient way to apply the style to all 85 occurrences.
parts.answer: Create a character style (e.g. Company-name) and use Find and Replace: find 'Indus Weave', replace with the same text but with the Company-name style as replacement formatting, then Replace All.
parts.working: 1 mark: Find and Replace (Replace All). 1 mark: replacement formatting set to the character style.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one risk of using Replace All and how to reduce it.
parts.answer: It may change text that should not be changed, for example the name inside a quotation or a web address; review the changes afterwards (or use Find Next and replace one at a time / match case).
parts.working: 1 mark: unintended replacements. 1 mark: proofread / match case / whole words / check each one.

author: HomiLabs

stem: An international aid organisation has offices in Pakistan, Jordan and Kenya. Documents are written in English, Urdu and Arabic. Head office wants one corporate house style for all offices.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the issues the organisation should consider when designing a single house style for all three offices.
parts.answer: The chosen fonts must support Urdu and Arabic script as well as English, so a font family with matching scripts is needed; Urdu and Arabic are written right to left, so alignment, page layout and logo position rules must work in mirrored form; font sizes may need adjusting because some scripts appear smaller at the same point size; colours and images must be culturally acceptable in each country; templates and styles must be shared with every office and staff trained. Benefits: a consistent, recognisable brand worldwide. Conclusion: one house style with language-specific variations defined in it.
parts.working: Up to 5 marks for issues/benefits, 1 mark for reasoned conclusion. Points: fonts must support all scripts | right-to-left text affects alignment/layout/indents | logo placement in mirrored layouts | relative font sizes differ between scripts | cultural meaning of colours/images | templates must be distributed and kept up to date | training and checking in each office | benefit – global brand consistency.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A house style for exam revision booklets states: 'No widows or orphans; no blank pages; each section heading must be on the same page as the paragraph that follows it.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a widow and an orphan in a document.
parts.answer: A widow is the last line of a paragraph that appears on its own at the top of a new page (or column); an orphan is the first line of a paragraph left on its own at the bottom of a page (or column).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how paragraph style settings can be used to meet all three parts of this house style rule.
parts.answer: Turn on widow/orphan control in the body text style so single lines are never left alone; turn on 'keep with next' in the heading styles so each heading moves to the page of the next paragraph; use page breaks only where required (or page break before in a style) and remove empty paragraphs so no blank pages are created.
parts.working: 1 mark: widow/orphan control. 1 mark: keep with next on headings. 1 mark: remove extra blank paragraphs/unneeded page breaks to avoid blank pages.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how a student could check the whole booklet for these errors before printing.
parts.answer: Use print preview (multi-page view) and look at the top and bottom of every page.
parts.working: B1: print preview / proofread each page / show formatting marks to find empty paragraphs.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the three layers used in web development.
parts.answer: Content layer, presentation layer, behaviour layer.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which layer each of these belongs to: (i) a CSS file that sets the font colour of headings; (ii) a script that checks a form has been filled in before it is sent; (iii) the HTML table that holds the page text.
parts.answer: (i) presentation; (ii) behaviour; (iii) content.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the purpose of the head section and the body section of a web page.
parts.answer: The head contains information about the page that is not displayed in the page itself, such as the title, metatags and links to stylesheets; the body contains the content shown in the browser window, such as text, images, tables and links.
parts.working: 1 mark: head – page information/metadata/title/stylesheet links not displayed in the page. 1 mark: body – the visible content.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two items that are placed in the head section.
parts.answer: The page title; the link to an external stylesheet.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: title | meta tags (charset, keywords, description, author, viewport) | link to external CSS | internal <style> | base target | scripts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the purpose of each of these metatags: (i) description (ii) keywords (iii) author (iv) viewport.
parts.answer: (i) Gives a short summary of the page, which search engines may display in their results. (ii) Lists words that describe the page so search engines can match it to searches. (iii) Gives the name of the person who created the page. (iv) Tells the browser how to scale and size the page to fit the width of the device, so it displays correctly on phones and tablets.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct purpose.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the purpose of the meta tag <meta charset="UTF-8">.
parts.answer: It tells the browser which character set to use so that text, including special characters, is displayed correctly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the presentation layer should be kept separate from the content layer by using an external stylesheet.
parts.answer: One stylesheet can be attached to every page, so all pages look consistent; changing one rule in the stylesheet updates every page at once; the HTML files are smaller and easier to read and edit because they contain only content; and different stylesheets can be used for different devices or for printing without changing the content.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: consistency across pages/house style | change once – updates all pages | saves time when restyling | HTML simpler/shorter/easier to maintain | faster loading – CSS cached once | different styles for different devices/print | developers and designers can work separately.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the <link> to an external stylesheet is placed in the head section.
parts.answer: The link is information about the page rather than content to display, so it belongs in the head; the head is read before the body is shown, so the styles are ready and the page is displayed correctly formatted from the start.
parts.working: B1: head holds information about the page/resources, not displayed content | loaded before the body so styles are applied when the page is shown.

stem: A web page contains the hyperlink Sports news.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what happens when a user clicks the words Sports news.
parts.answer: The browser opens the page sports.html from the news folder on www.example.org, and it opens in a new window or tab because of target="_blank".
parts.working: 1 mark: opens the sports.html page at that address. 1 mark: in a new tab/window.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference between an absolute file path and a relative file path, and why relative paths are used for files within the same website.
parts.answer: An absolute path gives the full location from the root (e.g. a full URL or a drive letter on the developer's computer); a relative path gives the location relative to the current page (e.g. images/logo.png). Relative paths keep working when the whole website is uploaded to a server or moved to another folder, whereas absolute local paths (such as C:\Users\...) would break.
parts.working: 1 mark: absolute – full path from root/drive/URL. 1 mark: relative – from the location of the current file. 1 mark: relative paths still work when the site is moved/uploaded; absolute local paths break.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A web page has an external stylesheet that sets h1 { color: #000080; }, an internal style in the head that sets h1 { color: #008000; } (placed after the link to the external stylesheet), and one heading written as

Results

. State the colour in which the heading Results is displayed and explain why.
parts.answer: #800000 (maroon / dark red). Inline styles take priority over both internal and external styles, so the inline colour is used even though the internal style would normally override the external one.
parts.working: 1 mark: #800000. 1 mark: inline style has highest priority. 1 mark: internal (later) style would override external for other h1 headings.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the colour of a second h1 heading on the page that has no inline style, and explain why.
parts.answer: #008000 (green) – the internal style is read after the external stylesheet, so it overrides the external rule.
parts.working: 1 mark: #008000. 1 mark: later/internal rule overrides the external stylesheet.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the purpose of a bookmark (anchor) on a web page and describe how to create a link to one.
parts.answer:
A bookmark marks a particular position on a page so that a link can take the user straight to it, e.g. to a section further down a long page. Give the target element an id, e.g.

Fees

, and create a link with a hash before the id: Go to fees.
parts.working: 1 mark: purpose – jump to a specific point on a (long) page. 1 mark: set an id on the target element. 1 mark: link uses href="#id".

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a web developer should give every image an alt attribute.
parts.answer: The alt text is displayed if the image cannot load and is read aloud by screen readers for visually impaired users; it also helps search engines understand the image.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: shown if image fails to load | accessibility – screen readers | search engines index it | describes the image's purpose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what each of these HTML elements is used for: <tr>, <td>, <th>.
parts.answer: <tr> defines a table row; <td> defines a table data cell; <th> defines a table header cell (bold and centred by default).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the attribute colspan="2" does to a table cell.
parts.answer: It makes the cell stretch across (merge) two columns.

stem: A student describes the behaviour layer as 'the layer that makes the website look nice'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the student is wrong and describe what the behaviour layer does.
parts.answer: Making the page look nice is the job of the presentation layer (CSS). The behaviour layer uses a scripting language (such as JavaScript) to make the page interactive – for example responding to button clicks, validating form entries or showing and hiding content.
parts.working: 1 mark: appearance is the presentation layer / CSS. 1 mark: behaviour layer uses scripts/scripting language. 1 mark: example of interactivity (validation, pop-ups, menus, responding to events).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one reason why behaviour scripts are often kept in separate files.
parts.answer: The same script file can be used by many pages and changed in one place, keeping the HTML content simple.
parts.working: B1: reuse across pages | easier maintenance | content layer kept clean | cached by browser.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare a CSS class with an inline style for formatting part of a web page.
parts.answer: Both change the appearance of elements. A class is defined once in a stylesheet (e.g. .warning { color: #FF0000; }) and can be applied to many elements with class="warning", so changing the class definition updates all of them; an inline style is written inside one element's tag with the style attribute and affects only that element. Inline styles override class rules, but they mix presentation with content and are harder to maintain.
parts.working: 1 mark for a similarity (both apply formatting/CSS properties). Up to 3 for differences: class defined once and reused vs inline applies to one element | class in stylesheet vs style attribute in tag | changing class updates all vs edit each inline style | inline has higher priority | class keeps content and presentation separate.

stem: Before printing a 12-page charity report, a student is told to check the layout of the whole document.

parts.label: a
parts.text: List four layout problems the student should look for and correct.
parts.answer: Any four: widows or orphans; blank pages; a table split across two pages; a heading at the bottom of a page separated from its text; inconsistent spacing between paragraphs; images overlapping text or margins; text running beyond the margins; inconsistent fonts/styles.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A college in Peshawar prints its 40-page prospectus double-sided and binds it along the left edge of odd pages and the right edge of even pages.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what a gutter margin is and why one is needed here.
parts.answer: A gutter margin is extra margin space added on the binding edge; it stops text being hidden or hard to read where the pages are bound.
parts.working: B1 extra space on binding side. B1 text not lost in binding.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the page setting that makes the inside and outside margins swap on facing pages.
parts.answer: Mirror margins (book fold / facing pages).
parts.working: B1 mirror margins.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The page is 21.0 cm wide, the inside margin is 2.0 cm, the outside margin is 1.5 cm and the gutter is 1.0 cm. Calculate the width available for text.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the difference between a page break and a column break.
parts.answer: A page break forces the text after it to start on the next page; a column break forces the text after it to start at the top of the next column (on the same page if there is one).
parts.working: B1 page break → next page. B1 column break → next column.

stem: A table in a document lists eight cricket grounds in Pakistan with three columns: Ground, City, Capacity. The first row holds the column headings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to make the heading row stand out and repeat at the top of each page if the table splits.
parts.answer: Format the first row (e.g. bold and shaded/coloured background), and set it as a header row that repeats on each page.
parts.working: B1 format heading row – bold/shading/centre. B1 'repeat as header row' setting.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the alignment that should be used for the Capacity column and give a reason.
