parts.answer: Right aligned, so that units, tens and thousands line up and numbers are easy to compare.
parts.working: B1 right (accept decimal). B1 digits line up.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A new ground must be added between rows 4 and 5. State how this is done.
parts.answer: Place the cursor in row 4 and insert a row below (or in row 5 and insert a row above).
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

stem: A school timetable is laid out in a table with days in the first column and periods 1 to 7 across the top. On Friday, periods 6 and 7 are combined for Jumu'ah prayers and a sports session.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to make one cell span periods 6 and 7 for Friday.
parts.answer: Select the two Friday cells for periods 6 and 7, then use 'merge cells' so they become one cell.
parts.working: B1 select both cells. B1 merge.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the table gridlines should be shown (borders applied) when this timetable is printed.
parts.answer: So that the rows and columns are clearly separated on paper (gridlines that are not borders do not print).
parts.working: B1 easier to read / gridlines alone may not print.

author: HomiLabs

stem: One point (pt) is 1/72 of an inch, and one inch is 2.54 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the height in millimetres represented by a 36 pt heading. Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A sign must be readable from a distance and the letters need to be at least 2.5 cm high. Calculate the smallest whole number of points that gives at least 2.5 cm.
parts.answer: 71 pt

author: HomiLabs

stem: A task says: enter the title Clean Water For Thar exactly as shown, in a 24 point bold font, centre aligned.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three different formatting settings named in the task.
parts.answer: Font size 24 point; bold (font style); centre alignment.
parts.working: 1 mark each: 24 pt size; bold; centred.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the title must be typed exactly as shown.
parts.answer: The capital letters, spelling and spaces must match the original so the text is accurate (any error means the text is wrong).
parts.working: B1 accuracy – capitals/spaces/spelling must match.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A teacher asks students to hand in draft essays with double line spacing and wide margins.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why double line spacing and wide margins are useful on a draft.
parts.answer: They leave space between lines and at the edges for the teacher to write corrections and comments; the text is also easier to read and edit.
parts.working: B1 space for annotations/corrections. B1 easier to read/proofread.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a long science report, a subheading 'Results of the pH tests' appears as the last line of page 5, and the table that belongs to it starts on page 6.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why this is a layout error.
parts.answer: The subheading is separated from the content it introduces, so the reader sees a heading with nothing under it.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two different ways of correcting it.
parts.answer: Apply 'keep with next' to the subheading so it always stays on the same page as the following paragraph/table; or insert a page break before the subheading so it moves to page 6.
parts.working: 1 mark each: keep with next; page break before heading; (accept adjusting spacing only if it moves the heading to page 6).

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a fully justified paragraph, the measurement '25 kg' is split so that '25' ends one line and 'kg' starts the next.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to stop the number and its unit being split across lines.
parts.answer: Replace the ordinary space with a non-breaking space between 25 and kg.
parts.working: B1 non-breaking space.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why fully justified text sometimes shows large gaps between words, and state one way to reduce them.
parts.answer: Extra space is added between words so each line reaches both margins; with long words or narrow columns the gaps become large. Reduce by using automatic hyphenation (or left alignment / a wider column).
parts.working: B1 explanation of spacing to fill line. B1 hyphenation / left align / wider column.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A house style states: heading – 16 pt with 12 pt space before and 6 pt space after; body text – 11 pt with 0 pt before and 6 pt after.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A heading is followed directly by a body paragraph. State the space, in points, between the bottom of the heading and the top of the body text, assuming the larger of the two settings applies.
parts.answer: 6 pt (heading space after is 6 pt, body space before is 0 pt).
parts.working: B1 6 pt.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A body paragraph is followed by a heading. Calculate the total space between them if both settings are added together.
parts.answer: 18 pt

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two ways of enhancing text in a heading, other than changing the font size.
parts.answer: Any two: bold; italic; underline; change font colour; change font face; highlight/shading; all capitals.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: A poster designed on A4 paper (21.0 cm × 29.7 cm) is to be printed on A3 paper (29.7 cm × 42.0 cm) without changing its layout.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the scale factor applied to each side, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A heading was 40 pt on the A4 version. Calculate its new size, to the nearest whole point.
parts.answer: 57 pt

author: HomiLabs

stem: A small business in Sialkot that exports sports goods types every invoice and letter from a blank page, changing the margins, fonts and alignment each time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the use of a document template with preset page and text formatting for this business.
parts.answer: Benefits: consistent appearance on every document; saves time because margins, fonts, logo, alignment are already set; fewer formatting errors; staff need less training; professional image with overseas customers. Drawbacks: time and skill needed to design the template at first; may not suit every document type so several templates may be needed; staff may forget to use it or use an old version; changes to house style mean templates must be updated. Conclusion: benefits usually outweigh costs for a business producing many similar documents.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for benefits, up to 4 for drawbacks, max 5 if no reasoned conclusion. 1 mark per valid expanded point, total 6.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between the internet and the World Wide Web.
parts.answer: The internet is the worldwide network of interconnected computer networks (the hardware and connections); the World Wide Web is a collection of web pages/websites that are accessed using the internet.
parts.working: B1 internet = global network of networks / infrastructure. B1 WWW = web pages/sites (resources) accessed via the internet using HTTP/browser.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines
stem:
A passenger types this address into a web browser:
https://www.railbook.com.pk/timetables/karachi-lahore.html

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the protocol.
parts.answer: https
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the domain name.
parts.answer: www.railbook.com.pk (accept railbook.com.pk)
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify the folder (path) name.
parts.answer: timetables
parts.working: B1

parts.label: d
parts.text: Identify the file name.
parts.answer: karachi-lahore.html
parts.working: B1 must include .html

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines
stem:
A student finds information at:
http://climate.uni-example.ac.uk/research/glaciers/hunza.htm

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what the 'ac.uk' part tells the student about the website.
parts.answer: ac shows it belongs to an academic/educational institution (e.g. a university); uk is the country code for the United Kingdom.
parts.working: B1 academic/educational organisation. B1 country code – UK.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The website does not use https. Explain why this matters if the site had a login form.
parts.answer: Without https the data is sent unencrypted, so a username and password could be intercepted and read by someone else on the network.
parts.working: B1 http not encrypted / no SSL/TLS. B1 login details could be intercepted/read.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two ways a user can tell that a website uses a secure connection.
parts.answer: The URL begins with https (rather than http); a padlock symbol appears in the address bar (clicking it shows a valid digital certificate).
parts.working: 1 mark each: https; padlock icon; valid certificate details.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a hyperlink.
parts.answer: Text or an image on a web page that, when clicked, takes the user to another web page, another part of the same page, or opens a file/email.
parts.working: B1 clickable text/image. B1 moves to another page/location/file.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give three features of a web browser that help a user to find pages again or move between pages.
parts.answer: Any three: bookmarks/favourites; history; back and forward buttons; tabs; address bar; home page button; hyperlinks; search within the address bar.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines
stem: A student in Hyderabad wants information about mangrove forests in the Indus Delta but not about mangroves in other countries. A search for the single word mangroves returned millions of results.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe three ways the student could refine the search to get more useful results.
parts.answer: Any three: add more specific keywords such as 'Indus Delta' and 'Pakistan'; put an exact phrase in quotation marks, e.g. "Indus Delta mangroves"; use operators such as AND / + to require words and − (minus/NOT) to exclude words; use advanced search filters such as date, region, file type or domain (e.g. .edu.pk).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three described methods.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines
stem: Many students use the internet rather than school library books for their projects.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain three ways a student could judge whether a website is reliable.
parts.answer: Any three: check who the author/organisation is and their expertise; check the date it was last updated; look at the domain type (e.g. .gov or .edu is more likely reliable); cross-check the facts with other sources; look for references/citations; check for poor spelling and grammar or heavy advertising; check whether it is biased/selling something.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three explained.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using the internet rather than printed books to find information for a geography project.
parts.answer: Advantages: information is often more up to date; huge amount available; quick to search with keywords; available at any time from home; multimedia such as videos and maps; usually free. Disadvantages: information may be unreliable or biased because anyone can publish; too many results to sort through; may find irrelevant pages; distractions; needs a device and internet connection; risk of plagiarism or copyright issues; books are often checked/edited before publishing.
parts.working: Max 4 for advantages only or disadvantages only. 1 mark per valid point; 6th mark for a reasoned conclusion.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a search engine finds and ranks the web pages it shows in its results.
parts.answer: Web crawlers (spiders/bots) automatically visit pages and follow links; the content and keywords of each page are stored in an index; when a user enters a search the engine looks up matching pages in its index rather than the live web; results are ranked by an algorithm using factors such as relevance of keywords, number and quality of links to the page, how recent it is and location/popularity.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: crawler/spider; follows links; index built; search looks up index; ranking algorithm; ranking factors.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a web browser and a search engine.
parts.answer: A web browser is software installed on the device used to display web pages from a URL; a search engine is a website/service used inside the browser to find web pages that match keywords.
parts.working: B1 browser = software that displays/retrieves web pages. B1 search engine = finds pages from keywords.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by an Internet Service Provider (ISP).
parts.answer: A company that provides users with access to the internet (usually for a monthly fee).
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two services, other than internet access, that an ISP may provide.
parts.answer: Any two: email accounts; web hosting; security/filtering such as parental controls or firewalls; online storage; technical support; IP address allocation.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the differences between a blog and a wiki.
parts.answer: A blog is usually written by one person (or a small group) and only they can edit it; entries appear in reverse date order; readers can usually only comment. A wiki can be edited by many users, who can add, change and delete content; it is organised by topic pages, not date; it keeps a history of edits.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three linked differences (authorship, who can edit, organisation by date vs topic, comments vs editing, edit history).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines
stem: An online forum helps parents in Karachi share advice about schools.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a moderated and an unmoderated forum.
parts.answer: In a moderated forum posts are checked by a moderator (before or after posting) and unsuitable posts are removed; in an unmoderated forum posts appear without any checking.
parts.working: B1 moderated – checked/administrator removes inappropriate posts. B1 unmoderated – no checking.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the forum owners choose to make it moderated.
parts.answer: To remove offensive, abusive, false or spam posts and keep users (and children's information) safe.
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines
stem: A web page for a science fair contains a link to the website https://www.examplemuseum.org/space.html

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the HTML to show the text 'Space gallery' as a hyperlink to this page so that it opens in a new browser window or tab.
parts.answer: Space gallery
parts.working: B1 with correct URL. B1 target="_blank". B1 text Space gallery and closing .

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why an absolute URL is used here rather than a relative one.
parts.answer: The page is on a different website, so the full address (protocol and domain) is needed; a relative path only works for files on the same site.
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether the internet should be policed.
parts.answer: For policing: helps stop illegal material and criminal activity (e.g. fraud, terrorism); protects children from unsuitable content; reduces false information and cyberbullying; protects copyright. Against: material is already illegal under existing laws; difficult and expensive to enforce worldwide because no single body owns the internet; limits freedom of speech/information; may be used by governments for censorship; people can bypass controls. A reasoned conclusion.
parts.working: 1 mark per valid point; max 4 if only one side; 6th mark only with a conclusion.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines
stem:
A school website stores its pages in this folder structure on the web server:
/index.html
/events/sports.html
/events/images/trophy.jpg

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the relative URL that sports.html should use to link back to index.html.
parts.answer: ../index.html
parts.working: B1 ../index.html

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the relative path that sports.html should use for the image trophy.jpg.
parts.answer: images/trophy.jpg
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one advantage of using relative rather than absolute URLs for links within the same website.
parts.answer: The links still work if the whole website is moved to a different domain or server (or tested locally), because they do not contain the domain name.
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between cc and bcc when sending an email.
parts.answer: Recipients in cc (carbon copy) receive a copy and their addresses are visible to all other recipients; recipients in bcc (blind carbon copy) receive a copy but their addresses are hidden from the other recipients.
parts.working: B1 cc – copy sent, address visible. B1 bcc – copy sent, address hidden.

stem: A school in Quetta sends a weekly email newsletter to the parents of 600 students.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the school should put the parents' addresses in the bcc field.
parts.answer: So parents cannot see each other's email addresses, which protects their personal data/privacy and stops addresses being misused for spam or 'reply all'.
parts.working: B1 addresses hidden / privacy / data protection. B1 avoids misuse e.g. spam or reply-all chains.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how an email group (contact list) would help the school.
parts.answer: All 600 addresses are saved under one group name, so the newsletter is sent by typing just the group name; this saves time and avoids missing anyone or typing addresses wrongly.
parts.working: B1 one name for many addresses. B1 saves time / fewer errors / nobody missed.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by spam.
parts.answer: Unsolicited (unwanted) emails sent to many people at once, often advertising.
parts.working: B1 unsolicited/junk bulk email.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give three ways of reducing the amount of spam received.
parts.answer: Any three: use a spam filter; do not reply to spam or click 'unsubscribe' on suspicious messages; do not publish your email address on websites/forums; untick boxes that allow companies to share your address; use a separate address for online sign-ups; block the sender.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe four rules of netiquette that should be followed when writing emails.
parts.answer: Any four: do not use capital letters for whole sentences (seen as shouting); do not use abusive or offensive language; check spelling and grammar; use a clear subject line; keep messages short and relevant; respect privacy – do not forward others' messages without permission; do not send spam or chain emails; be careful with humour/sarcasm which can be misunderstood.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four.

stem: Ayesha wants to email holiday photos to her cousin in Toronto. The photos are 4.2 MB, 3.8 MB, 6.5 MB, 7.9 MB and 5.1 MB. Her email service allows attachments of up to 25 MB in total per message.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total size of the photos and state whether they can all be sent in one email.
parts.answer: 27.5 MB; no – this is more than the 25 MB limit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two ways Ayesha could still send all the photos.
parts.answer: Any two: compress the files (zip or reduce image resolution/quality); split them over two emails; upload them to cloud storage and email a link instead.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A trading company in Faisalabad currently posts letters to its suppliers in China and Turkey.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the use of email instead of posted letters for this company.
parts.answer: Benefits: arrives almost instantly regardless of distance; cheaper (no postage); can attach documents and send to many suppliers at once; replies are faster; copies are stored and searchable. Drawbacks: needs devices and internet connection; risk of viruses/phishing in attachments; emails can be intercepted or sent to the wrong person; some formal documents may still need signed paper copies; may be filtered as spam and not read; information overload. Conclusion weighing these.
parts.working: 1 mark per point; max 4 if only one side; 6th mark for reasoned conclusion.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between 'reply', 'reply all' and 'forward'.
parts.answer: Reply sends a response only to the sender; reply all sends the response to the sender and everyone else who received the original (in To and cc); forward sends the original message (with attachments) to a new recipient chosen by the user.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe three features of an email that suggest it is spam or a scam.
parts.answer: Any three: sent from an unknown or odd-looking address; generic greeting such as 'Dear customer'; spelling and grammar mistakes; urgent requests or threats; offers that seem too good to be true (prizes, lottery wins); asks for personal or bank details; suspicious links whose address does not match the company; unexpected attachments.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: A web page for a charity book sale in Lahore must contain a hyperlink that opens the visitor's email software with the address sales@bookdrive.org and the subject Book donation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the HTML for this hyperlink, using the text Email us.
parts.answer: Email us
parts.working: B1 mailto: with correct address. B1 ?subject=Book donation (accept the space typed directly or as %20). B1 correct … with text Email us.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A software company in Islamabad gives employees a policy about how they must use company email.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain three things that such an email policy is likely to include and why each is needed.
parts.answer: Any three, each with a reason: only use email for work purposes – to reduce wasted time and system load; no offensive or discriminatory language – the company could be sued and its reputation harmed; do not send confidential data unencrypted or to outsiders – data protection laws; do not open unknown attachments – to prevent malware; emails may be monitored/stored – legal requirement and security; follow copyright law when attaching material; use a standard signature/house style – professional image.
parts.working: For each of three points: 1 mark for the rule, 1 mark for the reason (max 6).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Hamza's email address is hamza.r@unimail.edu.pk

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the user name (local part) and the domain name in this address.
parts.answer: User name: hamza.r; domain name: unimail.edu.pk
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the symbol that separates them and what it means.
parts.answer: @ – 'at', separating the user from the mail server/domain.
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a spam filter may sometimes put a genuine email in the junk folder, and what the user should do about it.
parts.answer: The filter uses rules (e.g. certain words, many recipients, unknown sender, links or attachments) and may wrongly match a genuine email – a false positive; the user should regularly check the junk folder and mark genuine emails as 'not spam' / add the sender to a safe senders list so the filter learns.
parts.working: B1 filter uses keywords/rules/sender reputation. B1 genuine mail matches these rules (false positive). B1 check junk folder / mark not spam / safe sender list.

stem: A hospital in Rawalpindi needs to send a patient's test results to a specialist at another hospital.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the precautions staff should take if these results are sent by email.
parts.answer: Any four: encrypt the email or the attachment / send through a secure email system; check the recipient's address carefully before sending (avoid autocomplete errors); password-protect the attachment and send the password by another method; include only the data that is needed; use a professional, clear subject line without personal details; follow data protection law and hospital policy; confirm receipt.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two advantages and one disadvantage of sending an attachment rather than pasting the text into the body of an email.
parts.answer: Advantages (any two): keeps the original formatting/layout; recipient can save, edit and print the file; non-text files such as images or spreadsheets can be sent; large documents keep the email body short. Disadvantage (any one): attachments may carry viruses; size limits; recipient needs suitable software to open the file; may be blocked by filters.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two advantages and one disadvantage.

stem: Bilal works in a call centre in Lahore, typing customer details for eight hours a day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two health problems Bilal could develop from this work.
parts.answer: Any two: repetitive strain injury (RSI) in the wrists/fingers; back and/or neck problems; eyestrain; headaches.
parts.working: 1 mark each. Do not accept 'pain' without location.

parts.label: b
parts.text: For one of the problems named, describe one way of reducing the risk.
parts.answer: e.g. RSI – use a wrist rest / ergonomic keyboard and take regular breaks; back pain – use an adjustable chair with back support and sit upright; eyestrain – take regular breaks and use an anti-glare screen.
parts.working: B1 prevention matched to the named problem.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by repetitive strain injury (RSI).
parts.answer: Damage/pain to the muscles, tendons or nerves of the fingers, hands, wrists or arms caused by repeating the same movements many times.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two causes of RSI when using a computer.
parts.answer: Any two: continuous typing on a keyboard; repeated clicking/using a mouse; poor wrist position; not taking breaks; repeated texting on a phone.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each of the following health problems, give one cause when using a computer.
Problem 1: eyestrain
Problem 2: neck pain
Problem 3: headache
parts.answer: Eyestrain – staring at a screen for a long time / screen glare or flicker / poor lighting. Neck pain – screen at the wrong height so the head is tilted for long periods. Headache – glare or flickering screen / poor lighting / looking at screen too long without breaks.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: A school in Karachi has opened a new computer room for students.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe four features of the room or its furniture that would help to reduce health problems.
parts.answer: Any four: adjustable chairs with back support; desks at the correct height; monitors that can be tilted/raised so the top of the screen is at eye level; anti-glare screens or blinds to reduce glare; good lighting; footrests; wrist rests / ergonomic keyboards and mice; enough space to move.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A graphic designer uses a computer for long periods each day. An eye specialist advises the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet (about 6 metres) away for 20 seconds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many of these short breaks the designer should take in a 7.5-hour working day.
parts.working: M1 7.5 × 60 ÷ 20 = 22.5. A1 22 complete 20-minute periods.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the rule helps prevent eyestrain.
parts.answer: Looking into the distance lets the eye muscles relax after focusing on a close screen for a long time.
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why sitting with poor posture at a computer can cause back problems.
parts.answer: Slouching or leaning forward for long periods puts strain on the muscles and spine of the back; without support the spine is not kept in its natural position, leading to pain.
parts.working: B1 poor posture / no back support for long periods. B1 strain on spine/back muscles.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two ways of preventing back problems.
parts.answer: Any two: use an adjustable chair with lumbar support; sit upright with feet flat on the floor or on a footrest; take regular breaks to stand and stretch; have the screen at eye level so you do not lean forward.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: Sana's monitor faces a large window and the afternoon sun shines on the screen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how this could affect Sana's health.
parts.answer: Glare/reflections on the screen make it hard to see, so she strains her eyes and may squint, causing eyestrain and headaches.
parts.working: B1 glare/reflection. B1 eyestrain or headache.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways of solving the problem.
parts.answer: Any two: move/turn the monitor so it is not facing the window (at right angles to it); fit blinds/curtains; use an anti-glare screen filter; adjust the screen brightness.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A data-entry company in Faisalabad has received complaints from employees about wrist pain, back pain and headaches.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the actions the company could take to reduce these health problems, including any drawbacks.
parts.answer: Actions: buy ergonomic keyboards, mice and wrist rests (reduces RSI); provide adjustable chairs and monitor stands (reduces back/neck pain); fit anti-glare screens and blinds, improve lighting (reduces headaches); schedule regular breaks and vary tasks; give training on correct posture; offer eye tests. Drawbacks: cost of new equipment; breaks reduce working time/output; staff may not follow advice; some solutions take time to show results. Conclusion: health measures reduce sick leave so are worthwhile.
parts.working: 1 mark per valid point; max 5 without drawbacks or conclusion.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why taking regular breaks from a computer helps to prevent health problems. Refer to two different problems.
parts.answer: Breaks rest the hands and wrists from repeated movements, reducing RSI; they also let the eyes rest from focusing on the screen, reducing eyestrain (and moving/stretching reduces back pain).
parts.working: 1 mark each for two problems linked to reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the causes and prevention of RSI and eyestrain.
parts.answer: Both are caused by using a computer for long periods without breaks, and both are reduced by taking regular breaks. RSI is caused by repeated hand/finger movements on keyboard and mouse, whereas eyestrain is caused by staring at a screen, glare or flicker. RSI is prevented with wrist rests and ergonomic keyboards/mice, whereas eyestrain is prevented with anti-glare screens, correct lighting and regular eye tests.
parts.working: 1 mark for a similarity; up to 3 for linked differences (causes/prevention). Must compare, not list separately.

stem: A teenager in Islamabad plays online games on a laptop on his bed for several hours each night.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three health problems that could result and give a cause of each in this scenario.
parts.answer: Back/neck pain – sitting hunched on the bed with no back support and the screen too low; RSI – repeated use of keys/mouse/controller; eyestrain/headaches – looking at the screen for hours, often in a dark room.
parts.working: 1 mark per problem with scenario-based cause.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student says, 'A laptop is better for your health than a desktop computer.' Evaluate this statement.
parts.answer: Points against: laptop screen is attached to the keyboard so the screen is usually below eye level, causing neck strain; small keyboard and touchpad can increase RSI; often used on laps or sofas with poor posture. Points for: the user can move it to a better-lit place; can be used standing; easier to take breaks and move. A laptop can be made healthier with an external keyboard, mouse and stand. Conclusion: neither is automatically healthier; it depends on how it is set up and used.
parts.working: 1 mark per valid point on either side; max 4 if one-sided; 6th mark for a reasoned conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two items of equipment that reduce the risk of RSI.
parts.answer: Any two: wrist rest; ergonomic keyboard; ergonomic/vertical mouse; voice-recognition software; adjustable desk/chair (so arms are at the correct height).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: An office manager measures one employee's set-up: the top of the screen is 15 cm above her eye level and the screen is 30 cm from her face.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two problems with this set-up and how each should be changed.
parts.answer: Screen too high makes her tilt her head back, causing neck pain – lower it so the top of the screen is at or slightly below eye level. Screen too close (30 cm) makes the eyes work harder, causing eyestrain – move it back to about arm's length (roughly 50–70 cm).
parts.working: For each problem: 1 mark for the effect, 1 mark for the correction.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A hospital is introducing tablet computers so that nurses record patient observations at the bedside instead of on paper.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two health risks to the nurses from using tablets in this way, and suggest a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Any two: neck strain from looking down at the tablet for long periods – hold it at eye level / use a stand on the trolley; RSI from repeated tapping/typing on a small screen – use voice input or a stylus and take breaks; eyestrain from small text – increase font size and screen brightness to suit lighting.
parts.working: For each risk: 1 mark risk with cause, 1 mark precaution.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name three microprocessor-controlled devices commonly found in the home.
parts.answer: Any three: washing machine; microwave oven; smart fridge; central heating/air-conditioning controller; burglar alarm; smart TV; dishwasher; robotic vacuum cleaner; bread maker; smart lighting.
parts.working: 1 mark each. Do not accept brand names.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two positive effects of microprocessor-controlled household devices on people's lifestyles.
parts.answer: Any two: they save time because people do not have to carry out manual tasks (e.g. washing), giving more leisure time; devices can be set to run while people are out; they can be controlled remotely (e.g. switching on air-conditioning before arriving home); energy savings when devices switch off automatically; improved home security.
parts.working: 1 mark each, described.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two negative effects.
parts.answer: Any two: people may become lazy and less physically active; people lose household skills; smart devices connected to the internet can be hacked, risking data and security; dependence on technology when devices fail; cost to buy and repair; people may socialise less.
parts.working: 1 mark each, described.

stem: Many new cars sold in Pakistan have microprocessor-controlled features such as parking sensors, anti-lock brakes and cruise control.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two advantages to drivers of microprocessor-controlled features in cars.
parts.answer: Any two: safer driving because sensors react faster than humans (e.g. anti-lock brakes stop skidding); parking sensors warn of obstacles, reducing accidents; cruise control keeps a steady speed, reducing fatigue and saving fuel; satnav reduces getting lost; better fuel efficiency.
parts.working: 1 mark each, explained.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two disadvantages.
parts.answer: Any two: drivers may rely on the systems and become less alert or lose driving skills; systems can fail or give false readings; more expensive to buy and repair; connected systems could be hacked; drivers may be overconfident.
parts.working: 1 mark each, explained.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a microprocessor-controlled washing machine increases the leisure time of the user.
parts.answer: The user selects a programme and the microprocessor controls filling, heating, washing, rinsing and spinning automatically, so the user does not need to stay with it and can do other things.
parts.working: B1 automatic control of the cycle. B1 user free to do other activities.

stem: A family in Islamabad installs smart devices (lights, door lock, cameras, thermostat) that can be controlled from a smartphone app over the internet.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the effects of these devices on the family's security and privacy.
parts.answer: Positive: can check cameras and lock the door remotely; alerts sent to phone if someone enters; lights can be switched on while away so the house looks occupied; logs show who came and went. Negative: devices can be hacked so criminals could unlock doors or watch camera feeds; personal data (when the family is home) collected by companies may be shared or leaked; weak default passwords; loss of internet or power may stop devices working. Measures: strong passwords, updates, two-factor authentication. Conclusion.
parts.working: 1 mark per valid point; max 4 if one-sided; 6th mark for reasoned conclusion.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how microprocessor-controlled devices can affect a person's physical fitness and social interaction.
parts.answer: Fitness: devices do manual work (e.g. robotic vacuum, remote controls) so people are less active, which can lead to an unhealthy lifestyle; but saved time may be used for exercise, and fitness trackers can encourage activity. Social: people may spend more time on smart TVs/gaming devices and less time with others; but devices such as smartphones/video calls help people keep in touch with distant family.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for fitness, up to 2 for social interaction; balanced points credited.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Some smart fridges can monitor the food inside and order more automatically. Evaluate the use of such a fridge for a busy family.
parts.answer: Benefits: saves time shopping; food is less likely to run out; can warn of expiry dates, reducing waste; can suggest meals. Drawbacks: expensive to buy and repair; may order items not wanted or at higher prices; needs internet and stored payment details, so security risk; privacy – data about eating habits collected; family loses the habit of planning meals. Conclusion.
parts.working: 1 mark per valid point; max 4 if one-sided; 6th mark for conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two microprocessor-controlled devices found in a car, other than the engine management system.
parts.answer: Any two: anti-lock braking system; airbags; parking sensors; cruise control; satellite navigation; climate control; lane-departure warning; automatic windscreen wipers.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: A microprocessor-controlled air-conditioner in a flat in Multan keeps the room at 24 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the microprocessor keeps the room at the required temperature.
parts.answer: A temperature sensor sends readings (converted by an ADC) to the microprocessor; the microprocessor compares each reading with the preset 24 °C; if it is higher it switches the cooling on (via an actuator/DAC), if lower it switches it off; this repeats continuously.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: sensor reading; ADC; compares with preset; switches cooler on/off via actuator; continuous loop.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the energy use of a home may go down when microprocessor-controlled devices are used, but the overall cost to the household may still rise.
parts.answer: Devices switch off automatically or run at efficient times (e.g. lights turning off in empty rooms, heating only when needed), reducing energy use; however the devices are expensive to buy, may need replacing or repairing by specialists, and many draw standby power or need internet subscriptions, so overall costs may increase.
parts.working: B1 automatic/efficient control saves energy. B1 high purchase/repair cost. B1 standby power or subscription/replacement cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two types of job that have been lost because of the introduction of IT.
parts.answer: Any two: manufacturing/production-line workers (replaced by robots); typing pool / secretarial staff; bank clerks/cashiers; car-park attendants; shop checkout staff; printing and typesetting workers; telephone operators.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two types of job that have been created by IT.
parts.answer: Any two: programmers/software developers; network managers/technicians; website designers; maintenance engineers for robots/computers; IT trainers; data analysts; cybersecurity specialists.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the working patterns of part-time working, flexible hours (flexi-time) and job sharing.
parts.answer: Part-time – working fewer hours per week than a full-time employee; flexible hours – working the full number of hours but choosing start and finish times (often around a core time); job sharing – two people share the hours and duties of one full-time job.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: A car factory near Karachi replaces many of its paint-shop workers with robots.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two effects of this on the workers who remain at the factory.
parts.answer: Any two, explained: they need retraining to operate/maintain robots, gaining new skills; work becomes less dangerous as robots do the hazardous painting (fumes); jobs may become more boring/supervisory; fear of further job losses; some may move to new higher-skilled, better-paid roles; may work different shift patterns as robots run continuously.
parts.working: For each effect: 1 mark identification, 1 mark explanation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A bank in Pakistan is closing several branches because more customers now use online and mobile banking.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the effects of this change on the bank's employees.
parts.answer: Negative: loss of jobs for cashiers and counter staff; staff may have to move/travel to other branches; need to learn new skills; job insecurity and stress. Positive: new jobs in call centres, IT support, cybersecurity and app development; chance of retraining to better-paid roles; possible flexible/home working for some staff; less handling of cash so safer. Conclusion weighing effects.
parts.working: 1 mark per valid point; max 4 if one-sided; 6th mark for reasoned conclusion.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how IT has made compressed hours and working from home possible for many office workers, and give one drawback for the employer.
parts.answer: Compressed hours: the full weekly hours are worked in fewer days, possible because systems are available all day and work is tracked electronically. Working from home: laptops, internet access, cloud storage, VPNs, email and video-conferencing allow staff to access files and communicate as if in the office. Drawback for employer (any one): harder to supervise staff / monitor productivity; data security risks on home networks; cost of equipment; team communication may suffer.
parts.working: B1 compressed hours described. B1 IT link. B1 home working technologies. B1 drawback.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a header and a footer in a document.
parts.answer: A header is an area in the top margin of each page; a footer is an area in the bottom margin; text or fields placed in them appear automatically on every page (of the section).
parts.working: B1 header top margin / footer bottom margin. B1 repeated on every page.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two items commonly placed in a footer.
parts.answer: Any two: page number; total number of pages; file name/path; date; author's name; copyright notice; company contact details.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why automated fields, rather than typed text, should be used for the page number and date in a header.
parts.answer: Automated fields update automatically – page numbers change when pages are added or removed and the date updates each time the document is opened/printed – so they are always correct without the user retyping them.
parts.working: B1 updates automatically. B1 example: page numbering after edits / current date when printed.

stem:
You are working on a report for a solar-panel company in Lahore. The page is A4 portrait with 2 cm margins. The instructions say:
• in the header: your name left aligned, and an automated date right aligned
• in the footer: an automated file name centred, and an automated page number right aligned
• no other text in the header or footer

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the steps to place the automated date at the right of the header.
parts.answer: Open/edit the header, move to the right-hand position (right tab stop at the right margin or right-align), then insert a date field set to update automatically.
parts.working: B1 open header and right align / right tab at margin. B1 insert date field (update automatically).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the right-aligned items must line up with the right margin of the page.
parts.answer: The house style requires header/footer items to align with the margins of the body text; if the tab stop is beyond or short of the margin, it will not match the text and will look unprofessional/be marked wrong.
parts.working: B1 consistent alignment with body margins.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the type of field that should be used to show the file name in the footer.
parts.answer: An automated file name field (inserted from the field list, not typed).
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

stem: A document's header has a centre tab and a right tab. The page is A4 portrait (21.0 cm wide). The margins are changed to 2.5 cm on the left and 2.5 cm on the right.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate where, measured from the left margin, the right tab stop must be placed so that the right-aligned item lines up with the right margin.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate where the centre tab stop must be placed, measured from the left margin.
parts.answer: 8.0 cm

author: HomiLabs

stem: A report is changed to A4 landscape (29.7 cm wide) with a left margin of 2.0 cm and a right margin of 1.5 cm. The header's tab stops were set for portrait pages at 8.75 cm (centre) and 17.5 cm (right), which matched the portrait text width with the same margins.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the new positions, measured from the left margin, for the centre and right tab stops.
parts.answer: Centre 13.1 cm; right 26.2 cm.
parts.working: M1 text width 29.7 − 2.0 − 1.5 = 26.2 cm. A1 centre 13.1 cm, right 26.2 cm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what will appear wrong in the header if the tab stops are not changed.
parts.answer: The 'right-aligned' item would end at 17.5 cm, well short of the right margin, and the centred item would not be in the centre of the page.
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

stem: A school annual report has a cover page followed by 18 pages of content. The cover must not show a header, footer or page number.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the header and footer setting that removes them from the cover only.
parts.answer: Different first page.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: The first content page must show page number 1. Describe how this is achieved.
parts.answer: Format the page numbers to start at 0 for the cover (so the next page is 1), or put a next-page section break after the cover and set page numbering in the new section to start at 1.
parts.working: B1 page number format / start at. B1 correct start value (0 on cover, or 1 in new section after break).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A project file has 26 pages. Pages 1 and 2 are the title page and contents page and must not be numbered. Page numbering starts at 1 on page 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the page number printed on the last page.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The footer shows 'Page X of Y', where Y is the total number of numbered pages. Write the footer that appears on the 10th physical page.
parts.answer: Page 8 of 24

author: HomiLabs

stem: The footer of a 23-page leaflet uses automated fields to show 'Page X of Y'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what the footer shows on the seventh page.
parts.answer: Page 7 of 23
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Two extra pages are added in the middle of the leaflet. State what the footer now shows on the last page.
parts.answer: Page 25 of 25
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

stem: A novel by a writer in Karachi is printed double-sided as a book. The book title must appear at the top left of even-numbered (left-hand) pages, and the chapter title at the top right of odd-numbered (right-hand) pages. Page numbers appear on the outside edge of each page.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the header setting needed so that odd and even pages can have different headers.
parts.answer: Different odd and even pages.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where the page number should be aligned on odd pages and on even pages.
parts.answer: Odd (right-hand) pages: right aligned. Even (left-hand) pages: left aligned.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why each chapter must be in a separate section for the chapter title to change.
parts.answer: Header content is the same throughout a section; a section break at each chapter allows a different header, once it is unlinked from the previous section ('link to previous' turned off).
parts.working: B1 headers apply per section. B1 unlink from previous / new section per chapter.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A spreadsheet records rainfall for ten cities in Pakistan. Before printing, you are told to place your name, centre number and candidate number in the header, and an automated file path in the footer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the automated file path is useful on the printout.
parts.answer: It shows exactly where the file is saved (drive, folders and file name), so it can be found again.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two other automated fields that can be inserted into a spreadsheet header or footer.
parts.answer: Any two: page number; number of pages; date; time; file name; sheet (tab) name.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A database report lists all students in a school sports club, grouped by house. You must add a report title, page numbers, the house name before each group, and a count of all students at the end of the report.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State the section of the report in which each item should be placed:
(i) the report title shown once at the start
(ii) the page numbers
(iii) the total count shown once at the end
parts.answer: (i) report header; (ii) page footer (or page header); (iii) report footer.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference between the report header and the page header.
parts.answer: The report header appears once at the start of the report (first page only); the page header appears at the top of every page.
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

stem: A presentation about water conservation for a Year 8 class has 15 slides. Slide numbers and the presenter's name must appear in the footer of every slide except the title slide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the footer items should be set on the master slide.
parts.answer: Items placed on the master slide appear on every slide automatically in the same position and style, so they are consistent and only need to be added once (and changed once).
parts.working: B1 appears on all slides. B1 consistent / saves time / one change updates all.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the setting that stops the footer showing on the title slide.
parts.answer: Don't show on title slide.
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

stem: A letter has a top margin of 3.0 cm. The header starts 1.25 cm from the top edge of the page. The header contains a logo.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the greatest height the logo can have without pushing into the body text area.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The original logo is 6.0 cm wide and 2.4 cm high. Calculate the largest width it can have, with its aspect ratio maintained, so that it fits this height. Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two reasons why an office might require the file name to appear in the footer of every printed document.
parts.answer: Any two: so the electronic copy can be found quickly; to identify which version of the document was printed; helps if pages from different documents get mixed up; consistency with house style.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: A clinic in Quetta wants a letter template. The clinic's name and logo must be at the top of every page, and the address, phone number and website at the bottom of every page.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the clinic should use a header and footer for these items rather than typing them at the top and bottom of the body text.
parts.answer: Header/footer content repeats automatically on every page and stays in the same place even when the body text is edited or extends to more pages; text typed in the body would move with the text and only appear on the first page.
parts.working: B1 repeats on every page. B1 does not move when body text changes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one setting that keeps the contact details on the first page only, if the clinic decides later pages need only a page number.
parts.answer: Different first page (with the contact details in the first-page footer and a page number in the other pages' footer).
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a header and a heading.
parts.answer: A header is text placed in the top margin that repeats on every page; a heading is a title within the body text that introduces a section and appears only once where it is typed.
parts.working: B1 header – top margin, every page. B1 heading – in the body, introduces a section, appears once.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a footnote and a footer.
parts.answer: A footnote gives extra information or a reference linked to a numbered mark in the text and appears at the bottom of the page where the mark is; a footer holds the same items (e.g. page number) on every page.
parts.working: B1 footnote linked to a reference mark/specific text. B1 footer repeated on every page.

stem: A legal contract was signed on 3 March. The contract document has a date field in the header that updates automatically. It is reprinted on 10 June.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the date shown in the header of the reprinted copy and explain why this is a problem.
parts.answer: 10 June – the automatic field shows the current date, so the header no longer shows the date of signing and could cause confusion about when the contract was agreed.
parts.working: B1 10 June. B1 problem explained.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the header should have been set up.
parts.answer: Insert the date as fixed text / a date field set not to update automatically (or type the signing date).
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

stem: A university thesis has 6 introductory pages (title, declaration, acknowledgements, abstract, contents and list of tables) before Chapter 1. The introductory pages must be numbered i, ii, iii …, and Chapter 1 must start at page 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to set up the page numbering.
parts.answer: Insert a next-page section break before Chapter 1; in the first section set the page number format to lower-case Roman numerals (i, ii, iii); in the second section unlink the footer from the previous section, choose Arabic numerals (1, 2, 3) and set numbering to start at 1.
parts.working: B1 section break. B1 Roman numeral format in section 1. B1 Arabic format starting at 1 in section 2 (unlinked).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the page number printed on the abstract, which is the fourth introductory page.
parts.answer: iv
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

stem: A portrait report contains one landscape page holding a wide table of exam statistics. After changing that page to landscape, the student notices that the right-aligned page number in the footer of the landscape page is now in the middle of the page.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why this has happened.
parts.answer: The footer's right tab stop is still at the position set for the narrower portrait page, so on the wider landscape page it is no longer at the right margin.
parts.working: B1 tab/alignment set for portrait width. B1 landscape text width is greater.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how to correct it without affecting the portrait pages.
parts.answer: In the landscape section, unlink the footer from the previous section and move the right tab stop to the new right margin (or use right alignment).
parts.working: B1 unlink from previous section. B1 move tab to new right margin.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A spreadsheet of monthly sales for a shoe shop in Sialkot must be printed showing the formulas, on a single landscape page, with your name in the header and the page number in the footer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: List three print/page settings that must be made, apart from the header and footer.
parts.answer: Any three: show formulas (formula view); landscape orientation; fit to one page wide/one page; show row and column headings; gridlines if required; columns widened so formulas are fully visible.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the column widths should be checked before printing the formulas.
parts.answer: Formulas are often longer than their values, so narrow columns would cut them off and they could not be read in full.
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

stem: Five students in a group each write a chapter of a project about Pakistan's renewable energy. The chapters will be combined into one file.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two problems that could occur in the headers and footers when the chapters are combined, and how they can be avoided.
parts.answer: Any two: different fonts/sizes/alignment in each student's header – agree a template/house style for headers and footers; typed page numbers restart or are wrong – use automated page number fields after combining; different information in each header – decide content beforehand; section breaks carried in may stop headers continuing – check 'link to previous'.
parts.working: For each: 1 mark problem, 1 mark solution.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State where the words 'Private and Confidential' should be placed so that they appear on every page.
parts.answer: In the header.
parts.working: B1 header (not typed at the top of the body text).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why these words should be typed as ordinary text rather than inserted as an automated field.
parts.answer: The words never change, so they are fixed text; automated fields are only needed for information that changes, such as the date or page number.
parts.working: B1 text is fixed/does not change; fields are for changing data (date, page number, file name).

author: HomiLabs
stem: A three-page letter from a law firm in Karachi must show the words 'Private and Confidential' at the top of every page.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two reasons why the text in headers and footers is usually smaller and less prominent than the body text.
parts.answer: Any two: it is supporting information, not the main content; so it does not distract the reader from the body text; it must fit in the margin area; consistent professional appearance / house style.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: After finishing a document, a student checks the header and footer before printing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three things the student should check.
parts.answer: Any three: all required items are present (e.g. name, date, page number); items are in the correct position/alignment and line up with the margins; fields are automated, not typed; spelling of typed text is correct; they appear on every page required (or not on the first page if set); no extra text has been added.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A database report lists 48 orders for a bakery in Hyderabad, sorted by delivery date, with a calculated Total column for each order. The report runs over 3 pages.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The manager wants the overall sum of all order totals shown once at the end. State where this calculation should be placed.
parts.answer: In the report footer.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what would happen if the sum calculation were placed in the page footer instead.
parts.answer: It would be printed at the bottom of every page, and depending on the software it may show only that page's total or repeat the overall total, so the report would be confusing/incorrect.
parts.working: B1 appears on every page. B1 gives page/partial totals or repeated values – not a single overall total.

parts.label: c
parts.text: On average, how many orders appear on each page if the orders are split as evenly as possible?

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A user types '1' at the bottom of page 1, '2' at the bottom of page 2 and so on in a 10-page document instead of using a page number field. Describe two problems this may cause.
parts.answer: Any two: if text is added or deleted, the numbers move to the wrong position on the page (into the middle of a page); numbers will be wrong if pages are added/removed and must be retyped; takes much longer; inconsistent position/format.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: A 40-page guide to the Karakoram Highway has five chapters. Each page header must show the name of the chapter it is in.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the type of break that must be inserted at the start of each new chapter (chapters 2 to 5).
parts.answer: A section break (next page).
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Chapter 1 starts on page 1. State how many of these breaks are needed and how many sections the document then has.
parts.answer: 4 section breaks; 5 sections.
parts.working: One break before each of chapters 2–5 = 4 breaks; sections = breaks + 1 = 5. B1 both.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe what must be done in the header of chapters 2 to 5 before typing the new chapter name.
parts.answer: Turn off 'link to previous' so the header is not the same as the previous section's.
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

stem: An examination board requires candidates to put their name, centre number and candidate number in the header of every printed page of practical work.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the details are required on every page rather than only on the first page.
parts.answer: Pages can become separated or mixed with other candidates' work; having the details on each page means every page can be identified and returned to the right candidate.
parts.working: B1 pages may be separated. B1 each page identifiable.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why using the header is better than typing these details at the top of the body text on each page.
parts.answer: The header repeats automatically on every page and stays in place if the body text is edited; typing on each page is slow and the text would move as content changes.
parts.working: B1 automatic repetition. B1 fixed position / saves time.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A workbook for a cricket academy in Rawalpindi has three sheets named Batting, Bowling and Fielding. Each sheet is printed on two pages. The footer must show the sheet name on the left and 'Page X of Y' on the right, where Y counts the pages of that sheet only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the sheet name should be an automated field rather than typed text.
parts.answer: If a sheet is renamed, or the header/footer is copied to other sheets, the field shows the correct name automatically.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the footer text printed on the second page of the Bowling sheet.
parts.answer: Bowling (left) and Page 2 of 2 (right).
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: If all three sheets were instead printed as one job with continuous page numbering, state the footer on the second page of the Bowling sheet.
parts.answer: Bowling (left) and Page 4 of 6 (right).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by software copyright.
parts.answer: The legal right of the creator/owner of software to control how it is copied, used, changed and distributed.
parts.working: B1 legal protection/ownership – others need permission to copy or distribute.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two actions that would break software copyright.
parts.answer: Any two: making copies of the software and giving or selling them to others; installing it on more computers than the licence allows; using parts of the code in your own program without permission; renting or lending it out without permission; removing or bypassing the copy protection / using a cracked key; modifying it and distributing it without permission.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by software piracy.
parts.answer: Illegally copying, distributing or using software without a valid licence / the copyright owner's permission.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two reasons why software piracy is harmful to software companies.
parts.answer: Any two: loss of sales income; less money to invest in developing new software and updates; jobs may be lost; harm to reputation if pirated copies contain malware or faults.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe three methods used by software producers to prevent their software being copied illegally.
parts.answer: Any three: a unique product/licence key must be entered during installation; online activation links the key to one device so it cannot be reused elsewhere; the user must accept a licence agreement before installing; holograms on packaging show it is genuine; a dongle (hardware key) must be plugged in for the software to run; the original disc/memory stick must be present to run it; the program code is encrypted and needs a key to run.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three described.

stem: A college in Peshawar has 120 computers. A design program is installed on all of them, but timetabling means that at most 30 students ever use the program at the same time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a concurrent-user licence.
parts.answer: A licence that allows a set maximum number of people to use the software at the same time, regardless of how many computers it is installed on.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of concurrent-user licences the college needs and explain why this may be cheaper than licensing every computer.
parts.answer: 30 licences; the college pays for 30 simultaneous users instead of 120 individual installations.
parts.working: B1 30. B1 fewer licences than computers.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A school in Lahore needs a mathematics program on 40 computers. Single-user licences cost Rs 4,500 each. A site licence for the whole school costs Rs 150,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost of buying single-user licences for all 40 computers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how much the school saves by buying the site licence.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one other advantage of a site licence for the school.
parts.answer: More computers can be added later without buying extra licences (within the site); easier to manage one licence.
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

stem: An architect's office in Islamabad can buy design software for a one-off payment of Rs 60,000 per user, or pay a subscription of Rs 1,500 per user per month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of months after which the total subscription cost equals the one-off payment.
parts.answer: 40 months

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of the subscription for the office, apart from cost.
parts.answer: Advantage: updates/new versions and support are included; can easily reduce the number of users. Disadvantage: the software stops working if payments stop; often needs internet to check the licence; price may rise.
parts.working: B1 advantage. B1 disadvantage.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A software audit at a logistics company in Karachi finds the accounts program installed on 75 computers, but the company owns only 60 licences. Each extra licence costs Rs 8,200.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost of buying enough licences so that all installations are legal.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one other way the company could become legal.
parts.answer: Uninstall the program from the 15 unlicensed computers.
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a product key on its own may not stop software piracy, and how online activation improves protection.
parts.answer: A product key can be copied and shared with others, so many people could install the software with the same key; it may also be generated by key-generating programs. Online activation sends the key (and details of the device) to the producer's server, which checks it has not already been used on more devices than allowed and ties it to that hardware, so a shared key will be rejected.
parts.working: B1 key can be shared. B1 or generated / no check of number of uses. B1 activation checks key with server. B1 linked to hardware/limits number of installs.

stem: Zain bought a licensed copy of a video-editing program. His friend asks Zain to install it on the friend's laptop as well.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why Zain should not do this.
parts.answer: The licence usually allows use on one computer only, so installing it on another person's laptop is illegal copying/breaks copyright; the producer loses the income from a sale.
parts.working: B1 licence limits installations/is for Zain only. B1 breaks copyright law / illegal / unfair to producer.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the differences between freeware, shareware and free (open source) software.
parts.answer: Freeware is free to use but is still protected by copyright, the source code is not available and users may not modify it. Shareware is free to try for a limited time or with limited features, after which the user must pay to continue. Free/open-source software is supplied with its source code, which users may study, modify and redistribute, subject to the conditions of its licence.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: A student in Multan downloads a 'cracked' copy of an expensive photo-editing program from a file-sharing site, saying that the company is rich and will not miss the money.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the legal, ethical and practical issues of the student's action.
parts.answer: Legal: it breaks copyright law and the licence terms; the student could be fined or face legal action. Ethical: it is unfair to the developers who are not paid for their work; it is effectively theft; argument that the company is rich does not make it right. Practical: cracked copies often contain viruses/spyware that can steal data; no updates or technical support; may stop working; a free alternative or student discount could be used instead. Conclusion.
parts.working: 1 mark per valid point; at least two of legal/ethical/practical needed for full marks; 6th mark for reasoned conclusion.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a hologram on software packaging helps to protect copyright.
parts.answer: Holograms are difficult to copy, so they show buyers that the product is genuine; customers and shops can recognise counterfeit (pirated) copies that lack the hologram.
parts.working: B1 hard to copy. B1 identifies genuine copy / detects fakes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a dongle is used to protect software.
parts.answer: A dongle is a small hardware device plugged into a USB port; the software checks for the dongle and will only run while it is connected, so copies of the software are useless without it.
parts.working: B1 hardware device plugged into computer. B1 software only runs when it is present.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one disadvantage of this method for a legitimate user.
parts.answer: Any one: if the dongle is lost or damaged the software cannot be used; it takes up a USB port; it can only be used on one computer at a time.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why copyright laws are especially important for software.
parts.answer: Software can be copied quickly, easily and cheaply; every digital copy is identical to the original; copies can be distributed worldwide over the internet in seconds; developers invest a lot of time and money, so the law protects their income and encourages new software.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: a
parts.text: When installing software, the user is asked to accept a licence agreement. Give three things the agreement is likely to state.
parts.answer: Any three: the number of devices/users the software may be installed on; that the software must not be copied or distributed; that it must not be modified or reverse engineered; whether it can be used for commercial purposes; that the user does not own the software, only a right to use it; the length of the licence; limits of the producer's responsibility.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why software provided as an online (cloud-based) service is harder to pirate than software installed from a disc.
parts.answer: The program code runs on the company's servers rather than being copied onto the user's computer; users must log in to an account, so access is controlled and checked each time; a licence that is not paid for can be cancelled immediately.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: A security program is sold in packs, each licensed for up to 5 devices. A family in Rawalpindi has 4 laptops, 6 smartphones and 2 tablets that all need protecting.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the smallest number of packs the family must buy.
parts.answer: 3 packs

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why installing the program from 2 packs on all 12 devices would be wrong.
parts.answer: Two packs cover only 10 devices; using it on 12 breaks the licence terms/copyright.
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how 'trial versions' of software help software producers sell their product while still protecting it.
parts.answer: Users can try the program free for a limited time or with limited features, which encourages them to buy; after the time ends the software stops working (or features stay locked) until a licence key is purchased; so the full program is not given away.
parts.working: B1 try before buying / advertising. B1 time-limited or feature-limited. B1 needs purchase/key to unlock full version.

stem: A teacher in Gujranwala is making a presentation for 12-year-old students and wants to use photographs and music she found on the internet.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why she should check the copyright of the photographs and music before using them.
parts.answer: The material belongs to its creator and is protected by copyright; using it without permission (or outside its licence terms) may be illegal, so she must check whether it is free to use, needs permission, or must be credited.
parts.working: B1 protected by copyright / owned by creator. B1 need permission or licence / acknowledgement.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two ways she can use suitable images legally.
parts.answer: Any two: use images that are copyright-free or licensed for reuse (and follow the licence terms, e.g. credit the creator); ask the owner for permission; buy a licence from a stock image library; take her own photos.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: For a coursework project, a student copies large sections of program code from a website and submits it as his own work.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why this is wrong.
parts.answer: It may break the copyright of the code's author if permission/licence terms are not followed; it is plagiarism – presenting someone else's work as your own, which is dishonest and breaks exam/school rules.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the student should have done if he wanted to use some of this code.
parts.answer: Check the licence allows reuse and acknowledge/credit the source clearly (or ask permission).
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

stem: A software house in Lahore needs an office program for 25 staff. An annual licence costs Rs 9,600 per user. A volume discount of 15% is given for 20 or more users.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total annual cost for 25 staff after the discount.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Two staff leave, so only 23 licences are needed. Calculate the new annual cost.
parts.working: 23 × 9,600 × 0.85 = 187,680. B1 (still ≥ 20 users so discount applies).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A programmer buys a licensed app and changes its code so that it works in Urdu, then sells the new version online.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain whether this is allowed under normal software copyright.
parts.answer: Not allowed: the programmer bought only a licence to use the app, not ownership of the code; licences normally forbid modifying/reverse engineering the code; selling the changed version distributes the copyright owner's work without permission, so it is illegal (unless the licence, e.g. some open-source licences, specifically permits it).
parts.working: B1 licence = right to use, not to change. B1 modification/reverse engineering forbidden. B1 distribution/selling without permission illegal.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A publisher sells ePublications that can only be opened on the buyer's registered devices. Describe how this protects the publisher's copyright.
parts.answer: The file is encrypted and linked to the buyer's account/devices, so if it is copied to another person's device it cannot be opened, stopping illegal sharing.
